News.title: Car stolen with toddler still inside before being dumped five miles away
News.content:
Car stolen with toddler still inside before being dumped five miles away

The Volvo was stolen after the keys were left in the ignition, while the child's parents were nearby, before being taken on a high-speed joyride with the infant still inside

View Image Police photo of a Citroen Berlingo that may have been in convoy with the stolen Volvo containing a child (Image: WYP)

A two-year-old child was inside a car when it was suddenly stolen and driven at “excessive speed”, before being abandoned next to a canal.

‌



The car was taken from the Long Thorpe Lane area of Lofthouse, between Leeds and Wakefield, on Wednesday evening, Yorkshire Live reports.

‌



There was a child inside the Volvo and the keys had been left in the ignition, while the child's parents were nearby, according to reports.

‌



The Volvo was driven to Woodlesford Lock, Leeds, where it was later found, West Yorkshire Police said.

The car was recovered within around 15 minutes and the two-year-old child was found safe and well. Police are now asking the public for information.

‌



The force said the Volvo was taken just before 8.30pm and arrived at Woodlesford Lock around 8.37pm.

The force said in a statement: “Detectives are keen to speak with anyone who saw, or who has footage of the grey Volvo XC90 as it travelled to Woodlesford Lock, where it was later found. It is believed to have arrived there at about 8.37pm.

"Enquiries suggest the Volvo, which had a ‘58’ plate and was said to be travelling at excessive speed, passed through Carlton, Rothwell and Woodlesford (via Holmsley Lane). It also appeared to be in convoy with a blue Citroen Berlingo."

Article continues below

Anyone with information or footage which may assist this investigation is asked to contact Leeds CID, quoting crime reference 13260446258.

News.title: Days out at UK seaside considered outdated as young people moan about seagulls, toilets and phone woes
News.content:
Days out at UK seaside considered outdated as young people moan about seagulls, toilets and phone woes

The poll, commissioned by eco-tech brand Hive, found eight in ten of people aged between 14 and 29 are no longer fond of visits to Britain's seaside resorts

View 3 Images Seagulls pinching chips is one of the major moans (Image: Getty Images)

The tide is turning on traditional bucket and spade beach holidays, according to research.

‌



A poll found 80% of those aged 14 to 29 reckon a day at the British seaside was old fashioned. And the Love Island generation weren’t slow to explain why a trip to the sea gives them the ick.

‌



The major moan for 70% of the 2,000 young people was their phone running out of juice. But other sources of stress include filthy toilets, problems finding a car parking space and seagulls swooping in to nick their chips. Physical conditions of the beach can also be annoying.

‌



View 3 Images Many are miffed by sand in shoes (Image: Getty Images/Connect Images)

Moment seaside cafe owner saves drowning children by throwing life rings READ MORE :

UK Heatwave: Yellow heat alerts issued as temperatures set to soar to 36C READ MORE :

People shared complaints it is too far from the car, the sea’s too cold, they get sand on their feet, or it is too pebbly. Phones seem to matter to Gen Z more than enjoying a day out.

‌



Many say poor signal does their head in or panic their tech will get trashed. More than one in 10 moan they can’t see their screen in the sun, and nearly as many sulk as there’s nowhere to charge their phone.

While 70% say a dying battery ruins the day, just 37% of Baby Boomers, aged 62 to 80, who managed to survive childhood without a portable power bank, agree. Three in 10 Gen Z and over a quarter of Millennials, aged 30 to 45, have left the beach early because their phone was running low.

View 3 Images Low phone battery was also a big concern cited by respondents to the poll (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Article continues below

Susan Wells, of eco-tech brand Hive, which commissioned the poll, said: “When the weather heats up, Britain heads to the coast, but beaches rarely offer power. Dead phones and no charging points have become a familiar frustration, especially when people rely on their devices for digital tickets, maps, messaging and mobile payments.”

Brits enjoy at least four beach days every summer with 90% saying that some of their best summer memories are from time spent there, proving a little sand in your shoes is still a price many are willing to pay.

When it comes to the most nostalgic seaside holiday memories from childhood, eating fish and chips wrapped in newspaper at the beach is rated by 55%, followed by more than half who valued time with the whole family. Other highlights include penny arcades, collecting seashells and eating sticks of rock.

News.title: Funeral home where 50 rotting bodies were discovered branded 'an abomination'
News.content:
Funeral home where 50 rotting bodies were discovered branded 'an abomination'

South Chicago Chapel Funeral Home was raided by cops on Thursday who made the shocking discovery, and officials revealed that the couple who ran the home had allegedly done it before

View 2 Images Workers remove bodies from the South Chicago Chapel on Friday (Image: Antonio Perez/TNS via ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Police have made a horrifying discovery after more than 50 bodies were found decomposing in an unrefrigerated room at a funeral home.

‌



The South Chicago Chapel Funeral Home in Chicago was being run by a couple who had previously operated another crematorium where similar horrific scenes allegedly occurred.

‌



Cops were called in to help with a license investigation at the funeral home on Thursday and reportedly found dozens of corpses. A team of investigators and forensic pathologists from the local Medical Examiner’s Office found bodies in “various states of decomposition,” a spokesperson said.

‌



“MEO staff are assessing the conditions of the remains, searching for documentation regarding identification of the deceased as well as death certificates,” the office said in a statement.

It is not known how long bodies had been at the funeral home or what tipped of authorities to investigate. Cops have said enquiries are ongoing and no arrests have been made yet.

View 2 Images Police officers outside South Chicago Chapel (Image: Pat Nabong /Chicago Sun-Times vi)

‌



The couple who run the funeral home, Johanna and Clark Morgan, had “egregious past practices” while operating the Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights, according to Susana Mendoza, who is in charge of licensing funeral homes in the state of Illinois.

Ms Mendoza told how the Heights Crematory had been shut down last year after investigators found multiple bodies stacked on top of each other inside broken refrigerators, the New York Times reports.

“Horrified. Again,” Ms Mendoza said in a statement. “The discovery of decomposing remains waiting to be laid to rest this week at a Southside funeral home is heartbreaking and an abomination.”

Article continues below

Officials have taken away Mrs Morgan’s license, who was listed as the registered funeral director, after Thursday’s grim discovery. State regulators wrote in a disciplinary filing that her “continued practice is a danger to the public safety, interest and welfare due to respondent allowing multiple decedents to be kept in an unrefrigerated area with deplorable conditions” that included rodent infestation.

Mr Morgan had already had his funeral director and embalmer intern license revoked in 2024 because he was operating on an expired license and had engaged in “unprofessional conduct,” officials said.

The horrific find comes after Hull funeral director Robert Bush was jailed for 20 years last week after police about 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes after raiding Legacy Independent Funeral Directors following a tip-off.

News.title: MI5 and GCHQ chiefs on hunt for young Russian-speaking spies to combat Vladimir Putin threat
News.content:
MI5 and GCHQ chiefs on hunt for young Russian-speaking spies to combat Vladimir Putin threat

Intelligence chiefs from MI5 and GCHQ are looking for young Russian speakers as part of a new recruitment drive in to work out what Russia is thinking and doing

View 4 Images MI5 and GCHQ are looking for young Russian-speakers to help combat the threat of Putin (Image: Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik K)

Young Russian-speaking spies are being recruited to help combat the threat from Vladimir Putin.

‌



Intelligence chiefs from MI5 and GCHQ are jointly launching an 11-week Language Talent Programme next month aimed at finding full-time Russian Language Specialists. A source said: “The ability to work out what Russia is thinking and doing has never been more important. It is absolutely vital we get the best young minds to help us.”

‌



The advert says wannabe spooks should be starting the final year of their degree this autumn, or have graduated in the last three years. They will be paid £6,380 to £7,059 for the 11-week programme, with locations including Cheltenham, London and Manchester.

‌



View 4 Images Some of the wannabe spooks will be based at the GCHQ building in Cheltenham (Image: GCHQ/PA Wire)

Vladimir Putin has backed himself into a corner as prodding NATO may have dire consequences READ MORE :

Ukraine and Europe developing new major new missiles capable of smashing Russia's ballistic threat READ MORE :

If they impress, they will be eligible for jobs starting on £37,892 to £40,248. People who speak Ukrainian are of particular interest to MI5. The advert adds: "If you can also speak and understand Ukrainian, please apply to MI5 as we are particularly interested in candidates with this ability.

"However, please note this isn’t essential and you’ll still be considered fairly and equally with your Russian qualifications."

‌



View 4 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin (Image: Russian President official/APAImages/Shutterstock)

Meanwhile, MI5 and GCHQ are also launching a separate 11-week Summer Intelligence Internship in Cheltenham and London, aimed at students from Black, Asian, mixed heritage or other ethnic minority backgrounds. The programme will be held at "Cheltenham (GCHQ) or London (MI5), with time potentially split across two London sites in Central and West London (TFL Zones 1 and 2)."

The advert explains: "People from a Black, Asian, mixed-heritage or other ethnic minority background and who are also from a socially or economically disadvantaged background are currently under-represented in the UK’s Intelligence Services.

Article continues below

View 4 Images Thames House serves now as the headquarters for the UK’s internal Security Service MI5 (Image: Getty Images)

"We invite applications to this 10-to-11-week internship from university students in their penultimate or final year of study (for the 2026/2027 academic year), who are specifically from these backgrounds."

The ad also says: “If you don’t live nearby – don’t let that stop you. We'll cover the cost of accommodation for the duration of the internship where required. Mentors, managers and buddies will be on hand to help you get the most out of your experience."

News.title: Hunter Biden fears he worsened Joe Biden's health and says cancer has spread
News.content:
Hunter Biden fears he worsened Joe Biden's health and says cancer has spread

Asked if he had made President Biden's life and health worse, Hunter said: "Of course I did. That's what addiction does." And he said his father's cancer had spread to his bones

View Image Hunter Biden said his father's cancer has spread to his bones (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Hunter Biden fears he may have worsened his father Joe's health through his decades of drug addiction, as he revealed cancer has spread to the President's bones.

‌



Asked if he had made President Biden's life and health worse, Hunter told BBC Newsnight: "Of course I did. That's what addiction does." He grew emotional as he discussed his father’s condition, describing it as very sad to watch. "The cancer has spread, metastasised into his bones and further," he said. "It’s very painful and it's very debilitating in many respects.”

‌



He said his father always left the door open for him to return to the fold when he was ready, but acknowledged the toll his behaviour had taken on his Joe and his family.

‌



"My dad never let me off the hook," Hunter said. "But what my dad did was always make it clear that when I was ready to come back, the door was open and that he loved me just as much, no matter what. And what my dad did when I fell down this well of despair is he shined the light down and helped guide me out. And that's a beautiful thing, but it's not without its cost. And the cost is that it never goes away. That stress."

Biden, 83, was the oldest man to serve as US President and his age was a source of concern for much of his four years in office. He and his White House advisers have faced intense criticism for allegedly concealing the extent of his problems, especially after he was forced to abandon his bid for re-election after a disastrous debate with his eventual successor, Donald Trump.

‌



The former president revealed his cancer diagnosis in May of last year, less than four months after he left the White House. Hunter said the diagnosis had been tough on the family.

“The only thing that I'd say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good,” he said.

But he said his father remains “out there," speaking publicly about the issues that are important to him. “He’s still doing his thing," he said. “He so believes in this country." Biden will publish a memoir, “Promise Me, America,” after the mid-term elections.

Article continues below

In his last act as President, Joe Biden issued a pre-emptive pardon to Hunter, to shield him in case Trump pursued him with vindictive prosecutions. Hunter expressed gratitude for the move - but admitted he was conflicted about whether it was the right thing to do for the country and for his father's legacy.

"Was it good for our Constitution?" He said. "Was it for the American people? Was it a good for my dad's legacy? No, on all counts. It was not. It was something that is easily criticised and for good reason. And I can't pretend otherwise. All I know is that I'm grateful that he did it for me and all I can say to anybody out there. Is that what would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me and left me to the whims of Donald Trump? What would you think of a dad that would say, I'll put you in a prison controlled by a guy who's made it clear that he's willing to do just about anything to get his way for himself?."

He added: "It's not fair. I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father."

News.title: Man guilty of murdering teenager in Wembley weeks after his 18th birthday
News.content:
Man guilty of murdering teenager in Wembley weeks after his 18th birthday

Tyrece Balcha, 18, was shout outside a nightclub in South Way, Wembley, following an altercation inside the venue - his heartbroken family have paid tribute to his kindness, warmth and sense of humour.

View 3 Images Ashley Wallace, 40, was found guilty of murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life (Image: Metropolitan Police)

A man has been convicted of gunning down “loving son, brother and friend” Tyrece Balcha just weeks after his 18th birthday in a shooting outside a Wembley nightclub.

‌



Ashley Wallace, 40, of Shenley Road in Southwark, south London, was found guilty of murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life at the Old Bailey on Friday.

‌



Police and paramedics were called to a nightclub in South Way, Wembley at 5.30am on Sunday, 21 September, 2025 following reports of a shooting in the street.

‌



Tyrece Balcha, aged 18, was found outside the premises, with multiple gunshot wounds. He was rushed to hospital but despite medics’ best efforts he passed away five days later.

Officers spoke to witnesses and analysed CCTV which showed that Tyrece had been involved in an altercation inside the club prior to the shooting. He was pursued outside and shot, the jury heard.

View 3 Images Tyrece Balcha had recently turned 18 when he was murdered (Image: Metropolitan Police)

‌



Afterwards, Wallace left the scene in a vehicle, which was parked nearby. Cops traced Wallace to a car in South East London, and he was arrested on the same day Tyrece died.

A revolver was found hidden inside the vehicle, and forensic officers subsequently found Wallace’s DNA on the weapon. The bullet found at the murder scene was later matched to the gun.

At the same trial, two men were found not guilty of murder. A woman was found not guilty of possession of a firearm, possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and perverting the course of justice. The jury could not reach a verdict on a fourth man.

‌



Detective Chief Inspector Phil Clarke – who led the investigation – said: “Throughout this investigation and subsequent trial, the victim's family have conducted themselves with remarkable dignity and patience. We are grateful for their continued support and cooperation, and we hope today's verdict provides them with some measure of justice."

“During this investigation, my team used CCTV and forensic evidence, which allowed them to build a remarkably detailed picture of the murder, leading to today’s conviction.”

Tyrece’s mother, Bonnie, said after the verdict: “Today's verdict brings a measure of justice for Tyrece, and we are grateful Ashley Wallace has been found guilty of his cold and senseless murder.

‌



“While this verdict is important, it does not bring our son back or ease the pain we have lived with every day since we lost him. Tyrece's life was cruelly taken from him eight weeks after he had turned 18 years old. He was a loving son, brother and friend with the biggest heart, an infectious smile and a personality that drew people towards him.

“Anyone who knew Tyrece knew his kindness, warmth and sense of humour.

View 3 Images Ashley Wallace, 40, was found guilty of murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life (Image: Metropolitan Police)

‌



“Our hearts have been shattered. His sisters miss him every day, and his little brother had only just turned one year old when Tyrece died and will never truly get the chance to know him.

“We will make sure that his memory lives on and that he is always remembered for the wonderful person he was, not for the way his life was taken. We pray that Tyrece can now rest in peace, knowing that justice has been served.

“We would like to thank the police and prosecution team for their unwavering dedication, compassion and determination throughout this case. Their commitment to securing justice for Tyrece means more to us than words can express.

‌



“We would also like to thank our family, friends, and the many people who never even knew Tyrece but offered kind messages, prayers and support.

“Your compassion has reminded us that there is still so much goodness in the world, even in the midst of unimaginable heartbreak.

“We now await sentencing and kindly ask for privacy as we continue to heal from the trauma of both losing Tyrece and reliving the circumstances of his death throughout the trial.”

Article continues below

Wallace will be sentenced at a later date.

News.title: 'Arrogant dad made incredible five-word demand when I took my daughter to the cinema'
News.content:
'Arrogant dad made incredible five-word demand when I took my daughter to the cinema'

The astonishing demand left the parent furious. "I can't believe I have to deal with this nonsense and I am not going to be bullied in front of my daughter," they said.

View Image There are few things better than a trip to the cinema (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

Taking a trip to the cinema is easier than ever these days. Once upon a time you had to check the local newspaper for showing times, or pop by the cinema itself to find out when the movie you wanted to see was on, and then queue up at the box office and hope tickets didn't sell out.

‌



Or you could ring the cinema to check times and book tickets, but this was often more trouble than it was worth, and could end up landing you with a hefty phone bill on top of the cost of the ticket. These days it's simple - you can check showing times easily online, and book the tickets there and then if you like, cutting out the queues and the risk of missing out.

‌



Another big change older film fans will have seen is allocated seating. These days most cinemas allocate a specific seat with each ticket, and usually allow customers to choose where they want to sit when the book, as long as someone hasn't booked it already.

‌



But this was less common in years past, and especially before the dawn of the major multiplex chains we see in towns and cities around the UK today. In many cases, the cinemas would sell as many tickets for a screen as there were seats, leaving it to customers to pick where to sit for themselves, similar to a bus.

And it was apparently this which led to a bizarre incident. Writing on Reddit, a parent revealed a strange episode that occurred when they took their daughter to the cinema, only for another film-goer to make a truly baffling demand, reports the Irish Mirror.

Explaining what happened, they said it was "a story from many years ago, before seat allocation in movie theatres". "I arrived at the cinema early with my school-aged daughter to see one of The Lord of the Rings movies," they said.

‌



"We picked the best seats, up towards the back and in the centre. The cinema was not very full, with whole rows empty. Usually you do not really interact with strangers at the cinema, everyone tends to be quite respectful.

"In comes [a] group of two dads with about four children in tow. Entitled dad asks 'Can you both move so we can sit there?' Not an 'excuse me', or 'please' or any reasoning.

"I reply, 'No'. He continues rather more aggressively, 'You can sit somewhere else'.

‌



"Not sure what this guy's issue was. I reply again, 'No I arrived here early to get good seats'. I can't believe I have to deal with this nonsense and I am not going to be bullied in front of my daughter.

"The guy looks like he is about to have a fit when his friend starts physically pulling him away and placating him. At least one of them was a reasonable fellow, though no apology for the rude behaviour. Luckily that was the end of it."

‌



Fellow Reddit users praised the parent for refusing to back down, while others shared similar stories. One said: "I’ve had that happen before. Some lady asked us to move over so her kids could sit there. That would’ve put me behind a tall guy. I said no, we came early to pick out our seats so that wasn’t happening."

Another said: "Probably the same guy that walks into a shop that has a line and walks right up to the front of the line expecting to be checked out right then and there.

"My bet is this guy grew up being given anything and everything by his parents, never taught how to respect others but basically shown that you're better than others and entitled to whatever you want, whenever you want. It's only a matter of time until he makes the mistake of demanding something from the wrong person... and I'm just gonna leave it at that."

Article continues below

And someone else said simply: "The guy was just trying to bully you to get what he wanted - first come, first served, and he was not first."

News.title: Man slashed and stabbed in Nottingham nature reserve
News.content:
Man slashed and stabbed in Nottingham nature reserve

Police officers found a man with knife wounds to his chest, back and legs while out on routine patrol in Nottingham on Friday evening

View Image The victim was found by officers during a routine patrol on Oxclose Lane outside the Golden Phoenix (Image: GoogleMaps)

Cops on a routine patrol in a Nottingham nature reserve on Friday made a horrific discovery.

‌



The officers, who were just doing their route, came across a man with slashes and stab injuries on his chest, back and legs.

‌



The 32-year-old man was walking on Bembridge Drive in the north of the city, close to the Sandy Banks Nature Reserve when the attack took place yesterday evening.

‌



Police said two men got out of a car at 7.08pm and launched a brutal attack on the man. The attack continued into the nature reserve on the steps leading into it, the force added.

“The victim sustained slash and stab injuries to his chest, back and legs and he was found by officers during a routine patrol on Oxclose Lane outside the Golden Phoenix,” Nottinghamshire Police said in a statement.

‌



The officers who found the bloodied man called paramedics who rushed the victim to hospital. Police have said that his injuries are not thought to be life threatening or life altering.

Detective Inspector Stuart Barson said: "We are actively investigating this attack and officers are in the area conducting house to house inquiries.

"The victim sustained multiple stab and slash wound injuries and we need to find those responsible for this.

Article continues below

"Anyone with information should call 101 quoting incident 699 of 7 August. If you wish to remain completely anonymous, make a report to CrimeStoppers online or call 0800 555 111."

News.title: Victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures' over murderer and rapist
News.content:
Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.

Andrea Simon called for a review on the "failure to monitor him appropriately" when the 40-year-old was known to police as a sexual predator.

British Transport Police said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.

Meanwhile, the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant is facing a misconduct investigation.

On Friday, Levy was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London while he was being monitored by the Met Police for being a convicted sex offender. He had previously committed a string of sex attacks.

The BBC reported how a series of grave failings by police, prosecutors and the courts left Levy free to murder, rape and sexually assault women.

Levy is due to be sentenced on Wednesday.

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Chasing a ghost: how BBC tracked a fugitive spy chief after months-long hunt
News.content:
For months we drew a blank in our hunt for Luka.

And then we had our first breakthrough.

One of those listed in the book, who we tried calling again, finally answered the phone.

He had been the guard for Luka's apartment block, he told us, and eventually agreed to give us the number for someone he said had been Luka's personal bodyguard - a man we are calling Mahmoud.

It took weeks to secure an interview with Mahmoud. Meetings would be scheduled but he would not show up, or he would request a meeting in a private space such as a car or apartment, which our reporter judged too much of a risk.

They eventually met at a hotel one night, just before midnight. Broad-shouldered and physically imposing, Mahmoud seemed to be considering every answer carefully before he spoke.

He told us he was angry with Luka for leaving him behind when the regime fell. As word had spread in December 2024 that Assad's rule was on the brink of collapse - with rebels advancing on the capital - Luka had said he would stay and defend Damascus, Mahmoud told us. But by the early hours of the next morning, Luka had disappeared, taking a large sum of money with him from the office safe, Mahmoud said.

Mahmoud refused to share any contact details for Luka or his family, but did give us a number for Luka's driver, who he believed had driven the former spy chief out of the capital that night.

This man proved even harder to reach.

When he answered the phone, his voice was nervous and unsteady. He repeatedly insisted he was just a driver, and knew nothing of Luka's activities. Multiple meetings with us were never kept, and eventually he stopped replying.

We turned our attention to Luka's possible escape routes, including neighbouring Lebanon - where the Iran-backed group Hezbollah had close links with the Assad regime.

One senior source in the Lebanese government told us he understood Luka had passed through Lebanon on a "good Russian passport but with a different name", before flying out to Russia.

We managed to find a man, now based in Lebanon, whose name was listed in Luka's contacts book, but under a number that no longer worked. He is one of many wanted by the new Syrian government, because of his close association with the Assad regime.

This man, who we cannot identify, said he had a number for Luka.

We saw it, and realised it had a Russian country code.

Russia was a key backer of the Assad regime, and in the days after his fall, Assad released a statement confirming that he had fled there. Many of his inner circle were believed to have followed him.

Back in Luka's apartment in Damascus, we had found clues that Luka also had strong links to Moscow - awards from Russia's foreign spy service, and even a New Year's card addressed to him from a senior Russian official.

Now, the Russian telephone number for him suggested we finally had proof that he was - as we had predicted - in Russia.

News.title: Sturgeon hasn't spoken to Murrell since he was jailed for embezzling SNP funds
News.content:
Sturgeon also told Dale that she only discovered Murrell was due to plead guilty a week before his first public court appearance.

It later emerged he had been negotiating his plea for months, a fact which she said "hit me like a tonne of bricks".

Sturgeon said: "He was still lying to me right up until the day he pled guilty."

The former first minister added: "He was very isolated over that period, he very rarely left the house, he wasn't communicative, I was a bit worried about his well-being and his mental health.

"And then, now I think: 'What a mug, why were you worried about him?' He didn't worry about me. He didn't worry at all about what he was doing.

"What he has subjected me to is beyond anything I could ever have comprehended.

"I don't understand why he did it, he had no need to do it, I don't think I will ever understand his motivations.

"But whatever that motivation was, he could not have stopped and ever thought about me.

"But I was, until recently, still worrying about him."

Sturgeon - who had stepped down as first minister in March 2023 - was arrested In June 2023 but was later told that she was no longer under investigation.

The former first minister announced her separation from Murrell last year.

News.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
News.content:
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

News.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
News.content:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

News.title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back and 'a bit more real'
News.content:
Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.

The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention â "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.

He's right â digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.

There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18â30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.

So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?

For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".

She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.

"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.

That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids â where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image â are also popular on socials right now.

With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.

"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.

"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."

News.title: How a former GB Olympian curbed his porn problem - and the signs and steps to recovery
News.content:
Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn.

"Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do was open those sites," he revealed.

By age 12, he was regularly visiting what he calls "hardcore" sites. As his career progressed - which included representing his country in the Olympics - he was watching adult content several times a day.

Now aged 30, the Olympian has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset.

"You can't be the person who is trying to quit porn. You have to be someone who doesn't watch porn, and that takes a lot of work," he said.

So how can you spot when a porn habit has become unhealthy, and how can you tackle it?

Although it has become a common phrase, "porn addiction" is not an officially recognised condition in its own right.

"We know a lot of people have a problem with porn," explains sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves, who says the matter has become more prevalent among clients at his private practice.

But experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction" â like someone might experience with drugs, for example â and how best to deal with it.

Researcher Campbell Ince, from Australia's Monash University, says the vast majority of clinicians now agree people can suffer from "problematic porn use", but there is still a lot to figure out about its causes and treatments.

This means there is no definitive list of symptoms or treatments available to those worried they may be addicted.

Some clinicians approach it as a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a condition recognised by the World Health Organization.

This is sexual behaviour that "feels out of control, is causing significant distress, and despite repeated attempts to control it, they can't," explains psychotherapist Dr Paula Hall, who works privately at the Laurel Centre, a sex and porn addiction centre, and also runs a not-for-profit service.

The NHS does say, external it is possible to be addicted to "just about anything", including sex.

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."

Stephenson said a lovely evening with friends had turned into a horrible morning.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites," she said.

"It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realised what had happened."

News.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
News.content:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple's manager Vickie White confirmed the split, which was first reported by the Sun newspaper, external.

She said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago.

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.

News.title: Hundreds flying out of Birmingham Airport left without luggage
News.content:
She described seeing a "build up" of luggage at the airport, after problems with the luggage belt, but had been assured by staff that it would be loaded on to the plane.

But on arrival at Dalaman they were told by the pilot that no bags had been loaded.

"We have heard nothing about compensation, no communication when our luggage is expected, we've heard nothing about who is liable for it. Is it the airport? Is it TUI? Is it our travel insurance? Who are we meant to go to? We've had nothing from anybody", Chapman said.

"It's just radio silence from the airport, apart from literally telling people 'we've got an issue'".

The first day of their holiday was spent travelling to a shopping centre to buy essentials for "for the next few days" but she added "we have no idea how long this is going to last".

"There are families all over the world at the moment with nothing and no idea of what's going on," she said.

"It's really important that Birmingham Airport are held accountable, and sort this out."

News.title: Man guilty of fatal shooting of teen outside club
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of fatally shooting an 18-year-old outside a Wembley nightclub.

Tyrece Balcha was found with gunshot wounds outside the Crystal Club in Atlantic Crescent at about 05:30 GMT on 21 September 2025. He was taken to hospital, where he died four days later.

A jury at the Old Bailey found Ashley Wallace, 40, of Shenley Road, Southwark, guilty of murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

At the same trial, two men were found not guilty of murder. A woman was cleared of possession of a firearm, possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, and perverting the course of justice. The jury did not reach a verdict on a fourth man.

CCTV footage showed that Balcha had been involved in an altercation inside the club before being followed outside and shot.

Wallace fled the scene in a vehicle and was arrested on 25 September after police traced the car to south-east London.

A revolver carrying Wallace's DNA was found inside the vehicle, and investigators established that the bullet recovered from the murder scene had been fired from the gun.

News.title: Siân Phillips to step back from acting aged 93 after memory issues
News.content:
One of Wales' most celebrated actresses, Dame SiÃ¢n Phillips, is stepping back from full-scale stage acting after experiencing memory issues during rehearsals.

The 93-year-old made the decision after struggling to remember her lines while preparing for a recent production, according to The Times.

However, Phillips said she would continue performing in smaller projects, including a production with Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Her career has spanned more than 80 years across stage, television and film.

Phillips told The Times she decided to stop taking on major stage productions after struggling to remember her lines during rehearsals for Atonement at Chichester Festival Theatre earlier this year.

According to the newspaper, she said she would continue performing in her show It's All Greek and is also due to appear in Samuel Beckett's Rockaby for Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Born in Betws, near Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, in 1933, Phillips grew up speaking Welsh before learning English by listening to the radio.

She began performing as a child, appearing on Welsh-language radio from the age of 11, before studying at the University of Wales and later winning a scholarship to the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.

She performed in radio productions such as The Archers and an adaptation of John le Carre's Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy, opposite Sir Alec Guinness.

Before her acting career took off, she worked for BBC Wales as a bilingual announcer and newsreader.

Phillips went on to become one of Britain's most acclaimed actresses, appearing in productions including Doctor Who, Calendar Girls, Dune, and I, Claudius.

She won a Bafta for her portrayal of Livia in the BBC's I, Claudius and received a Tony Award nomination for playing the title role in Marlene.

She was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 2000 for services to drama, and then a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in 2016.

News.title: The 'cheap Cotswolds' attracting new residents
News.content:
More people are leaving cities behind in search of cheaper homes, more space and easier access to the countryside, with the Forest of Dean emerging as an increasingly popular destination for buyers priced out of nearby Bristol.

The Gloucestershire district, which lies between the River Severn and the Welsh border, has long been known for its ancient woodlands, market towns and rural communities.

Estate agents say it is now drawing new residents from across the South West who want countryside living without the price tag associated with the nearby Cotswolds.

Local estate agent Glen Webb said many buyers see the area as a more affordable alternative to one of England's most sought-after rural locations: "The Forest is really such a brilliant asset to Gloucestershire. It's a cheap version of the Cotswolds and people sort of love it for that reason."

News.title: Bristol Airport disruption a 'shambles' as flights restart
News.content:
Widespread disruption continues at Bristol Airport after a runway defect saw all flights suspended.

Hundreds of passengers were stranded after the airport's runway was closed from 18:00 BST on Friday until 08:00 on Saturday. While the runway has since reopened, the airport's website says the majority of flights are delayed or cancelled.

A spokesperson for the airport apologised for any inconvenience caused and advised passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline.

Dave Blackwell, travelling home from the Greek island of Rhodes, said it had been "a shambles" since his flight back to Bristol was diverted to Newcastle.

"We were in Rhodes Airport for three hours with no information. Now we have all been told our flight is going to Newcastle and then a five or six-hour bus ride - why Newcastle? How appalling," he said.

News.title: Passengers 'stranded' at locked train station
News.content:
Translink has apologised after rail passengers were left stranded on a platform when a late-night train arrived into a station that was already shut for the night.

A group of about 30 customers were stuck on the platform at Newry Train Station for more than 45 minutes in the early hours of Saturday.

One of the passengers, Anne Greer, told BBC News NI it raised safety questions for the public transport company as the customers had no safe way to exit the station.

Translink said the firm was "looking into the incident" but added its train crew "remained with the passengers to ensure their safety while the issue was resolved".

The train was among a number of extra late-night services which are running to and from Belfast during the Fleadh Cheoil na hÃireann (Music Festival of Ireland).

It was scheduled to leave Belfast at 23:59 BST on Friday and it arrived in Newry at about 01:20 BST on Saturday.

"To our surprise the entire station was closed, so we couldn't exit," Greer said.

"So we're all trapped on the platforms for over 40 minutes."

She said the train crew "helped as much as they could, but there was nothing they could do".

"They were completely gobsmacked as to why they've arrived into a completely closed and locked train station."

Greer said she and other passengers tried to contact Translink but they could only find phone numbers for call centres which had also already closed for the day.

Wes Streeting, the newly appointed Defence Secretary, has revealed he has encountered an "unbelievable volume" of online homophobia since taking up the role, surpassing all previous experiences in his career.

Speaking at the Edinburgh Fringe, Mr Streeting noted that while his appointment three weeks ago was "almost entirely unremarked upon in the media," the online reaction has been starkly different.

He attributed the abuse to individuals who "cannot cope with the idea" of a gay Defence Secretary.

Despite the negativity, he views the position as a chance to demonstrate "strength" and "challenge this sort of stereotype that clearly persists in dark corners of the internet."

Despite the negativity, he views the position as a chance to demonstrate ‘strength’ ( Jane Barlow - WPA Pool/Getty Images )

Despite the decriminalisation of homosexuality in 1967, it remained a criminal offence for military personnel until 1994.

Even after that date, homosexuality remained classed as “conduct prejudicial to good order and discipline” until 2000, meaning service personnel could still be dismissed for being gay.

Mr Streeting added: “I am proud of the fact that in my lifetime we’ve gone from gay people not being allowed to serve in the military to a gay Defence Secretary.

“And in my first week, someone in the MoD said to me, you know, as a gay man, I’m really proud that we have our first gay Defence Secretary, and it means a lot to many of us who remember the bad old days.”

Prior to his appointment, Mr Streeting had been considered a potential challenger to Andy Burnham in the contest to succeed Sir Keir Starmer.

But once Sir Keir announced his resignation and Mr Burnham formally launched his bid for No 10, Mr Streeting said he would not stand in the leadership contest.

He told the audience in Edinburgh that he had spoken to Mr Burnham during the Makerfield by-election campaign and decided there were not enough “fundamental differences” between the two men to justify standing.

He said: “I sort of went in with the aim of saying I think we can show a different way of doing politics in terms of how we debate the future of the Labour Party and how we conduct ourselves in a contest.

“And we sat around over a cup of tea, talking about what had gone wrong. And inevitably, when you talk about what’s gone wrong, you give hints to each other about what you think you need to do to make it right.

“And the more we were talking, the more I was thinking, how much do I fundamentally disagree with this guy on anything?”

Mr Streeting said he had told Mr Burnham he would back him on the Friday after the Makerfield by-election, and agreed to make the announcement the following Monday.

He said he and his partner had “gone into hiding over the weekend”, adding: “I sort of spent three days desperate to tell people.

“And the moment I did, I felt like the weight of the world had been lifted off my shoulder.”

Asked whether he thought Mr Burnham would be Prime Minister if he had not resigned as health secretary, Mr Streeting said: “Probably not.”

He added: “What I think my resignation did that week was force choices for others.”

Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the U.S. that supplies drinking water to more than 20 million people, has hit a record low.

The reservoir, located behind Hoover Dam on the Arizona-Nevada border, fell to 1,040.5 feet above sea level at 1 a.m. MST on Friday, marking its lowest level since it was first filled in the 1930s, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, CNN reported. The drop surpasses the previous record low of 1,040 feet, set in July 2022.

While water levels climbed slightly above 1,040.50 feet before sunrise Friday, officials say the drop is a sign of the challenges ahead.

"It's grim, and we obviously need to do something – and fast," Brad Udall, a senior climate scientist at Colorado State University's Colorado Water Center, told USA Today.

Lake Mead is a critical water source for the Southwest, providing drinking water for between 20 and 25 million people. It is part of the larger Colorado River Basin system, which supplies water to around 40 million people across seven states, tribal communities and parts of Mexico.

open image in gallery Lake Mead dropped to a new record-low elevation of 1,040.5 feet Friday morning, breaking the previous low set in July 2022 ( Reuters )

open image in gallery As water levels drop, the receding water exposes hidden shorelines, old rocks, land and objects that stayed underwater for decades ( Reuters )

The Colorado River also plays a major role in American agriculture, providing irrigation for about 5 million acres of farmland. That includes farms in California’s agricultural regions that produce a significant portion of the country’s fruits and vegetables.

Because of below-average snowmelt runoff from the Rocky Mountains this year, officials announced a plan in April to keep more water in Lake Powell rather than releasing it downstream to Lake Mead. The move was designed to protect Lake Powell’s water levels during a dry year, but it also means less water is flowing into Lake Mead, contributing to its continued decline.

The Bureau of Reclamation warned at the time that keeping more water in Lake Powell would speed up Lake Mead’s decline and could reduce Hoover Dam’s hydropower capacity by up to 40 percent as early as the fall.

Before the adjustment, Lake Mead was projected to fall to about 1,055.99 feet by the end of September. With less water released from Lake Powell, projections showed it could drop closer to 1,035 feet.

The reservoir’s dramatic decline has reshaped the landscape around Lake Mead. As the water recedes, it has exposed previously submerged shorelines, rocky terrain and areas that have been underwater for decades. The July 2022 record low drew national attention when it exposed a body found inside a barrel, several sunken boats and other remains.

Earlier this week, Colorado officials announced a program aimed at easing the Colorado River water crisis would pay people in Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico to use less water. While it could save enough water to supply hundreds of thousands of homes for a year, officials say much larger cuts are needed.

A separate federal plan, announced July 31, could require Arizona, California and Nevada to reduce Colorado River use by up to 3 million acre-feet annually, which is enough water to supply about 6 million households for a year.

Demi Vollering launched a blistering attack to win the eighth stage of the Women’s Tour de France and take the yellow jersey heading into Sunday's final stage.

The Dutchwoman upped the pace on Saturday's fourth and final small climb and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney cracked with about six kilometres to go, sitting back down in her saddle as 2023 Tour winner Vollering surged ahead.

As Vollering zoomed along the famed Promenade des Anglais by the seaside in Nice, Niewiadoma-Phinney and former Giro d’Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini could not close the gap.

Vollering raised her arms triumphantly at the line, then sat on the ground and panted heavily as she tried to get her breath back. Longo Borghini was second and Niewiadoma-Phinney was third, both 17 seconds behind.

The day belonged to Vollering, who won the Giro d’Italia this year to complete the hat trick of Grands Tour wins.

She is eight seconds ahead of Niewiadoma-Phinney, the 2024 champion, in the overall standings. The Polish rider took the yellow jersey with a brilliant solo win up Mont Ventoux on Friday, and rode a yellow bike to go with it on Stage 8.

Stage 9 features four sharp climbs of Col d’Èze, which is nestled in the hills overlooking the tiny principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on a final day mountain stage to win the race by just four seconds. Vollering will have to ensure it's not a case of deja vu.

Earlier, defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot was forced to withdraw from the Tour having been struggling with an illness.

Manchester United face their highest-profile pre-season friendly of the summer as the tour of Scandinavia continues with a clash against double reigning Champions League winners Paris Saint-Germain.

The Swedish city of Gothenburg plays host to the heavyweight clash, as Michael Carrick’s side look to build on a friendly campaign that has seen them win their previous two matches – including a 2-1 comeback win over Atletico Madrid in Stockholm last time out.

PSG are an intimidating foe, although their star-studded squad will likely still be missing a number of players who played for France during their run to the semi-finals at the World Cup last month and they lost their previous friendly 3-0 to Mallorca. However, they will still provide a fascinating test as Carrick gears up for his first full season at the helm.

Follow all the action with our live blog below:

News.title: Joao Pedro double and Caicedo stunner give Chelsea win over AC Milan
News.content:
Chelsea 3 AC Milan 0

Chelsea cruised to a 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Saturday. Goals from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to their second win on their Far East tour.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head intothe break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Moises Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

The London side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto. Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Chelsea had further chances to extend their lead in a dominant second-half performance but were unable to add to their three goals.

Chelsea conclude their tour of the Far East with a game against Johor Darul Ta’zim on Sunday in Malaysia before returning home.

Their final pre-season game will be against Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge before beginning their Premier League campaign at Fulham.

AC Milan take on Amorim’s former club Manchester United next Saturday before they kick off their Serie A campaign at Torino on August 23.

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.title: The best luxury hotels in the Cotswolds
News.content:
From gracious old farmsteads and magnificent manor houses to an ancient coaching inn creaking with Tudor character, the top luxury hotels in the Cotswolds combine a wonderful sense of history with contemporary style and outstanding modern British cuisine. Whether near picturesque Broadway in the north of the region or close to Bath in the south, location is a key attribute to them all: some offer serene escapes in acres of their own rolling parkland; others sit amid superb gardens; and several take over classic honey-stone villages that look as if they have been beamed in from a halcyon era of the past.

They all excel in providing creature comforts, whether crackling fires by kick-back sofas, canopy beds with soft throws, or suites with terraces and hot tubs. Facilities are top-notch too, ranging from beautiful bars and quiet terraces to blissful spas with inviting pools and even an opportunity for equine adventures. Read on to discover our pick of the best luxury hotels in the Cotswolds.

News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”
