“Media freedom cannot mean immunity from scrutiny, just as political speech cannot mean immunity from political accountability,” Simuuwe said, describing Chavula’s assertion that Hichilema would lose the 2026 election as a political position rather than media analysis. “If Mr Chavula wants to join politics, he is welcome. We will meet him there, as a political opponent, not as a media owner.”

Neither party has confirmed whether a formal complaint has been lodged with the IBA. As of publication, no further public exchange had followed Simuuwe’s statement.

World.title: SENZENI – Who Will Be Sacrificed?
World.content:
Filming for Senzeni has officially wrapped, director Cosmas Ng’andwe announced this week, sparking celebration on set.

Ng’andwe, the Lusaka-born filmmaker and CEO of Cosca Films, shared a behind-the-scenes video on his Facebook page on Thursday, 6 July, showing cast and crew marking the end of production. He is best known locally as an actor, comedian and master of ceremonies, and won the AMVCA Trailblazer award and a Ngoma Award in 2025, cementing his status as one of Zambia’s most recognisable young filmmakers. Senzeni marks one of his most ambitious projects yet, bringing established Nollywood names into a Zambian-led production.

Nollywood veteran Kanayo O Kanayo featured in the clip, praising his time working with the team. Born Anayo Modestus Onyekwere, he arrived in Zambia on 26 July 2026 to take up one of the film’s lead roles. He is best known for characters tied to ritual sacrifice for wealth, a theme that fits the film’s premise.

Fellow Nollywood actor Tony Umez also joins the cast. Umez started out in stage plays during secondary school before entering Nollywood in 1993. His first two roles went unpaid, prompting a brief break from acting. He returned in 1997 with The Princess, then built his reputation with the 1998 hit Died Wretched.

Ng’andwe used the video to tease the film’s trailer, due for release soon, and confirmed Senzeni will premiere in November.

The title translates to “what have we done?” Senzeni follows a young man whose search for the truth about his family’s past pulls him into a web of secrets and betrayal, forcing him to decide what legacies are worth fighting for.

World.title: Zambia election choice: continuity under UPND or uncosted change under Tonse Alliance
World.content:
The August 13 general election has taken shape as a choice between economic continuity and campaign uncertainty, with President Hakainde Hichilema‘s United Party for National Development (UPND) and the opposition Tonse Alliance offering starkly different pictures of the country’s direction.

On one side stands an incumbent anchoring his re-election bid on macroeconomic stabilisation, debt relief and agricultural recovery. On the other stands an opposition coalition whose campaign has increasingly turned toward security warnings and allegations rather than sustained policy debate.

When Hichilema took office, he inherited a defaulted economy with a negative 2.8 percent GDP contraction. The centrepiece of the turnaround since then has been a debt restructuring programme now saving Zambia US$1.9 billion every year, funds redirected into free education, public service recruitment and localised development rather than foreign Eurobond repayments.

That approach has been tested by the worst drought in living memory. While Tonse Alliance candidate Brian Mundubile pointed to rising food prices, the administration says it focused on building supply and resilience, delivering what officials describe as the highest maize harvest since independence. Inflation dropped from 6.7 percent in June to 6.4 percent in July, with mealie meal prices falling from K300 to K240 in several regions.

During a recent campaign stop, Hichilema addressed the criticism directly: “Yes, the basket is high because of the drought we inherited from the past, but we have stopped the bleeding. Economics is measured in real terms, not nominal slogans.”

The contrast in governance approach was highlighted during Mundubile’s recent appearance on the BBC’s Focus on Africa programme. Asked by journalist Dingindaba Jonah Buyoya to outline concrete plans for job creation and industrialisation, Mundubile responded with a broad pledge: “We will put women, youth, and the poor at the centre.”

The Tonse Alliance campaign has promised a K2,000 salary increase for civil servants, a higher Food Reserve Agency maize price for farmers, cancellation of water utility debts and free school uniforms and books nationwide. When pressed on how these commitments would be funded without triggering a new debt crisis, the campaign offered no detailed costing, despite the Alliance having published a manifesto.

By contrast, the UPND administration points to figures already reflected in the national payroll: 45,000 teachers and 20,000 health workers recruited, and the Constituency Development Fund expanded to move resources from Lusaka ministries directly into local communities for clinics, classrooms and feeder roads.

With the election days away, the UPND has focused its campaign on the Copperbelt, home to 1,296,446 registered voters, Zambia’s second-largest voting bloc. Hichilema won the province with 56.4 percent of the vote in 2021 and has since toured Mufulira, Lufwanyama, Kalulushi and Chambishi to expand that margin, pairing structural investment messaging in urban mining centres with agricultural support and Social Cash Transfer messaging in rural areas such as Lufwanyama and Masaiti.

Addressing a crowd in Lufwanyama, Hichilema linked the province’s development gains directly to his call for continuity: “Your show of gratitude towards free education, increased CDF, and employment opportunities is highly acknowledged. In order for these developments to continue trickling down, we call on you to protect this progress.”

As the campaign has intensified, Tonse Alliance leadership has raised a series of security allegations. Alliance secretary general Celestine Mukandila alleged, without presenting evidence to the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) or police, that foreign nationals from Tanzania, Malawi, Congo and Angola were crossing into border districts to vote using illegal documents. Alliance chairperson Binwell Mpundu separately alleged that three security personnel sent to Russia for VIP protection training had been abducted upon their return to Lusaka.

These claims have not been substantiated through ECZ or police channels. A related episode of political friction in Mongu was similarly leveraged by opposition figures to suggest broader instability, though isolated incidents have not translated into wider unrest; Western Province, like the rest of the country, remains largely peaceful.

Elections ultimately turn on two questions: whether a candidate understands the country’s challenges, and whether they present a realistic, funded plan to address them. On August 13, Zambians will decide between continuing the current debt restructuring, agricultural recovery and infrastructure programme under Hichilema, or a change in direction under an opposition coalition that has yet to detail how its commitments would be financed.

World.title: Election promises: Do they really influence voters?
World.content:
With polling day fast approaching, Zambians are once again weighing a familiar question: do campaign promises actually shape how people vote? Writer and political commentator Alfred Sayila argues that the electorate has grown far more discerning since independence, no longer taking rhetoric at face value regardless of which party makes the pledge.

Since 1964, campaign promises have been used unsparingly by ruling parties to win support, and at times those promises have helped opposition parties ascend to power. But voters have come of age. They now sift through political rhetoric with far greater discernment, separating substance from spin.

Founding President Kenneth Kaunda used to say no one can take Zambian people for granted. He learned this the hard way in 1991, when the crowds he had commanded at rallies for 27 years turned against him at the ballot box, handing victory to Fredrick Chiluba, a man Kaunda had once dismissed as a political dwarf because of his short stature.

If that rejection could befall a leader who delivered real development, peace and unity, the consequences for candidates offering only unfulfilled pledges could prove far harsher. Voters increasingly ask a pointed question before casting their ballots: what did previous leaders fail to do that they now claim they will finally accomplish? Unfulfilled promises, in the eyes of many voters, carry little more weight than lies, and no late window-dressing can restore lost confidence.

Cheap electioneering built on empty promises breeds suspicion among an electorate that has already walked that road before. Rallies, dances, hymnals, handouts and donations often amount to little more than vote-chasing theatre, while the real decision in most voters’ minds is settled long before polling day.

Several campaign pledges circulating this election season raise questions about feasibility. These include promises to build universities in rural capitals, construct skills centres nationwide, build an international airport in a terminus town, further increase the Constituency Development Fund, install solar plants everywhere, employ millions of people and pay farmers within three working days of submitting claims. Such promises invite an obvious question: where would the funding come from, since many are not backed by demonstrated fiscal detail?

Some pledges being presented as new are, in fact, programmes with long historical roots. Free education, for instance, existed in a form during the colonial era through Native Authorities, which offered access to schooling with only small fee contributions, alongside bursaries for vulnerable children. School feeding programmes for boarders also existed under colonial-era grants administered through native authorities, structures that functioned similarly to today’s Constituency Development Fund. The first post-independence government under Kaunda largely consolidated and diversified what it inherited rather than inventing entirely new systems.

The point extends even to the “One Zambia, One Nation” ethos some politicians now invoke. Cross-country transfers of civil servants during the colonial period, though designed to serve a divide-and-rule strategy, inadvertently mixed tribes and cultures across regions, a process the mining industry on the Copperbelt also accelerated. That intermingling laid groundwork Kaunda later built on with his unifying slogan, and its legacy persists in families that settled far from their ancestral regions, illustrating that many of today’s talking points describe processes already well underway long before current candidates entered public life.

Politicians should therefore be cautious about presenting themselves as pioneers of ideas that predate them. Making a promise is one thing; having the resources to deliver it is another. Pointing to numbers of newly employed civil servants offers little persuasive weight, since recruiting public workers is a routine government function and a perpetual drain on the treasury rather than an extraordinary achievement. A more meaningful measure of good governance lies in creating conditions for private-sector job creation and supporting small and medium enterprises.

A genuinely good government also lightens the burden on citizens through subsidies on food, medicine, fuel, fertiliser and seeds. Free education alone means little if households sending children to school are stalked by hunger, and in some areas free education has led to overcrowding, poor facilities and staff exhaustion, undermining the quality of instruction it was meant to improve.

Campaign messaging, Sayila argues, would be more credible if grounded in physical projects already initiated or completed, rather than repeated promises. Voters today want to see improvement in living standards through affordable prices, not abstract statistics about inflation or exchange rates; they want that progress reflected in real purchasing power and reduced cost of living.

Ultimately, elections are rarely won through last-minute campaigning, colourful posters, slick s or borrowed slogans. They are won when politicians own their mistakes and credibly promise to do better. A candidate’s underlying character tends to show through regardless of rehearsed charisma, and unconvincing promises rarely manage to sway voter judgement in the end.

Given the closeness expected in this race, with no single presidential candidate likely to muster the 50-plus-one threshold in the first round, the Electoral Commission of Zambia carries a democratic duty to ensure the process remains free and fair, with the possibility of a run-off remaining real.

World.title: Mast Editorial: Police IG must prove critics wrong on election violence
World.content:
The Inspector General of Police, Graphel Musamba, issued a statement condemning the wave of violence linked to United Party for National Development (UPND) cadres in the run-up to Thursday’s general election. A Mast Editorial said the statement was welcome, but warned that words alone would not be enough to convince a sceptical public.

The piece argued that with polling day approaching, police carry a constitutional and moral duty to ensure all candidates, particularly opposition contenders, can campaign without being attacked or threatened by either cadres or officers themselves. It noted that the ruling party had campaigned largely unimpeded, while opposition figures had repeatedly found themselves on the receiving end of disruption.

The real test now, the editorial said, was whether Musamba’s officers would act against identifiable UPND cadres accused of targeting the campaign of NRPUP presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu. It linked the pattern of violence to what it described as divisive rhetoric from President Hakainde Hichilema at rallies, and to instructions allegedly issued by a Nigeria-based figure calling himself Prophet Seer 1.

Several specific incidents were raised, demanding direct answers from the IG. Where were police, the editorial asked, when officers reportedly tried to stop an Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) sanctioned opposition rally in Ndola, and when cadres allegedly descended on a hotel and lodge in Kitwe housing members of Mundubile’s campaign team, damaging vehicles while officers looked on.

An incident in Solwezi was also raised, where musicians supporting Mundubile’s campaign were allegedly attacked by people travelling in UPND-labelled vehicles, alongside a case in Mwembeshi East, where cadres reportedly raided a rally for an independent candidate and assaulted musician Clifford Dimba, known as General Kanene, leaving him with head injuries from a machete attack.

Further questions concerned Northern Western Province, where cadres allegedly trailed Mundubile’s entourage, and Luampa in Western Province, where his convoy was reportedly blocked and stoned, injuring a police chief inspector. A separate reference was made to Mongu, where officers reportedly detained members of Mundubile’s musical entourage, including a comedian, and where the candidate was allegedly forced to flee a peaceful rally under tear smoke.

Musamba was called on to respond directly to Mundubile’s claim that UPND cadres have been absorbed into the Zambia Police Service, issued uniforms and firearms, and deployed to obstruct his campaign while concealing their identities behind face masks. These allegations, the editorial stated, remained unanswered by the IG.

While acknowledging that video and photographic evidence of the cited incidents circulates on social media, the piece stressed continued confidence in the Zambia Police Service, adding that the institution’s conduct, not its statements, would be the true measure over the remaining election period.

World.title: REA Completes Luwingu’s K19.4 million  Grid Extension
World.content:
The Rural Electrification Authority (REA) has completed the implementation of the over 19.4 million Kwacha Tungati Grid Extension Project in Luwingu District in Northern Province.

Rural Electrification Authority Chief Executive Officer Alex Mbumba says the project is aimed at increasing the number of households connected to the national grid.

Engineer Mbumba says the project which was awarded to a Turkish based contractor Laatu Energy Solutions Limited is expected to benefit about 636 beneficiaries who will be connected to the supply of electricity which has been constructed in the area.

The Chief Executive Officer was speaking when he paid a courtesy call on Luwingu District Commissioner Chomba Chileshe in Luwingu.

He added that the project has given electricity supply to Tungati Combined School, Local Court, Market, Tungati Min Hospital, Kuta Primary School, Chibofwe Primary School, Sokontwe Primary School and Surrounding areas.

He explained that the supply of electricity to the area is expected to enhance the existing economical activities currently taking place on a micro scale such as retail trading, alcoholic beverage trading and maize-milling in the community.

Engineer Mbumba stated that the completion of the Tungati Grid Extension Project will encourage entrepreneurs in the area to set up businesses which communities had challenges accessing.

He emphasized that the implementation of the Tungati project will bring social and economic benefits which will improve the livelihood of the people of Tungati Chiefdom.

The Chief Executive Officer also highlighted that over 41 beneficiaries are expected to get connected under ASCENT subsidy program which is currently in force

And Luwingu District Commissioner Chomba Chileshe Commended government for completing the project on time saying people can now start benefiting from it.

Mr Chileshe indicated that since independence people of Tungati Chiefdom used to cover long distances to acquire services which need electricity.

He also disclosed that health facilities in the area used to have problems keeping vaccines and other essential drugs which needed refrigeration and that with the completion of the project these services will no longer be challenging to them.

Mr Chileshe further indicated that even vulnerable people in communities are now able to have their houses connected to electricity because of the subsidy programme which has been introduced.

He urged communities where REA has installed the electricity infrastructure not to vandalize the infrastructure aimed at improving their livelihood.

World.title: VEEP Urges Clergy to Pray for Peaceful Elections
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has called on the clergy to continue praying for unity, peace and love ahead of next Thursday’s general election, saying the values are essential for peaceful polls and national development.

Mrs Nalumango urged church leaders to pray for the country’s leadership and the nation as a whole to ensure Zambia holds peaceful elections.

Speaking when she met members of the clergy in Mkushi, the Vice President said love, peace and unity were critical to promoting national development, adding that Zambia needs God’s intervention to achieve its development aspirations.

She further urged Zambians to reject the spirit of division, confusion and disunity.

Mkushi Ministers Fellowship Chairperson, Reverend Adams Chilowana, said the church remains committed to praying for peace and unity as the country heads to the general election.

Reverend Chilowana disclosed that church mother bodies in the district will next week hold special prayers for peaceful elections.

Meanwhile, traditional leaders in Mkushi have commended the government for the prompt payment of farmers supplying maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA).

Speaking on behalf of seven chiefs who met the Vice President, Senior Chief Shaibila said farmers are receiving their payments on time and appealed to the government to maintain the status quo.

World.title: Government hails Joseph Katema’s enduring development legacy
World.content:
Government has eulogised the late former Cabinet Minister, Joseph Katema, as someone who made a significant contribution to the development trajectory of the country, through implementation of sound policies that attracted donor funding.

Speaking during the burial ceremony in Lusaka, Deputy Secretary to Cabinet, Oliver Kalabo, who was speaking on behalf of the government, has since called on the public service to emulate his selfless service to the country.

Dr Kalabo said that the late former cabinet minister facilitated mobilisation of donor support to complement government efforts in implementing policies and programmes targeted at improving the livelihood of the citizens.

“The nation may wish to know that the late Honourable Dr Joseph Katema, was admired for embracing servant leadership, when he served as a cabinet minister,” said Dr Kalabo.

Widow to the late cabinet minister, Antonette Katema, whose speech was read by her close friend, Suzyo Simbyakula, remembered her late husband as a humble man with a heart without limits when it came to helping others.

Mrs Katema said that the departure of her late husband has left a vacuum that cannot be expressed in words.

Cathedral of the Child Jesus Administrator, Benedict Chanda, said that the church has embraced the bereaved family with prayer, and asks God to strengthen them with his grace.

Fr Chanda also called for the need to honor the memories of Dr Katema with tribute and commitment to living a life of honesty, justice, reconciliation and service.

World.title: Africa: Africa Has Ideas - What It Lacks Is a Fair Hearing from Global Capital
World.content:
Africa Has Ideas - What It Lacks Is a Fair Hearing from Global Capital

guest column

Why good African businesses and projects can struggle to cross the funding redline

Africa has never suffered from a shortage of ideas.

It suffers from a shortage of capital willing to believe in those ideas.

Across the continent, entrepreneurs are building businesses, engineers are designing infrastructure, farmers are developing agricultural value chains, innovators are creating technology solutions and governments are proposing projects capable of transforming entire economies.



Yet again and again, they encounter the same wall:

Where is the money?

This is one of Africa’s great economic paradoxes. The continent has enormous natural resources, a young and expanding population, growing consumer markets and extraordinary entrepreneurial energy. Yet many African businesses and projects that could create jobs and generate wealth struggle to obtain the capital required to move from concept to implementation, or from a small enterprise to a large-scale business.

The uncomfortable truth is that Africa’s financing problem is not simply a shortage of capital.

There is plenty of capital in the world

The problem is that too much of that capital sees Africa first through the lens of risk — and only afterwards through the lens of opportunity.

That distinction matters.

The African funding redline

For years, African countries have effectively operated under a financial redline.

The language may be sophisticated: sovereign risk, country risk, credit risk, currency risk, liquidity risk and political risk.

But the consequence is simple:

Money becomes more expensive.

When the perceived risk of a country is high, investors demand a higher return. Governments pay more to borrow. Local financial institutions operate in a more expensive funding environment. Businesses then face higher interest rates and tougher investment requirements.

A project that might be financially viable at one cost of capital can become impossible when the financing cost rises significantly.

This creates a vicious circle.

A country perceived to be risky pays more for capital.

Higher borrowing costs put pressure on public finances.

Weak fiscal positions reinforce perceptions of risk.

Investors demand even greater returns.

And the cycle continues.

The entrepreneur at the end of that chain is often the one who pays the price.

This is not an argument that Africa has no risks.

Of course it does.

Every investment has risk.

The question is whether the financial system is sophisticated enough to distinguish between risk and opportunity — and between one African project and another.

Are we rating Africa instead of rating projects?

Perhaps one of the most important questions Africa should now be asking is this:

Are we properly assessing African projects, or are we allowing the reputation of the continent to influence our assessment before the project has even been examined?

A renewable-energy project backed by credible long-term agreements is not necessarily the same risk as a speculative start-up.

A profitable agricultural-processing company with established export markets is not the same proposition as an untested business.

An infrastructure project with predictable revenues is not the same as a project that exists only on paper.

Yet the African label can sometimes become an additional invisible risk premium.

This is where the conversation around international credit ratings and financial institutions becomes important.

Credit ratings have a legitimate purpose. Investors need independent mechanisms to assess creditworthiness.

But ratings also influence the cost of capital.

And when a continent is repeatedly perceived through a high-risk lens, the consequences extend far beyond sovereign borrowing.

They affect banks.

They affect businesses.

They affect infrastructure.

They affect entrepreneurs.

They affect the ability of African economies to convert natural resources, human capital and good ideas into productive investment.

The cost of being misunderstood

The greatest danger is not that investors identify genuine African risks.

The danger is that perceived risk becomes detached from actual opportunity.

Consider the African entrepreneur who has developed a viable business but cannot obtain expansion capital.

Consider the manufacturer who wants to build a factory but faces financing costs that make production uncompetitive.

Consider the farmer who wants to move from exporting raw commodities to processing them locally.

Consider the engineer who has designed an energy project but cannot secure affordable project finance.

In each case, the problem may not be the absence of an opportunity.

It may be the cost and structure of capital.

And this has consequences for entire economies.

If a factory is not built, jobs are not created.

If a processing plant is not financed, raw materials continue to leave the continent without capturing their full value.

If infrastructure is delayed, businesses face higher operating costs.

If businesses cannot scale, governments collect less tax.

If young people cannot find productive employment, demographic growth becomes a social challenge rather than an economic dividend.

So the financing question is not merely a question for bankers.

It is a question for anyone concerned about Africa’s development.

Something important may be changing

This is why a development announced by the Liquidity and Sustainability Facility deserves considerably more attention than it is likely to receive outside financial circles.

The LSF has welcomed the launch of the L&G LSF African Government Bond (USD) UCITS ETF, developed by Legal & General Asset Management and described by the LSF as the first of its kind available in Europe.

To the average African entrepreneur, an African government bond ETF may sound remote from the daily struggle to raise capital.

But it represents something much bigger:

an attempt to change the financial infrastructure through which the world accesses African markets.

The LSF has been working to address the structural problem of illiquid secondary markets for African sovereign debt, which can contribute to higher borrowing costs.

In 2024, it collaborated with S&P Dow Jones Indices to create the iBoxx LSF USD African Sovereigns Index, providing a standardized benchmark for African sovereign Eurobonds.

Now that benchmark has become the basis for a publicly accessible ETF.

That matters because capital likes familiarity.

Global institutional investors managing billions of dollars cannot individually analyse every African bond or every African opportunity.

They need benchmarks.

They need transparency.

They need liquidity.

They need standardized investment structures.

And when those structures exist, African assets become easier to access.

This is bigger than one ETF

The LSF says indices and ETFs can help broaden the investor base, increase secondary-market activity, improve price discovery and, over time, potentially reduce the liquidity premium paid by issuers.

That is an important development.

But it should also provoke a much bigger question:

What happens if this thinking is extended beyond sovereign bonds?

What if African infrastructure can be packaged into investment structures that global institutional investors can understand?

What if African renewable-energy projects become part of standardized investment portfolios?

What if African agricultural value chains can attract pension and insurance capital?

What if African companies can increasingly access corporate bond markets?

What if African pension funds can invest more effectively in African infrastructure?

What if global investors can obtain exposure to African growth through transparent, liquid and professionally structured vehicles?

That is where the conversation becomes transformational.

Because Africa does not merely need more money.

It needs better channels through which money can reach productive opportunity.

The entrepreneur is waiting

Somewhere in Lagos, Nairobi, Accra, Johannesburg, Kigali, Lusaka, Harare, Dar es Salaam or Dakar, there is an entrepreneur sitting on a business idea that could employ hundreds or thousands of people.

Close 

Somewhere there is an engineer with a viable energy project

Somewhere there is an agricultural entrepreneur who knows how to turn raw commodities into higher-value exports.

Somewhere there is a technology founder building a solution for a market of hundreds of millions of people.

Somewhere there is an infrastructure developer who has completed the feasibility studies, identified the market and assembled the partners.

And somewhere there is a banker telling them:

“The project is good. But the risk is too high.”

That sentence has probably killed more African opportunities than a lack of African ingenuity ever has.

The answer should not be to pretend the risks do not exist.

The answer is to build financial mechanisms capable of distinguishing between bad projects and good projects in difficult markets.

That is a very different proposition.

Africa should not have to beg for capital

There is another mindset Africa needs to abandon.

The continent should not have to spend eternity travelling around the world asking investors to “believe in Africa.”

At some point, Africa must be able to say:

Here is the opportunity. Here is the data. Here is the structure. Here is the return. Here is the risk. Make your investment decision.

That is what mature capital markets do.

They do not require investors to fall in love with a continent.

They provide investors with information and instruments through which they can make rational decisions.

The LSF describes its ambition as moving beyond individual transactions and creating durable financial-market infrastructure for African economies.

That is the direction Africa should pursue.

The continent does not need another room full of people promising to invest.

It needs financial plumbing that makes investment possible at scale.

And if that plumbing can eventually connect global capital to African businesses, infrastructure and productive industries, the consequences could extend far beyond the financial markets.

Because the real prize is not an ETF.

The real prize is what happens when capital starts building an African industrial economy.

That is where the next conversation must begin.

World.title: Namibia: Stars, UNAM's African Opponents Announced
World.content:
African Stars will face Mangasport of Gabon while Unam FC will face Kabuscorp of Angola in the qualifying rounds of the CAF Champions League and CAF Confederations Cup respectively.

Stars will face Mangasport in the first qualifying round of the CAF Champions League after the draw was made in Cairo on Thursday. Stars will play the first leg of the qualifying round away in the Gabonese town of Moanga on the weekend of 4-6 September, while it will host Mangasport in Windhoek in the return leg between 11-13 September.

Mangasport is one of Gabon's most successful teams having won the premier league ten times since 2000 as well as for the past two seasons.

The winners of the first qualifying round will progress to the second qualifying round to be played over two legs on 16-18 October and 23-25 October, to decide the 16 teams that will qualify for the group stages of the competition.



Unam FC will take on Kabuscorp in the first qualifying round of the CAF Confederation Cup. They will play the first leg in Windhoek between 4 and 6 September and the return leg in the Angolan capital between 11 and 13 September.

Kabuscorp won the Angola Cup in 2025, while they have only won the Angolan premier league (Girabola) once, in 2013.

World.title: Nigeria: Police and Obsession With Extortion
World.content:
column

Extortion, both official and unofficial, is now commonplace in Nigeria. Many Nigerians have been extorted at one point or another, with just as many Nigerians participating in extorting others. This social disease is especially endemic to Nigerian public and civil servants. Many of them, not content with their salaries, seize every opportunity they have to extort Nigerians.

The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) and the Independent Corrupt Practices Commission (ICPC) were established to fight economic and financial crimes in Nigeria. So it was truly ironic when sometime last month Musa Aliyu, SAN, the chairman of the Independent Corrupt Practices Commission (ICPC), ran into some policemen who were clearly oblivious of his identity and proceeded to extort him to the tune of N53,000. The act promptly landed them in hot water. But it was only because they ran into someone in a position to take it up.

Every day, the Nigerian police extort many Nigerians. This stubborn streak of extortion, which runs deep in the Nigeria Police, is as subtle as it is systemic. Usually when a complainant reports a case to the police, the extortion begins. They are often asked to bring money for all manner of things. When the suspect is arrested, the police also begin to collect money from them.

As for the ones who man Nigeria's highways, the less said about them, the better. The brazen extortion by the police has sometimes turned tragic, with motorists and passengers killed for as little as N20.



Nigeria has a corruption problem, and it is important to state that extortion does not stop at the table of the police. Many Nigerian civil and public servants do not believe that they can do their jobs without extorting Nigerians. So, despite their salaries, they seize every opportunity to milk Nigerians of their hard-earned money.

What is to blame for this failure that is moral as well as professional? While it would be easy and lazy to use the poor welfare of police officers in Nigeria as a shield, the whole story is not one of vulnerability and insecurity. It goes beyond that. Largely, it is a question of values.

What values do those who serve Nigerians as security personnel possess? It is difficult to see that they barely have any. For many of them, the only thing that matters is money. That is why they are in service. Anything else can wait.

Many Nigerians have long lost confidence in the Nigeria Police. For many of them, it is better to resort to self-help or to quietly lick their wounds than report any matter to the Nigerian police.

Close 

This mentality of helplessness and wariness has been shaped by years of difficult encounters with the police. Security never works well in an environment where pecuniary considerations are given preeminence. The authorities of the Nigerian police must fix what is an institutional cancer.

It Is easier said than done, however. Extortion is deeply ingrained in civil and public service in Nigeria. Many Nigerians see nothing wrong with it. This mindset is precisely what needs to change if Nigeria is to successfully tackle what is at once an institutional as well as social and moral crisis.

Kene Obiezu is a lawyer and writer

World.title: Nigeria: The Right to Disagree
World.content:
column

The notion that public policy critics cannot be wrong is misconceived, writes Bolaji ADEBIYI

The recent disagreement between President Bola Tinubu and a delegation of the Catholic Bishops' Conference of Nigeria on the country's state of affairs ought to be normal in a democratic setting, but for the misconceived notion that public policy critics cannot be wrong. This misconception is evident in the sharp critique, by habitual government critics, of the president's spokespersons' response to John Cardinal Onaiyekan's account of last week's presidential meeting with the bishops.

It was Cardinal Onaiyekan who brought the disagreement into the open during an interview with ARISE TV, a national broadcast network with a wide international audience. In describing the meeting, the widely respected clergyman portrayed the president as aloof and insulated from the grave situation facing the vast majority of the people he governs. He thought the president was arrogant for insisting on macroeconomic stability brought about by his reforms, which has not translated into improved living standards for the people. Finally, he opined that the president appeared bent on winning the 2027 general election despite growing concerns about the integrity of the electoral umpire.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Whilst the status of the presidential audience is unclear, the responses from the president's minders suggest that the presidency considered the clergyman's action inappropriate, given the one-sided presentation of the encounter, which portrayed their principal in a bad light. This is even more so when there was no official communique that would have enabled the public to conduct an objective analysis of what transpired. Coming from a man with access to a religious constituency of over 30 million adherents, the presidential spokesmen are justified in issuing a firm rebuttal to the clergyman's rebuke of their principal in an impending electioneering season.

Opinions are divided over the public spat, as expected. Critics, largely opposition politicians and their allies, argue that the Cardinal spoke truth to power, condemning the presidential response as insensitive and intolerant of public opinion. The Presidency and its supporters argue that public policy analysts and critics must speak from a position of factual knowledge, rejecting the notion of all-knowing public policy critics who cannot be wrong.

Snippets from the meeting's accounts on both sides suggest that President Tinubu disagreed with the Catholic clergymen's positions on all the issues raised, whether the economy, security, or the electoral process. Whilst the bishops contended that the economic reforms were not improving the people's quality of life, the president thought otherwise, even when he admitted the attendant challenges that were being addressed. The clergy believed that the country was bleeding; the president countered that there were significant improvements in tackling insecurity. Finally, the Catholic leaders opined that the electoral umpire had lost public confidence. The president was not persuaded and asked for the facts behind their claim.

Basically, the issues are not new. They have been in the public domain since the economic reforms were inaugurated at the start of the Tinubu administration. The reforms were accompanied by high inflation, with dire consequences for energy, food and transport costs, which adversely affected the mass of the people's living standards. The federal government acknowledged the pain and responded with palliative measures, promising that relief would come as the economy stabilises. Three years later, there is near consensus among global rating agencies and acclaimed economists that the nation's macroeconomy has stabilised and positioned Nigeria for growth and sustainable development via global private investment.

The economists who rated the reforms positively cited economic indicators showing that inflation is trending downward, forex has stabilised, external reserves are climbing at unprecedented levels, and foreign direct investment has grown phenomenally. However, there is also a consensus that these microeconomic improvements have not translated into enhanced living standards for the majority of the people, a development that President Tinubu has seized every speaking opportunity to acknowledge and to pledge his administration's commitment to alleviating.

The Catholic bishops' visit to the Presidential Villa to restate this notorious fact, with Cardinal Onaiyekan's insinuation that President Tinubu, surrounded by sycophantic aides, is oblivious to it, could seem more like playing to the gallery than speaking truth to power. Their position would have been meritorious if they had proposed an alternative strategy for the president to translate macroeconomic gains into better living standards for the people. After all, the central issue of widespread hunger and poverty is essentially a microeconomic matter within the remit of subnational governments at the state and local levels. Otherwise, the bishops ought to have addressed the contradiction between the quantum leap in the Federation Accounts Allocation to the states, arising from the reforms, and the underperformance of subnational economies, which is breeding these widespread complaints.

This cup-is-half-empty perspective, which apparently shaped the bishops' opinion on the economy, permeated their country-is-bleeding perception of the nation's security situation. Again, the clerics stated the obvious, discountenancing the government's efforts to address the challenge and its incremental success. President Tinubu's disagreement with them is not without merit.

Non-state actors' violent attacks on the people have been met with maximum force by the nation's security forces. Cooperation among intelligence agencies has been aligned with the increasing efficiency of the military forces, resulting in the decimation of the rank and file of bandits, terrorists, and religious insurgents. The leadership of the marauders has virtually been sought out and destroyed, to the admiration of even US President Donald Trump.

All of these came on the back of improved defence and security funding, which has enabled the security forces to be better equipped with more efficient technology and military platforms. There have been structural reforms, too, including the push for state police to increase security presence across the country, the expansion of forest guards to reclaim ungoverned spaces, an increase in army divisions from eight to twelve to reduce response times, presidential approval for the recruitment of more boots on the ground, and enhanced emoluments for the security forces.

Close 

The bishops' failure to recognise these significant strides, preferring to highlight daily reports of violence while ignoring the deluge of media coverage of the security forces' counter-insurgency successes, could not have been acceptable to a president who could not have solved decades-old crises in three years.

However, it is significant that neither Cardinal Onaiyekan's account nor those of the clerics suggested any hostility from President Tinubu during the encounter, except that the president stood his ground and robustly defended his policies and programmes.

Beyond the policy disagreement, which is normal in a democratic setting, the challenge seems to be the failure of the men of God and their supporters to recognise that their right to criticise the president does not preclude his freedom to disagree with their views. This appears to be the bug that has bitten perennial government critics and opposition politicians, who cannot take as much as they give.

Adebiyi, a Fellow of the Nigerian Guild of Editors, writes from Abuja

World.title: Nigeria: Presidency, the Cardinal and Many Truths
World.content:
analysis

Maturity is the capacity to hold more than one truth at once, contends Joshua J. OMOJUWA

The trouble with our public conversation is not that people disagree. It is that too many of us have never made peace with a simple fact of adult life: more than one truth can exist at the same time. You can respect a man and still tell him he is wrong. You can praise a stance on Monday and puncture a different one on Friday. You can love your country and criticise its government in the same breath. None of this is contradiction. It is the ordinary texture of an honest mind. Yet we now live in a country where this has to be taught, and taught, of all people, to some who host our morning shows.

Take the matter of Cardinal Onaiyekan. When His Eminence sat for that Arise TV interview and drifted into claims that bordered on the partisan, questioning the independence of INEC as though something in its structure had changed since the last time we voted, he stepped off the pulpit of the statesman and onto the platform of the partisan. Presidential aide Temitope Ajayi responded with a statement he titled "Cardinal Onaiyekan, Abuse of Clerical Privilege." I said, in reply to that piece, that the moment a statesman is seen to be partisan, he forfeits the immunity of neutrality and exposes his flanks to counterattack. That was not an attack on the Cardinal. It was an acknowledgment that Mr Ajayi, like any citizen, has the right to answer back. A robe does not exempt an argument from scrutiny. It never has.



Here is where the comedy began. A self-styled journalist decided that my position contradicted an earlier tweet in which I had praised the Cardinal. He went digging, and he surfaced my old words as though he had caught me in a lie. When I pointed out the poverty of that reading, he dug again and found yet another tweet, this one where I had commended him, the journalist, for doubling down during an interview. He presented it as a gotcha. I told him what I still believe: only a certain kind of mind reads an autopsy and goes looking for compliments in it. It takes a specific poverty of self-regard to comb through a critique in search of a pat on the back.

The deeper problem is not one confused man on a television set. It is a professional space where, on account of naked partisanship, some who call themselves journalists, and I will concede that a few of them are, have retreated into a bubble of their own truth. Not a perspective. A bubble. A closed room where their side is always right, where every criticism is a betrayal, and where the ability to hold two ideas at once has quietly atrophied. A truth that cannot survive contact with a second truth is not truth at all.

Let me turn to a heavier matter, because the same intellectual laziness shows up where it does real damage. When President Trump made his notorious remark about our country, I was in North America, and I spent that time defending the dignity of Nigeria to people who were only too eager to believe the worst of us. That work matters. Since then, the President and the United States government have become partners in progress, which is how diplomacy is supposed to work: you defend your house, then you build with your neighbour.

So imagine my astonishment when Peter Obi, reaching for something with which to wound President Tinubu, chose to reach instead for the insult that President Trump once hurled at our country. He repeated it. He took a foreigner's slur about Nigeria being a disgraced nation and he put it back into circulation, in his own mouth, as a weapon in a domestic quarrel. How does a man who aspires to be President of Nigeria recycle an insult against the very country he wishes to lead?

Let us be clear, because clarity is the whole point of this piece. You are free to have a go at your President. I have done it in these very pages. Some of the columns I have written here are direct criticisms of President Tinubu's policies, and I will write more, because that is what honest citizenship looks like. I have knocked governments and praised the same governments later, sometimes in the same year, and I make no apology for it. Consistency is loyalty to the truth, not loyalty to a side. But there is a canyon between telling your government it is wrong and telling the world your country is worthless.

Not knowing the difference between those two things is one of the many reasons Peter Obi will never be President of Nigeria. The most he will ever attain is what he has already attained. "Peter Obi is my President" is a sentence straight from the book of coping mechanisms, a consolation chanted by people who mistake a hashtag for a mandate. More than one truth can exist, and here is one of them: a man can seemingly mean well and still be temperamentally unfit for the highest office, undone not by his enemies but by his own inability to tell a domestic disagreement from a national disgrace.

Close 

I will close with a smaller example that carries the same lesson. Whenever I write that the government must fight harder against fake drugs, a certain crowd materialises to have a go at me, as though the campaign against counterfeit medicine were a plot against legitimate business. They cannot hold the two truths in one hand. A government can wage war on the poisonous, criminal underside of an industry while fiercely protecting the honest industry itself. Fighting fake drugs is not an attack on pharmacy. It is the defence of every Nigerian who swallows a tablet and trusts that it will heal rather than kill.

Maturity is the capacity to hold more than one truth at once. Its absence is the quiet crisis of our public life. We would argue far better if more of us simply learned to say: both of these things are true.

Omojuwa is chief strategist, Alpha Reach/BGX Publishing

World.title: Nigeria: FHA and Affordable Housing
World.content:
The authorities could do more to meet the housing needs of the people

Labour impact assessment studies in countries with similar demographics and economies as Nigeria estimate that no fewer than five direct jobs can be generated with every new home, and two indirect jobs in housing-related expenditure. At present, the federal government runs housing initiatives like the Renewed Hope Housing and the National Housing Programmes. Beyond the job prospects, public housing accounts for less than 10 per cent as most depend on the informal sector for their housing needs. But even when mass housing projects can be part solution to unemployment while meeting the residential needs of many, experts do not believe that the current approach by the Federal Housing Authority (FHA) will produce the desired results.

Created under the National Development Plan in 1973, the FHA is essentially mandated to coordinate, drive, and execute government housing agenda to the low, medium, and high-income groups. Over the years, FHA has been able to deliver thousands of housing units across the nation, despite obvious challenges. However, what is worrying is that many of its old estates are in bad shape: they are ill-kept. Many are increasingly falling into slums. The issue is not only about standards but poor conception, as well as the manner in which the houses were allocated in the past, and whether the current approach could not be different.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

As part of the efforts to deepen access to affordable housing across the country, the FHA said on Wednesday that it has secured prime land in 28 states. "We have also commenced the process of construction in some of the states, having procured the contracts," said FHA Executive Director, Estate Services, Ezekiel Etuk, at the groundbreaking ceremony for the FHA Green City Estate in Abuja. "We are currently working on the FHA Estate, Bwari, Abuja, which comprises 336 units, with the target date of commissioning before the end of this year."

Over several decades, the FHA has built many estates across the country. Perhaps the most prominent among them is FESTAC Town, initially dubbed "little London". Built in 1977 with substantial resources to house participants of the Second World Festival of Black Arts and Culture of 1977, the federal government allocated the houses and landed property to winners, after a ballot. Like Gowon Estate (Ipaja Federal Housing Estate also in Lagos}, initially built for FESTAC, it is seedy with plenty of crimes. The sewage system in both estates has collapsed, leading to constant outflow of dirt and waste. In 2022, the then Housing Minister instructed the agency's Southwest Zonal management to explore private sector funding to stem the infrastructural decay in the estates. But nothing came out of it, as the estates continue to deteriorate.

Close 

Developments in Nigeria contrast with some other climes where public housing contributes largely to social engineering. In the United Kingdom for instance, there are council apartments built and either sold or let to individuals. The councils maintain, collect rents, and administer sales mortgages. Unfortunately, local governments in Nigeria have been rendered prostrate by the governors. Many believe the federal government should keep its hands off retail housing provision as they are far too removed from the people. The suggestion is for the empowerment of both the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria (FMBN) and the Nigeria Mortgage Refinance Company (NMRC) for the task of providing affordable housing to Nigerians.

There are existing examples to draw from. At the industry level, there are houses built and owned by private people and companies. These constitute the housing stock and determine the supply and demand of housing in an open market. But they are very expensive with short-term mortgages being financed by banks. This is an area the FHA should work on with other stakeholders if it is to fulfill its mandate to Nigerians.

World.title: Couples asking wedding guests for cash spark fierce debate over manners and tradition
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A celebrity couple asking wedding guests to help fund their nuptials is being branded "tacky" by some, while others insist cash is king.

American actress AnnaLynne McCord, known for her roles on "90210," "Nip/Tuck" and "Days of Our Lives," and her English former professional rugby player fiancé, Danny Cipriani, set up a page on Honeyfund, an online wedding and honeymoon registry, inviting people to contribute to wish-list elements of their "dream wedding."

The registry lists wedding expenses ranging from $100 to $600, including the marriage license, reception beverages, photography, rehearsal dinner and floral arrangements.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Tacky is an ugly word, but it’s really unkind to ask your guests to give you money for any occasion," Texas-based etiquette expert Diane Gottsman told Fox News Digital. "It really is impolite to straight out ask for cash. You let your family do the talking for you. You let your website do the talking for you."

Gottsman said every couple needs a registry to give options for guests, but asking directly for cash sets the wrong tone immediately.

Cash is easy to give, she added, and is acceptable to include as a request on a website for honeymoon funds, a down payment for a home, etc., but it shouldn’t be the only option. Some guests prefer to give a gift, and it should be left up to them.

"A gift is not an admission ticket to your wedding," Gottsman said. "A registry makes it easier, but guests can do whatever they would like. It’s a gracious act of giving that they’re doing for you."

Several Reddit discussions about cash wedding registries suggest attitudes vary, with some users saying the practice is a modern, accepted trend. Gottsman clarified that a cash option is perfectly acceptable, but asking guests to pay for the wedding itself is "off-putting."

One Reddit forum asked, "Is it bad to ask for money instead of gifts?"

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"No, most people do this now, majority of weddings I’ve been to the last few years all were mainly cash registries," one user replied.

"We did, and didn’t get any backlash and got money from everyone, except one friend who offered us either money or getting a meat subscription box," another user responded. "And we love to cook and good meat is dang expensive so we took it, but we didn’t get any surprise gifts from people who refused to give us cash or anything like that."

A Redditor identifying as an Asian person said the only gift you give or receive in that culture is money.

"Can someone please explain to me why it is such a ‘bad’ thing to not have a physical registry? Like I don’t get it," the person wrote. "If I want something, you giving me the money will let me buy it. If I already have everything I need, money can help re-coop the cost of the wedding or literally anything else. Money is the best, most versatile gift."

"Why in American culture is it seen so negatively?" the person added. "I’m born and raised in the U.S., and I still never understood people’s issue with this."

CLICK HERE TO 

"It’s a general taboo around money in American culture," a fellow Redditor replied. "You’re not supposed to talk about money at all honestly. So asking for it or exchanging it directly is frowned upon. That’s why there’s such a culture around signaling wealth indirectly. Having a big wedding or designer bags is how to flaunt wealth, not posting a screenshot of your bank statement."

Someone else on Reddit asked if it would be rude to ask for money instead of gifts for her wedding, then edited the original post to say she decided against it and to include cash as an option among other gifts on her registry.

"Just have a honeymoon fund and few or no physical items on your registry and most people will take the hint," someone on the forum advised.

Gottsman encouraged couples to "think about the ask." They should throw a wedding they can afford, because asking for cash sets a different tone for the celebration.

If a guest is reluctant to chip in on a couple’s wedding, Gottsman said there’s a gracious way to decline.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Say, ‘I have something else in mind, and I’m really hoping you enjoy it,’ not, ‘I’m not giving you cash, because it annoys me,’" she said.

A timeless, go-to gift for a couple is something sentimental and thoughtful that you know the couple will like. If you don’t have any ideas, give them something they can return. Make sure you are always including a gift receipt, Gottsman said.

World.title: The 2026 Boston Red Sox are red hot and have proven all the haters wrong, including this idiot

Hand up. It's me. I'm the idiot.

Everything I've written about the 2026 Boston Red Sox has been wrong. Completely wrong. It was, and is, fake news.

Frankly, I don't know why I'm still allowed to even write about them at this point. But I'm here today, facing the music and extending an olive branch to the hottest team in ... baseball history?

RED SOX COME BACK FROM THE DEAD, MOVE INTO POSTSEASON CONTENTION WITH REMARKABLE 14-GAME WIN STREAK

The Red Sox might just be. This team is quite literally unbeatable. They can't lose. They won't lose. They refuse to lose.

Boston won again Friday night, dismantling the A's, 13-1, for its ninth straight win. The Red Sox are now 27-3 over their last 30 games. They're 33-7 over their last 40. They haven't lost a series in June, and are one win away from their second double-digit winning streak in as many months.

Somehow, the Sox have gone from the worst team in the American League, to leading the league in run differential (+89), sitting comfortably in a playoff spot and knocking on the door for the division lead.

Everyone was wrong. Everyone has egg on their face. And I'm right there at the front of the line.

The Red Sox are setting every record imaginable

Name a record, and the Red Sox have probably broken it this summer. This one is probably my favorite:

Per Elias, the 2026 Red Sox are the fastest team in MLB history to go from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over at 44 days. The previous quickest was 59 days by the 1914 Braves.

Goodness gracious. Where do I even start?

I said they'd regret firing Alex Cora. I was wrong. Interim manager Chad Tracy will undoubtedly be Manager of the Year. Does he even qualify? No clue. But he should.

I called Craig Breslow a clown. I said he put together one of the worst rosters in Red Sox history. I was wrong. Apparently, he built a monster.

I called for owner John Henry to sell the team, and I wasn't alone. All of Fenway Park chanted it back in May. He was HATED in Boston. Despised. Couldn't show his face.

Fast-forward three months, and look who was a man of the people earlier this week:

Amazing.

I spent much of the first two months of the season absolutely burying new third baseman Caleb Durbin. He was Alex Bregman's replacement, and was horrific. It looked like the biggest Red Sox whiff since the Mookie Betts debacle.

Durbin has been one of the best players in all of baseball this summer. A lot of fans credit him for starting this run in June when he played through a dislocated finger and hit a go-ahead home run against the Yankees.

Hard to argue:

Breslow didn't whiff on Durbin. I did. I was wrong.

Last week, I said the Sox should get rid of Jarren Duran at all costs at the trade deadline. He just had another embarrassing outburst in a win over the A's, and fans were DONE with him. At the time, he was literally the worst hitter in all of baseball, hitting .195.

"Remember the Titans" star Ethan Suplee spent years dramatically transforming his body, but the actor says the breakthrough that finally helped him maintain his weight loss came when he stopped viewing it as something he could permanently "cure."

Suplee explained he saw the biggest change when he began treating his relationship with food and weight much like his sobriety — a lifelong condition requiring honesty, communication and accountability.

Reflecting on his recovery journey with Fox News Digital, Suplee said repeated attempts to get sober failed because he believed he could simply complete rehab and move on. He believed taking 30 days away from drugs and alcohol meant the problem had gone away.

"I haven’t had drugs or alcohol in 30 days," he recalled. "That means I’m cured."

'REMEMBER THE TITANS' STAR ETHAN SUPLEE ISSUES WARNING ABOUT WEIGHT LOSS DRUG CRAZE

It wasn't until he embraced ongoing accountability and open communication that he found lasting success, a lesson he later realized applied just as much to maintaining his weight loss.

"My condition isn’t a condition with a cure," Suplee explained. "It’s a condition that I can learn to manage."

He added, "I did not apply that to weight loss for many, many years. I kind of was doing everything in my head, and the big boon to actually being able to maintain it was finding a group of people to be accountable to."

The man who once famously said "I am not a role model" joined "The Kittle Cast" with NFL tight end George Kittle and his wife, Claire, and was giving out some rather sage advice about aging athletically.

The tensions between the far-left and more establishment wings of the Democratic Party are not going away, as evidenced by some sharp comments from former presidential nominee Hillary Clinton this week.

"Pivot" podcast host Kara Swisher noted to Clinton that the Democratic Party is having a tense internal struggle between its more establishment and progressive wings to the point that Republican opposition has learned to capitalize on it.

"I think there's no doubt that, you know, the Republican Party is the Trump cult and the Democratic Party is a bigger tent. You know, we do have a broad cross-section of people, what they believe, what their experiences are. I think that's an advantage," Clinton said. "But we also have to win general elections."

Clinton noted that many Democrats now will have to learn to pivot and support the progressive Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign to defeat Republican Mike Rogers, while El-Sayed’s supporters will have to learn how to re-integrate defeated Haley Stevens and her supporters who they were "vilifying" online and in person.

World.title: Senate confirms Todd Blanche as attorney general after weeks of uncertainty
World.content:
The Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as U.S. attorney general early Saturday in a mostly party-line vote, capping off weeks of uncertainty and despite bipartisan concerns about his ability to run a Justice Department independent of President Donald Trump’s impulses.

Blanche, who was formerly Trump’s personal attorney, was confirmed by a vote of 50-49, with only two Republican senators, Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, voting against him along with all Democrats.

The vote was held after 4 a.m. on Saturday, as a late-night session ran over into the early hours ahead of a planned Senate recess.

“I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation’s 88th Attorney General,” Blanche said in a post on X, adding: “I am grateful to the Senate for staying late to complete this process.”

His confirmation had been in jeopardy, largely over concerns about his handling of the so-called anti-weaponization fund, which was established in connection with a purported settlement between private citizen Trump and the federal government he now controls. That fund could have been used to give money to Trump allies who claimed they were victims of government overreach, including people who were charged in connection with the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack. Blanche had also signed off on another part of the deal that gave Trump, his family members and his businesses immunity from tax audits.

Earlier Republican holdouts, Sens. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, ultimately backed Blanche after receiving various assurances from the nominee, including an order rescinding the $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund. (A legal loophole could still revive the fund, however.)

Lawmakers from both parties had also expressed discomfort about Blanche’s personal history with the president.

“The problem with confirming Todd Blanche is that he has never been able to shed his role as criminal defense lawyer for Donald Trump. He just can’t do it,” Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., said ahead of the Senate Judiciary Committee’s vote advancing Blanche’s nomination. “He will never do what’s best for the American people. He will only do what’s best for Donald Trump, and you cannot leave someone like that as the nation’s No. 1 law enforcement official.”

Blanche took over as acting attorney general in April after Trump forced out his predecessor, Pam Bondi. Trump had become frustrated with Bondi over the lack of action from the DOJ against his political foes.

Blanche told NBC News in April, after he took over the Justice Department in an acting capacity, that Americans should be “happy” with Trump’s involvement in the Justice Department’s operations.

Weeks after Bondi’s dismissal, the Justice Department indicted former FBI Director James Comey, who is accused of threatening the president’s life by posting a photo of seashells in the shape of “8647” to Instagram.

Critics have questioned whether Blanche will stand up to Trump’s future desires to target his political enemies.

“The biggest concern is whether he is now going to be emboldened to go even more gung-ho on Trump’s campaign of using the Justice Department for retribution,” former federal prosecutor Laurie Levenson told NBC News in an interview prior to his confirmation. “There are no guardrails.”

Trump’s attorneys general in his first term also departed under pressure to act on the president’s behalf. Jeff Sessions was forced out after the 2018 midterms in part due Trump’s frustration with his recusal from the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, an investigation that led to the Mueller report. Former Attorney General William Barr left after Trump tried to enlist the Justice Department in his efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss, a campaign that culminated in the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.

World.title: Iran says deal on Strait of Hormuz is close but will not open the waterway by itself
World.content:
Iran said on Saturday that a deal with Oman on control of the Strait of Hormuz was close but would not be enough to free up the waterway, and the United Arab Emirates said Iran had hit another ship there.

A U.S. official, who declined to be identified, said on Friday that Washington anticipated an agreement soon between Iran ⁠and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, so that normal oil traffic could resume.

Agreement between the two countries over control of the strategic waterway is seen as crucial to a wider agreement to end the conflict that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran and Oman were “very close” to agreement on a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz but that reopening the strait depended on other conditions, including U.S. compensation to Iran.

The previous shipping traffic separation scheme through ⁠the strait was no longer acceptable to Tehran, he said, adding that Iran was discussing a ​temporary route ⁠with Oman while technical and legal issues surrounding a permanent route were resolved.

Iran has responded to the U.S. attacks by targeting U.S. bases in Gulf states and Jordan, and shipping in the narrow strait, which carried a fifth of the world’s oil and gas shipments before the war.

The ⁠UAE said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a carrier affiliated with its state oil company with a missile as it transited the Strait of ​Hormuz, with no ⁠injuries reported, in the latest escalation in attacks on shipping ‌there.

There was no immediate comment from Iranian authorities. Iranian media quoted the UAE report without including the part in which the country blamed Iran for the attack.

U.S. to lift Iran blockade once deal is announced, official says

In recent weeks, the Trump administration has repeatedly signaled that a deal to open the strait could be ‌close, only to have Iran deny that talks are under way. It was unclear whether the latest ‌flurry of negotiations would yield a more lasting arrangement.

“There is progress between Oman and Iran on the strait, and we expect a deal soon,” a U.S. official told Reuters on Friday. “Once the deal is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports.”

“As always, U.S. actions will continue to be performance-based and tied to Iran’s implementation of its commitments,” the official said.

02:12 Iran and Oman negotiate over Strait of Hormuz control 00:00 00:00

Iran’s ⁠Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps also said on Saturday that re-opening the Strait of Hormuz depended on Washington accepting Iran’s conditions and was not related to the Iran-Oman negotiations.

IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi did not specify the conditions but said Washington must stop interfering in the regional negotiation process.

“Whenever the United States accepts Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will certainly be reopened,” he said, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency.

Sources said a deal would give Iran some control

A proposed deal between Iran and Oman to help end five months of war between Iran and the U.S. would give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through the strait, a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters on Wednesday, one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran.

U.S. officials have repeatedly insisted they would never agree to Iran controlling access ‌to the world’s most important trade route for energy supplies. It was not clear whether they had sought to change the parameters of ​the deal. Iran has used the hostilities to justify charging a toll on oil tankers. That, and the firing on ships that attempt to ‌cross the strait without its permission, has badly disrupted global shipments, causing energy ⁠prices to surge and fueling inflation.

Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, one of the world’s largest energy producers, said on Friday that 15 of ⁠its vessels had been struck in what it called unprovoked attacks while transiting the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the conflict. The attacks have killed one crew member and wounded 20 others, it ‌said. Iranian media often report attacks on ships saying ​they violated Iran’s directives, without specifying that Iran was behind the attacks.

Iranian strikes on Strait ‌of Hormuz shipping have been coupled with increased attacks by its Yemen-based ​allies, the Houthis, who have targeted ships at another oil chokepoint on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula between the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

World.title: Video shows hippo charging boat full of tourists in Botswana
World.content:
Video captured by a tourist aboard a boat in northern Botswana showed the heart-pounding moment the vessel had to outrun a charging hippo.

Oznur Bell, who took the video, was on the boat Sunday with her three children and a close friend as they traveled between camps during their stay in Botswana, she told NBC News.

“It was one of the most terrifying moments I’ve ever experienced,” Oznur said. “Once he started charging after us, the adrenaline was unbelievable.”

A video shows a hippopotamus jumping in the Okavango Delta in Botwana, on Sunday. Oznur Bell

One of the journey’s guides, who was operating the vessel, spotted the hippo and slowed the boat in an attempt not to disturb it, Oznur said. The vessel had just come upon an elephant, and she had her phone out when the hippo appeared, she said.

“I happened to have my phone in my hand because I was filming it,” Oznur said of the elephant. “By pure luck, I never put my phone away, which is the only reason I was able to capture what happened next on camera.”

The guide quickly realized the hippo had been provoked despite his efforts, she said.

Oznur remembers the guide saying, “Hold on — we need to speed up now before he decides to come after us.”

She continued, “The moment we accelerated, we looked back and realized the hippo was chasing us.”

Her video, posted to her Instagram account, shows the massive mammal extending its head and upper body out of the water in a marvel of propulsion that looks similar to a human breaststroke. The boat created a wake as it sped off and its operator smiled nervously.

“You can actually see the smiles on the guides’ faces, not because it was funny, but because it was a smile of pure relief,” Oznur said. “For a few moments, every single person in the boat was genuinely worried.”

It was a rare moment Oznur said she was glad she captured on video.

“Afterwards, the guides told us that although hippos are known to be extremely territorial, witnessing a chase like this is not something they see very often,” she said. “They said we had experienced a truly extraordinary encounter.”

Hippos, which are herbivores, are the third-largest land animal after elephants and white rhinos and can weigh as much as 8,000 pounds. Despite their mass, the mammals do know how to accelerate in water and on land.

“They have adaptations to their semi-aquatic environments allowing them to move swiftly on both water and land,” states the African Wildlife Foundation. “Their feet have four-webbed toes that splay out to distribute weight evenly and therefore adequately support them on land, and their short legs provide powerful propulsion through the water.”

The number of fatal encounters between hippos and humans is not known, but they’re estimated to cause a minimum of 500 deaths each year.

One of hippos’ biggest threats is human encroachment, according to the World Wildlife Fund, which lists the hippo as “vulnerable” but not endangered.

“I feel incredibly lucky that I happened to be filming,” Oznur said, “because otherwise this extraordinary encounter would have lived only in our memories.”
