World.title: A celebration of Mexican artist Arturo García Bustos, 100 years after his birth
World.content:
On Aug. 8, 1926, a child was born in the heart of Mexico City. Although he grew up to explore many places, his heart remained where his passion for art was first sparked, and he passed away in his house in Coyoacán on April 7, 2017.

Arturo García Bustos is recognized for his role in Mexican art history, notably as a student of Frida Kahlo and a dedicated artist whose legacy continues to inspire.

“The love that Frida instilled in us towards Mexican culture, towards our roots and popular customs, is still alive and present in my work,” the artist stated in a 1977 interview with El Día, underscoring his lifelong dedication to Mexican identity.

A childhood in the city

One cannot grow up in Mexico City without it leaving a mark. García Bustos was well aware of this, recalling fondly that as a primary school student, he would watch Diego Rivera working on his murals at the Secretaría de Educación Pública (Ministry of Public Education).

Little did he know that he would eventually marry one of Rivera’s close collaborators, Rina Lazo, and become closer to the master muralist than he could have ever imagined.

Living downtown put him at the center of a growing metropolis, where he attended public concerts, frequented local libraries and developed a keen eye for observing urban life.

A rebellious spirit

Ever the rebel, García Bustos broke away from the strict, rigid norms of the Academia de San Carlos, Mexico’s most prestigious art academy at the time. He transferred to La Esmeralda — a decision that altered his life forever. There, he not only found his true mentors, but also met Guatemalan-Mexican artist Rina Lazo, the woman he would marry and spend his life alongside.

In contrast with the San Carlos Academy, Frida Kahlo didn’t teach through theory. She avoided a clinical approach to creation, favoring a sensitive, vibrant perspective on the artistic process instead.

She challenged her students to observe the world deeply, asking them to count the subtle colors hidden in everyday objects. When her failing health made her commute to La Esmeralda impossible, she transformed her beloved Casa Azul in Coyoacán into a creative sanctuary. It was here that Arturo García Bustos became one of the four devoted pupils known as “Los Fridos.”

Kahlo’s mentorship catalyzed a breakthrough that launched García Bustos into the Mexican art scene. Kahlo actively championed her students’ careers, securing them local mural projects — like painting the walls of a nearby pulquería — and introducing their work to leading Mexican intellectuals.

García Bustos, the militant

La Esmeralda also connected Arturo to artist collectives that defined the trajectory of his work: the Taller de Gráfica Popular (TGP) and Artistas Jóvenes Revolucionarios. These groups were not merely social clubs; they were part of a broader movement given voice by printmakers and painters who proudly viewed themselves as visual working-class laborers.

Bustos quickly adopted graphic art as one of his primary media. At just 18 years old, he joined the Taller de Gráfica Popular — founded by Leopoldo Méndez, Luis Arenal and Pablo O’Higgins — to design flyers, posters and newspapers that documented global struggles and amplified labor union demands.

Through the TGP, García Bustos deepened his understanding of both printmaking and sociopolitical activism. Members divided their time equally between pulling prints and attending political assemblies or protests, bridging the gap between art and labor.

Simultaneously, young creators were forging their own spaces. The Artistas Jóvenes Revolucionarios collective brought together students seeking to display politically engaged artwork. Bypassing traditional galleries and museums, they exhibited in public parks and markets to invite direct dialogue with everyday citizens.

Inevitably, a teacher

Following in Kahlo’s footsteps, Arturo dedicated years of his life to education. Two institutions stand out in his teaching journey: the Escuela Nacional de Artes Plásticas in Guatemala and the Escuela de Bellas Artes de Oaxaca.

He was invited to Guatemala by writer and diplomat Luis Cardoza y Aragón — a move warmly supported by his wife, Rina Lazo. During his residency, he established a printmaking workshop that produced socially critical work, though political upheaval soon forced him to return to Mexico.

García Bustos shaped generations of talent, including renowned artist Francisco Toledo, through his dedicated work at the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Oaxaca, inspiring respect for his mentorship.

Artwork

There are two remarkable paths that García Bustos followed — or rather cultivated — throughout his career: muralism and printmaking. Perhaps at first sight they may seem far from one another, but they shared a common interest in getting art to the people. While the former is usually displayed publicly, the latter is, by nature, easy to reproduce repeatedly.

Regarding the first discipline, more than 10 murals can be attributed — individually or collectively — to García Bustos. His motifs always revolve around Mexican history, Indigenous traditions and social justice. Although all his work has been equally relevant, certain pieces have sparked debate and become landmarks where they were created.

In Oaxaca

One of his most significant murals, “Las Siete Regiones de Oaxaca,” created for the National Museum of Anthropology, exemplifies his dedication to Mexican history and cultural identity.

When Arturo created the murals for the Palacio de Gobierno de Oaxaca in 1980, there was much discussion about whether a non-Oaxacan artist should paint them; one of the main opponents was Oaxacan artist Rufino Tamayo. The protests eventually ceased once supporters argued that García Bustos had already given a great deal to the state through his teaching at the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Oaxaca.

In Mexico City

Additionally, he painted a stunning mural that thousands of people see every day at the Metro station Universidad in Mexico City, located at the heart of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México: “The University on the Threshold of the 21st Century.” In this piece, Arturo journeys through the different means of knowledge and education in Mexico. He also portrays key historical figures such as Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, his mentor Frida Kahlo and his lifelong partner, Rina Lazo.

Finally, one of his last murals adorns the walls of the Casa de Cultura de Azcapotzalco in Mexico City. Here, García Bustos not only showcases his technical expertise but also enriches a community cultural space with iconic moments from Mexican history.

On the 100th anniversary of his birth, Arturo García Bustos has become an undeniably influential figure in modern Mexican art, far beyond his status as one of Los Fridos. Ultimately, his legacy enriches Mexico’s public spaces and the generations of artists he inspired alongside Rina Lazo.

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: Beyond the lechero: Veracruz’s new wave of coffee culture
World.content:
When I first decided to leave the San Francisco Bay Area in California to live in Xalapa, Veracruz — the city where both of my parents once immigrated from decades ago, and where my mom eventually moved back to live — I never anticipated how much I would fall in love with one of Mexico’s best-kept secrets: Jarocho coffee.

The state’s adoration for, and history of, producing some of Mexico’s best coffee dates back centuries. This is, after all, where coffee cultivation began with the arrival of Europeans in the 1700s. While living here, I’ve been able to travel along the oldest coffee-producing trails on the continent, sipping my way through it all, and visiting coffee plantations to learn more about the process and conditions for cultivating coffee and its environmental impacts in modern times (spoiler: it’s harder than ever for producers to keep up with the global demand and maintain their practices from the past).

The rich coffee culture of Veracruz

In Mexico’s entirety, no state boasts the same pedigree of rich coffee lineage and ongoing traditions as deeply, and perhaps as invisibly, as Veracruz. Nowhere is that notion more evident than in the state’s largest city: the actual port itself.

Of course, Jarocho coffee is by no means completely unheard of or brand new, by any stretch of the imagination, particularly for those in the know. The sight of a “lechero” pouring frothy milk into a cup of espresso at El Gran Café de la Parroquia is a classic image of the Veracruz experience going back to 1808, when the cafe first opened as a tiny operation in front of the Parroquia de Nuestra Señora de la Asunción.

Now, it represents one of Mexico’s most iconic coffee rituals. Here’s how it works: patrons tap their glass with a spoon; a formally dressed lechero comes bustling over with a steaming pot of milk; the lechero evinces showmanship by pouring the milk from a spout at an impressive height, never spilling a drop. It may seem gimmicky for some, but throughout my life, it has always represented the Jarocho way of drinking coffee.

Café traditionalism

In addition to El Gran Café de la Parroquia (which eventually split into two separate factions due to ownership disputes in the 1990s), Gran Café del Portal in Veracruz’s historic center is also worth visiting for its colonial-era charm and sense of coffee traditionalism. Indeed, the port of Veracruz’s reputational coffee heritage has carried over into other parts of Mexico over the years, too; the most popular café in Coyoacán is named El Jarocho, which opened in 1953, and ships its coffee beans by the truckloads directly from Huatusco, Veracruz.

And yet, while becoming an intrinsic part of a classic tourist experience in Veracruz, the city has not always found a way to merge its glorious coffee past with its ongoing present and future. Until now.

A new generation of cafés

Currently, the specialty coffee scene in the port of Veracruz is booming in unseen ways, as a new wave of coffeemakers and baristas has entered the mix with a more contemporary approach, offering a cool range of Veracruz’s flavorful past in an aesthetic, renovated context. In just the past year and a half that I’ve lived in the state of Veracruz, I’ve noticed an uptick of youthful cafés in the puerto; it seems that every time I go for a weekend outing with my family, another one springs up.

So here are just a few of those cafes that should be added to your list. The next time you decide to visit Mexico’s oldest and most historically important port city — where imbibing a cup of coffee in the midday swelter is a way of life — you can experience its coffee renaissance for yourself.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Singular Coffee Roasters (@singular.coffee.roasters)

Located directly across the street from Playa de Oro, right on the border of Boca del Rio — a ritzier suburb a few miles away from the industrial center of Veracruz — Singular Coffee Roasters in many ways embodies the next generation of coffeemakers in the city. In addition to having a pristine view of the beach, where the nearby ocean scenically blows palm trees along the main avenue, the vibe is funky and hip, and the menu is top-notch.

Enjoy a tampiqueña de res (a thin cut of beef served with salsa, salad greens and beans) alongside an orange cold brew, a maracuyita (cold brew mixed with mashed passion fruit) or a matcha frappe. Or, keep it simple, and order a locally sourced cup of filtered coffee — with the option of adding coconut milk for an extra 20 pesos. Either way, it’ll be a refreshing way to start off your day before hitting the nearby Gulf’s waters to cool off from the oppressive weight of the year-round heat.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by IMPETUS – Casa Tostadora de Café (@impetus.mx)

With three locations sprinkled throughout the city, Impetus has become the “it” café in town. Recently named as one of seven finalists in Mexico’s nationwide Expo Café, the brand is certainly of the highest caliber, and the interior decor and design of each café matches the high-grade taste in each cup. Though their original location has been around for 10 years now, they’ve still retained the title as Veracruz’s leading specialty coffee purveyors with a seasonally changing menu. Available in multiple price tiers ascending from lowest to highest (coffee of the day, excellent or extraordinary), they’re known for their fine-tuned brewing methods. In true Veracruz fashion, you can cool off with a granizado de olla (shaved ice poured over with café de olla) or a chilled bottle of housemade cascarita (a fruity, tea-like beverage made by steeping the dried husks of a coffee cherry in water).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ETHOS Casa de Café (@ethos_casadecafe)

Small but mighty, this bite-sized café (it’s a small room that comfortably seats around 10 people, not counting the limited sidewalk seating available outside) was named as one of the Top 100 Coffee Shops in North America, Central America and the Caribbean islands. Aside from their regular pours — which are exceptional — they offer cold brews infused with in-house ginger ale, coffee liqueur frappes and dulce de leche espressos, among other inventive options like the Blue Velvet (a concoction of blue butterfly pea flower extract, lavender, organic vanilla and milk).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by VOLADOR – Café de Altura (@volador.mx)

Recognized as a two-time Expo Café winner for producing the best coffee in Mexico, this outpost can be found on a vibrant strip in Colonia Reforma (which, for my money, is the coolest and most diverse neighborhood in the state of Veracruz, replete with stylish bars, cafés, taquerias, Korean ramen, smash burgers, Middle Eastern dining, pizzerias and more, all connected by a tree-lined walking path that leads straight to the beach). Volador is the unequivocal king of coffee in this area, with a spacious environment and outdoor patio seating to accompany its vegan food options, salads and — for the over-18 crowd — carajillos (espresso and coffee liqueur) in mazapan or horchata varietals.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Avi Café (@avicafe_)

Specializing in brunch and sweet treats — in addition to their selection of coffee and teas — this dog-friendly café is charming and sprightly. Another of Colonia Reforma’s highlights, it opened at the end of 2024 and has added to Veracruz’s rising cafe presence. A pistachio tarta vasca (a dense Basque-style cheesecake) is ideally partnered with a tri-colored strawberry matcha, an iced taro or a classic espresso cortado.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @habibicafeteria

The latest newcomer to Veracruz’s growing and diversifying coffee scene, Habibi opened its doors earlier this summer and added something completely fresh and rare to the port city’s culinary sphere: a Turkish-inspired café. Found in the ever-trendy Reforma neighborhood, the decor here is a bit over the top and kitschy, but the spirit of the coffee and food is unique and notable. Order a Turkish coffee (which is brewed in hot sand) and, if you’re hungering or have a sweet tooth, add a side of gold-dusted dessert — or grab a loaded shawarma de pollo — and stay for the fun of it all. Pro tip: don’t forget the plátano macho-stuffed kibbeh.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Aquí si volvemos (@aquisivolvemos)

The tropical abundance of Veracruz’s ingredients reigns supreme at DeLirio. Take your pick of orange espressos, pineapple cold brews, maracuya cheesecakes, watermelon agua frescas, chilled cucumbers and lime frappes, and so much more. Despite its colorful vibrancy on the menu, it retains an understated interior style: An elegant, minimalist architecture highlighted by its mid-century-inspired curved walls and wicker chairs — all working in harmony to accentuate this chic café in (you guessed it) Colonia Reforma.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020) and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: MND launches new series on personal finance
World.content:
The team at Mexico News Daily is always trying to think of new content ideas to help better educate and inform our readers about Mexico. A few recent examples include our Expat Safety Perceptions Index, the MND Mexico Healthcare Survey, and the Sheinbaum, Mexico Economy, and Peso Indexes.

As we have been working on these content ideas over the past few months, we have received feedback from readers on other ideas, and we have identified some additional gaps as well. One of them is to create an index that focuses more on Mexico’s social progress (or lack of) versus more economically focused indicators. We are actively working on that one — stay tuned!

Another big gap we identified was regarding the whole issue of money and personal finance in Mexico. It occurred to us that there is often a real gap in knowledge when it comes to money in Mexico. Many people who are extremely sophisticated financially in their home country oftentimes don’t even have a bank account in Mexico. Others that I have met have little more than a local basic checking account with a debit card. Still others lose significant amounts of money on currency conversion.

The light bulb really went off when we were reviewing the results of the Expat Safety Perceptions Index. The data of our survey showed us that most expats/foreigners have not had personal safety issues and in fact, for the most part, feel very safe in Mexico. From a personal safety perspective, most feel pretty good. But that got us thinking and asking questions like:

1. What financial issues have you had in Mexico?

2. What are the financial risks the immigrants face here?

3. What are common mistakes that immigrants make with money here?

4. How many MND readers have been victims of a financial crime in Mexico?

5. What can you do to protect your finances in Mexico?

We believe that this is an extremely important topic and there is much to be learned and applied. As a result, Mexico News Daily will be going “all in” on this topic. We will start with a survey that we will be asking thousands of expats in Mexico to take. The results of this survey will be shared with our readers and will also help guide and define the topics of a new weekly series of “Mexico and My Money,” beginning next week. In this series, we will be covering everything from common mistakes made to best practices for protecting and growing your money in Mexico. We will cover topics like banking, exchanging money, rental income, investing, and dealing with contractors and local service providers.

Our goal is neither to scare you nor lead you to a false sense of security, but rather to provide you with the information, best practices and lessons learned of others to help you best manage your money in Mexico. Stay tuned, I am certain that we are all going to learn a lot from this survey and series.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: An award-winning bakery launches a definitive ‘map’ of Mexico’s abundant bread types
World.content:
Building on Mexico News Daily’s history of Mexican bread, published earlier this year, two Mexican bakers have created a new “map” that charts the vast, often overlooked world of Mexican breads — from conchas and bolillos to coyotas, pan de muerto and rosca de Reyes.

The Primer Mapa del Pan Mexicano — or First Map of Mexican Bread — is a research project by siblings Ariana and Julio González, the founding bakers at 13-year-old Buñuelo in Naucalpan, State of México.

Instead of sorting breads by state or region, the map tracks their baking lineage: dough, technique and tradition.

That framework shows how one preparation style can develop into breads with markedly different shapes, textures and uses, with seemingly unrelated pieces sharing production methods or customs.

The map includes sweet breads, or pan dulce, savory staples and festive breads such as pan de muerto for Día de Muertos and rosca de Reyes for Three Kings Day.

The savory family includes bolillo, telera, pambazo, cemita and hojaldra, breads commonly used in tortas and other Mexican sandwiches.

Other families include bizcocho — sweet, cake-like breads including conchas, nubes and pelones — and the cookie family, which includes cochinitos de piloncillo, coricos and coyotas, the last being Sonoran pastries typically filled with piloncillo.

Other breads in the festive category include pan de pulque, pan de yema and a specialty bread sold at festivals and patron saint celebrations in Puebla and Tlaxcala called pan de fiesta or pan de feria.

The González siblings — recently named Bakers of the Year by the Mexico Gastronomic Guide — developed the project through years of fieldwork at traditional and contemporary bakeries. Designer Marcela Morales turned the research into a reference piece.

The total number of Mexican breads remains an elusive proposition. Estimates often put the figure above 1,000 varieties, but the map is not presented as a census. Its 52 selections are representative samples meant to illuminate a larger and still-changing baking heritage.

“This map is not intended to be a definitive catalog of Mexican breadmaking, but rather an invitation to see it from a different perspective,” Julio González said, “We want people to understand that behind each piece there are techniques, traditions, and baking families that are all part of the same heritage.”

The map arrives after a period of renewed attention to Mexican breadmaking.

In late 2025, a British baker based in Mexico City voiced a blunt opinion about Mexican bread culture (or, in his opinion, lack thereof) and received widespread backlash, including a Mexico News Daily piece noting, “You’re free to dislike bolillos … Just don’t use cultural superiority as a seasoning.”

Then earlier this year, Panadería Rosetta in Mexico City was named one of the world’s 10 best pastry makers by La Liste, a prestigious Paris‑based global dining guide.

For now, the single-sheet map is being sold for 135 pesos (US $7.88) at Buñuelo, Av. Alcanfores 44-2 in Naucalpan. See the bakery’s Instagram for more details, including a planned digital version.

With reports from Food & Wine en Español and El Universal

World.title: Opinion: The real reason San Miguel de Allende feels so American
World.content:
Since I arrived in San Miguel de Allende over six weeks ago for a nine-week journalism internship, I have been trying to figure out why more international tourists do not come to central Mexico.

I have written about my experiences across the Bajío cities of Guanajuato and Quereétaro as well as Mexico City. I have been constantly surprised by the lack of American tourists, or sometimes even tourists in general, in what I felt like were incredible destinations for a vacation.

But I have yet to write about the tourists in the place where I’ve been living. A place flooded with local and international tourists on weekends and a place where the economy revolves around visitors. San Miguel is seemingly the one place in the region where American tourists are around every corner. So what sets San Miguel apart? Why do Americans flock here instead of Guanajuato or Querétaro?

It all started nearly 80 years ago when the emergence of art schools in San Miguel allowed Americans to take classes abroad. This, in turn, brought new business and development, with hotels opening throughout the city. San Miguel’s famous colonial streets were declared a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2008, spurring more development and tourism.

Now San Miguel is widely regarded as one of the top international destinations in Mexico, bringing in over two million visitors each year. There are an abundance of vineyards just outside the city limits, fine dining is around every corner and luxury hotels are found all throughout town.

As more and more foreigners came to San Miguel and as the arts scene continued to grow, the town became increasingly accommodating to American tourists. Americans tend to like to feel comfortable abroad, and the prevalence of English in the town takes away a massive hurdle that might deter Americans from going to Guanajuato or Querétaro, where English is less prevalent.

More Americans also means more American food, more American sports on TV, and more spaces designed to make Americans feel comfortable. Jewish delis, burger joints and microbreweries covered with TVs are easy to find — and they are harder to come by in Guanajuato or Querétaro. More places for Americans will always lead to more Americans.

The invention of social media has also greatly benefited San Miguel’s tourism industry. The Parroquia de San Miguel Árcangel — with its towering spires and jaw-dropping pink facade — looks glorious in an Instagram story. The courtyards and gardens throughout the town also make for great photos, and some have called San Miguel’s local Starbucks the most beautiful in the world.

Once San Miguel was named the best city in the world by Travel and Leisure magazine, more visitors than ever began to arrive.

San Miguel is also small and relatively relaxed. It’s dense and walkable, to the point that residents do not need a car to get around. It has a large local bar scene, but not many clubs. The weather is consistent and relatively mild year-round. All of these — along with cheaper prices than the United States — have made San Miguel a picture-perfect place for American retirees looking for something different late in life. With retirees generally less motivated to learn Spanish, the influx of English-speakers forced business to cater to that demographic.

While San Miguel is definitely popular, it still is not widely known in the United States. When most Americans think of tourism in Mexico, they imagine the picturesque beaches of Cancún, Los Cabos or Puerto Vallarta. Mexico City is rapidly growing as an international tourist destination and those seeking more of an adventure have probably heard of Oaxaca. Despite the high volume of arrivals, San Miguel de Allende does not have the same level of international recognition as other Mexican destinations.

And it shouldn’t. San Miguel is a small city that has already been drastically gentrified. Homes throughout Centro have been replaced by shops and restaurants, the cost of living continues to climb, and there is a lack of jobs outside of the tourism industry.

So what sets San Miguel apart? It’s at the top of tourism rankings, while other beautiful Bajío towns receive less attention. It has splashes of Mexican culture while still feeling comfortable for Americans.

Does that make San Miguel better than other cities? Yes and no. It feels more Americanized, which makes it attractive to American tourists. But the vibe isn’t just American — it’s international. Expats mingle with locals, and travelers from all over the world visit the cobblestone streets. It’s a destination for a reason, but a lot of those reasons can be found in a lot of other cities in the region — without the crowds, or price tag, that have followed San Miguel’s fame.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Seaweed diplomacy: Mexico and Japan to tackle sargassum crisis in new joint program
World.content:
The Foreign Ministry has announced that Japan will be participating in the development of a joint program to address the massive influx of sargassum on Mexico’s shores.

Japan — which has been actively collaborating with Caribbean nations to tackle the sargassum problems plaguing the region — will offer ocean-monitoring technology, specialized equipment including robotics and sensors and financial cooperation.

Additionally, Japan will provide sargassum-collecting ships and vessels adapted for the collection of the macroalgae at sea in order to strengthen Mexico’s capacity to address the situation along its Caribbean beaches.

The collaboration will also feature satellite monitoring, biological decomposition technologies for sargassum and technical training programs through Japan’s International Cooperation Agency, in coordination with Mexico’s Agency for International Development Cooperation.

The project will include academic research, as well as business-oriented research and development. This work will focus on processes for converting the sargassum, as a raw material, into commercially viable products, such as fertilizer, biofuels, building materials and soap.

The goal is to boost marine and nearshore coastal conservation efforts, support integrated coastal management actions and mitigate negative impacts on sectors such as fisheries, public health and tourism.

The announcement came during an Aug. 3 meeting between Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco and his Japanese counterpart, Toshimitsu Motegi, in which they agreed to establish a working group to advance new areas of collaboration to strengthen bilateral relations in the political, economic, scientific and technological spheres.

In a joint statement to the media, they announced the launch of a high-level economic dialogue to boost bilateral trade, which, from January to May this year, amounted to US $9.9 billion, a 4% increase compared to the same period last year.

A few days earlier, President Claudia Sheinbaum pledged 2 billion pesos in federal funds (US $115 million) to battle an influx of sargassum in the state of Quintana Roo.

These funds will be directed toward sargassum control efforts spanning roughly 30 miles of beachfront spanning resorts including Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Mahahual.

En reunión bilateral, ambos titulares de… pic.twitter.com/iaZwAhBjjV — Relaciones Exteriores (@SRE_mx) August 3, 2026

In October, Cancún will host the international EU-Caribbean Global Gateway Conference on Sargassum, with the aim of articulating joint strategies for the containment and management of biomass and sargassum.

The conference is expected to focus on regional cooperation, circular economy solutions and sargassum-harvesting technology.

World.title: The Mexican peso hits its strongest level against the dollar in 6 months
World.content:
Mexico’s currency gained 0.12% vs the U.S. dollar in Thursday trading, extending its rally to 10 straight days after the central bank left interest rates unchanged at its Aug. 6 monetary policy meeting.

The peso closed Thursday at 17.21 to the US dollar and dipped below 17.14 in early trading on Friday, an additional 0.58% gain and its strongest level against the U.S. dollar since Feb. 23.

Forbes México attributed Friday’s early action to a negative U.S. jobs report and said the peso is on pace to appreciate by 1.3% by the end of the week.

Mexico’s currency was also boosted by the central bank’s unanimous decision on Thursday to hold its benchmark rate at 6.50% for a second consecutive meeting, while hinting that rates would remain at the current level for the foreseeable future.

In a statement, Banxico’s board of governors said, “Headline and core inflation are expected to decline throughout the forecast horizon, albeit more gradually than previously anticipated.”

Headline inflation slowed in July for a fourth consecutive month though the central bank does not expect it to converge to its 3% target until late next year.

In a social media post, Gabriela Siller, director of analysis at Grupo Financerio BASE, said the peso is also appreciating “due to the carry-trade,” a strategy whereby an investor borrows money in a currency with a low interest rate and invests those funds into higher-yielding assets or currencies.

Siller said large global investors are borrowing in the U.S. and Japan, then investing in Mexico, indicating that the peso continues to benefit from a wide interest rate differential (Mexico’s 6.50% policy rate compares favorably to the U.S. Federal Reserve’s 3.50%-3.75% target range).

The newspaper El Economista said the U.S. jobs report (which noted that U.S. nonfarm payrolls fell by 23,000 jobs last month, following a downwardly revised increase of 20,000 jobs the previous month) prompted the market to reduce bets that U.S. interest rates will rise.

Monex Grupo Financiero concurred, saying in a statement that the peso’s advance against the dollar is “driven by the weakness of the dollar and a readjustment of expectations on the direction of the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy” at its next meeting in September.

With reports from El Economista and Forbes México

World.title: Where You Can Fly Nonstop to Costa Rica This High Season
World.content:
Getting to Costa Rica is about to get easier from a lot more places. Fourteen new or expanded nonstop flights start between October and March, and several of them connect cities that have never had a direct flight here. One heavily promoted route has already been cancelled, and it is worth knowing which. If you are planning a trip for the high season, or you have family flying down to visit, this is the list you need.

Every route below is confirmed by the airline, with start dates, days of the week and aircraft where those have been published. The expansion follows a strong year for arrivals. Between January and June, 1,605,360 travelers landed in Costa Rica by air, up 7.8% over the same six months of 2025 and the best first half on record.

New flights to San Jose

Las Vegas is off the table. Southwest announced a daily overnight Las Vegas to San Jose route in February, pushed the launch from October to November, then cancelled it in July before a single flight operated. The airline cited fuel costs and a decision to use its aircraft more efficiently, since an overnight leaves a plane parked in Costa Rica for hours. If you were waiting on that one, stop waiting.

That leaves the western United States where it was. From Nevada, Arizona and most of California you are still connecting through Houston, Miami or another gateway to reach Costa Rica.

Breeze Airways arrives from Tampa on October 3. This is the airline’s first-ever service to Costa Rica and makes the country its fifth international destination. Flights run Wednesdays and Saturdays on an Airbus A220 seating 137. Tampa has not had a direct link to San Jose in more than 25 years.

Air Transat starts Quebec City on December 15, once a week. Unlike most of the winter additions, this one is permanent rather than seasonal, and it brings the number of Canadian cities with direct flights to Costa Rica to seven.

Porter connects Toronto Pearson from December 2 through April 30, four flights a week on an Embraer E195-E2 seating 132. The aircraft has no middle seats.

Southwest adds Austin on March 13, 2027, Saturdays only. It is the only nonstop between Central Texas and San Jose. The outbound leaves Austin at 10:25 a.m. and lands at 2:05 p.m., with the return departing at 3:05 p.m. Tickets are already on sale.

New flights to Guanacaste

Liberia keeps pulling ahead. Daniel Oduber Quiros handled its busiest quarter ever in early 2026, and airlines have noticed. Air Canada flies Vancouver from December 13 through April 12, Mondays and Thursdays on a Boeing 737 MAX 8 seating 177. Canadian traffic through Liberia grew 28% in the first half of this year, which is the main reason so many of these routes point north.

WestJet adds Ottawa from December 20 through April 4, Sundays, on a 737 MAX 8 seating 174. Worth knowing before you shop: Porter already flies Ottawa to Liberia weekly through the winter, so from December you have two nonstop options on that route rather than one.

United flies Washington-Dulles daily from December 17 through January 4. Note how short that window is. It is a holiday-season route, not a winter-long one, and if you want it you should book early. The aircraft is a Boeing 737 MAX 9 with 179 seats including 20 in business.

That route also completes something unusual. United will now serve Liberia from all seven of its US hubs, alongside Newark, Denver, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Houston and Chicago. Delta returns to New York JFK from December 19 through April 10, Saturdays only, on an Airbus A321neo seating 194. Delta last flew this route in 2016, and it currently offers no service at all between New York City and Costa Rica.

Southwest adds Nashville from February 13 to March 6, 2027, Saturdays, on a 737 MAX 8. That is a four-week window, the shortest on this list.

Costa Rica gets its first flights from Poland

The most unexpected addition is a charter series. Rainbow Tours and LOT Polish Airlines will run eleven flights into Liberia on a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner seating 251, the first direct air link between Poland and Costa Rica. Warsaw Chopin operates weekly from October 8 to 29. Katowice takes over weekly from November 5 to December 17.

These are charter operations sold through a tour operator, so you will not find them on a standard flight search. If you have family in Poland planning a visit, that is the booking route.

More Seats from Europe

Three European carriers are adding frequencies rather than new destinations, which matters if you have struggled to find a seat on a specific day.

British Airways moves to Heathrow on October 25 and goes from three to five weekly flights through March, operating Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays on a Boeing 787-8. If you connect onward in Europe, this is the change that matters most. Heathrow is the airline’s main hub, and it has never had scheduled service to Costa Rica or anywhere in Central America until now.

Lufthansa moves from three to five weekly Frankfurt flights from October 25 to March 27, operating Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. The days change as well as the count, so check yours. The route currently runs Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays. Lufthansa is also switching to a Boeing 787-9 with its newer Allegris cabin.

Iberojet adds a third weekly Madrid flight on Thursdays from late November. The airline expects to make it permanent across 2027 and 2028.

The full list

Airline Route Starts Days Southwest Las Vegas to San Jose Cancelled Dropped before launch Breeze Tampa to San Jose Oct 3 Wed, Sat LOT (charter) Warsaw to Liberia Oct 8 to 29 Weekly British Airways London Heathrow to San Jose Oct 25 (3 to 5 weekly) Tue, Wed, Fri, Sat, Sun Lufthansa Frankfurt to San Jose Oct 25 (3 to 5 weekly) Mon, Wed, Fri, Sat, Sun LOT (charter) Katowice to Liberia Nov 5 to Dec 17 Weekly Iberojet Madrid to San Jose Late Nov (2 to 3 weekly) Adds Thu Porter Toronto to San Jose Dec 2 to Apr 30 4 weekly Air Canada Vancouver to Liberia Dec 13 to Apr 12 Mon, Thu Air Transat Quebec City to San Jose Dec 15 Weekly United Washington-Dulles to Liberia Dec 17 to Jan 4 Daily Delta New York JFK to Liberia Dec 19 to Apr 10 Sat WestJet Ottawa to Liberia Dec 20 to Apr 4 Sun Southwest Nashville to Liberia Feb 13 to Mar 6 Sat Southwest Austin to San Jose Mar 13, 2027 Sat

Before you book

Pick your airport before you pick your flight. Liberia puts you within a short drive of Tamarindo, Nosara, Playas del Coco, Papagayo, Flamingo and Santa Teresa. San Jose is better for the Caribbean side, the Central Valley, the southern Pacific and anywhere you need a domestic connection. Landing at the wrong one can add four or five hours of driving to your first day.

Watch the end dates as closely as the start dates. Several of these routes run for weeks rather than months, and a return flight that does not exist yet is a common way to get stuck paying for a connection you did not plan. Liberia also operates only between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m., so late arrivals are not an option there regardless of what a search engine shows you.

Seasonal routes get pulled when they do not sell. If a specific one matters to your plans, booking it early does more than save money, it helps keep the route on the schedule. That is also the argument for travel insurance on a seasonal route. If an airline drops the flight or shifts the schedule after you have booked hotels and tours around it, a policy that covers trip interruption is what stands between you and paying twice.

World.title: Costa Rica Approves New Rules for Nighttime Ambulance Flights
World.content:
Costa Rica has approved a national protocol governing nighttime air ambulance flights, closing out roughly ten months of uncertainty that began when Civil Aviation barred the practice at most of the airfields last October. Under the framework, night medical flights are permitted at six locations: the airfields at Limón, Palmar Sur and Coto 47 near Ciudad Neily, along with Tobías Bolaños in Pavas, Daniel Oduber in Liberia and Juan Santamaría in Alajuela.

Juan Santamaría must now serve as the arrival point for every nighttime medical flight in the country. The selection came down largely to which fields have runway lighting and a permanent police presence, both treated as prerequisites for safe operations after dark. Coto 47 has both, including a base of the Air Vigilance Service, and Palmar Sur received substantial state investment in lighting and security in recent years.

Left off the approved list are several airfields serving high-traffic tourist areas, among them Tamarindo, Quepos and Puerto Jiménez. Pilots had also identified Cóbano and Nicoya as essential for reaching patients in coastal and peninsular communities far from major hospitals.

The protocol restricts these flights to patients in critical condition whose lives are at immediate risk and who cannot safely wait for daylight. It sets out an eleven-step process that begins when the Costa Rican Social Security Fund identifies an emergency case, moves through coordination with the Air Vigilance Service and Civil Aviation, and ends with a private operator carrying out the flight once conditions and authorization align.

Officials say exceptions outside the formal protocol will still be permitted when a patient’s life is at stake. The rules were drafted jointly by the Ministry of Health, Civil Aviation, the Social Security Fund and the Air Vigilance Service, and are to be reviewed annually.

The finalized protocol ends a dispute that began with a directive issued on October 9 of last year, which prohibited takeoffs and landings between sunset and sunrise at uncontrolled airfields nationwide. Civil Aviation argued the flights had operated for decades without a formal regulatory framework and that medical operations must meet the same technical and legal standards as any other flight.

Transportation Minister Efraím Zeledón Leiva and Social Security Fund president Mónica Taylor defended the restriction at a press conference in February, characterizing the volume of genuinely urgent flights as minimal. Taylor said many transfers went to private hospitals and involved minor complaints. Zeledón referred to irregular commercial arrangements around the flights at Tobías Bolaños, and maintained that extreme emergencies were still being authorized.

That position drew immediate pushback from pilots, ambulance operators and physicians inside the Social Security system. The Fund’s own emergency and disaster center warned the restriction was delaying transfers of patients who needed higher-capacity hospitals, and the hospital in Ciudad Neily fell back on ground transfers with police escorts to speed the run into the Central Valley.

Ricardo Hernández, a paramedic and operations manager at the air and ground transport company SAAT, said roughly 700 people a year need urgent air transport in Costa Rica for medical reasons, and that close to half of all transfers happen at night. Operators separately reported hundreds of night ambulance flights annually before the restriction took effect, and said the country had recorded no accidents in night operations at uncontrolled airfields in eighteen years.

An analysis presented by pilots counted 3,130 nighttime ambulance flights over the previous decade, an average of about 285 a year, without a serious incident. Pilots also noted that the October directive landed at the start of high tourist season, when visitors are more likely to be injured in remote or coastal areas.

For anyone traveling to the more remote parts of the country, including popular surf and beach towns that are not on the approved list, the practical effect is unchanged. A serious nighttime medical emergency in those areas will still mean a lengthy ground transfer rather than an air evacuation, because every flight must now either originate or terminate at one of the six designated locations.

Civil Aviation issued temporary technical standards for qualifying airfields earlier this year while the permanent framework was being finalized. Those interim rules are now replaced. Whether additional airfields can be brought onto the list will depend on lighting, perimeter security and staffing upgrades that have not yet been funded or scheduled.

World.title: Belize @45 Workshop Explores Sovereignty and Nationhood
World.content:
Belize @45 Workshop Explores Sovereignty and Nationhood

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Workshop, a three-day professional development training, was held from August 5 to 7, 2026, bringing together educators from across the country to examine what Belize’s independence really means.

The training was a collaborative effort of the Institute for Social and Cultural Research (ISCR), the Belize Archives and Records Service (BARS), the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science & Technology (MOECST), specifically Ms. Ruby Reyes of the Belizean Studies Curriculum and Assessment Unit, the George Price Centre for Peace and Development, the University of Belize, and Galen University.

During the training, historian and diplomat Assad Shoman challenged educators to reflect on the “role of teachers and students in shaping Belize’s future.”

The event included virtual sessions and an in-person learning session at the George Price Centre for Peace and Development in Belmopan, equipping educators with new tools and perspectives to bring Belize’s history and independence journey to life for students.

Organizers emphasized that Belize’s independence is not simply an achievement of the past, but an ongoing process, underscoring the message: “Independence is the beginning!

World.title: Belizeans Travel Across U.S. for Passport and Nationality Services at Evanston Diaspora Hub
World.content:
Belizeans Travel Across U.S. for Passport and Nationality Services at Evanston Diaspora Hub

By Zoila Palma: Belizeans from across the Chicago area and several other parts of the United States travelled to Evanston this weekend to access passport and nationality services brought directly to the diaspora by Belize’s Ministry of Immigration, Governance and Labour.

The three-day Evanston Diaspora Hub runs from August 7 to 9. The event provides passport and nationality services, including first-time and renewal passport applications, as well as applications for Belizean nationality by descent.

The ministry says that the outreach provides a more convenient way to complete important documentation without having to travel to Belize. Belizean passport applicants are required to appear in person at an Immigration Office in Belize or at a designated Belizean diplomatic or consular mission, making mobile outreach efforts particularly valuable for Belizeans living far from those locations.

The Evanston hub also highlighted the strong community ties among Belizeans living in the United States. Some Chicago-area residents noted that they have built a vibrant Belizean community and are preparing to host a fundraiser on Saturday to provide scholarships to 14 Belizean-American students attending school.

Belize’s Ambassador to the United States, H.E. Nestor E. Mendez, visited the hub alongside Belize’s Ambassador for Diaspora Relations, Sandhya Murphy, as officials engaged with Belizeans accessing the services.

The Evanston initiative follows other diaspora outreach efforts by the Government of Belize in the United States. Earlier this year, approximately 230 passports and 17 nationality certificates were delivered to Belizeans abroad during another outreach initiative, reflecting continued demand for documentation services within Belizean communities across the United States.

World.title: Belizeans travel from across the United States to Evanston, Chicago, for immigration services at Diaspora Hub
World.content:
Belizeans travel from across the United States to Evanston, Chicago, for immigration services at Diaspora Hub

By Hugh O’Brien: Belizeans from across the Chicago area and the larger United States, including Texas, Washington and Colorado, travelled to Evanston this weekend to access passport and nationality services being offerred directly to the diaspora by Belize’s Ministry of Immigration, Governance and Labour.

The Diaspora Mobile Hub, being held from August 7 to 9, is providing Belizeans living in the United States with an opportunity to complete nationality and passport applications without having to travel to Belize or wait for an appointment at a designated Belizean diplomatic or consular mission.

While many of those attending came from Evanston, Chicago and surrounding communities, others travelled hundreds or even thousands of miles to take advantage of the outreach initiative. Several Belizeans from the Dallas area made the journey to Evanston to submit applications and complete other documentation processes.

In a public statement posted on its Facebook page, the Ministry said “Some visitors came to renew their Belizean passports, while others submitted first-time passport applications. Families also visited the hub to apply for Belizean nationality by descent, allowing eligible children and other descendants born outside Belize to formally establish their Belizean nationality.”

The Ministry said that these services are being provided through the Nationality and Passports Department as part of the Ministry’s broader effort to bring essential government services closer to Belizeans living abroad.

“For members of the diaspora, having services available in a U.S. city can significantly reduce the time, cost and logistical challenges associated with completing important documentation. Belizean passport applicants are required to appear in person at an Immigration Office in Belize or at a designated Belizean diplomatic or consular mission.”

For this reason, according to the Ministry, Evanston became a destination this weekend not only for Belizeans living in Illinois, but also for members of the diaspora who travelled from across the United States.

“For some families, the visit was simply about renewing a passport and maintaining the ability to travel using Belizean documentation. For others, particularly parents seeking nationality by descent for their children, the process represented another way of passing their connection to Belize from one generation to the next,” said the Ministry.

Belize’s Ambassador to the United States, H.E. Nestor E. Mendez, attended the Ministry’s immigration outreach alongside Belize’s Ambassador for Diaspora Relations, Sandhya Murphy.

Belizean nationality by descent is available to qualifying persons born outside Belize based on Belizean parentage.

The Evanston Diaspora Mobile Hub continues will conclude on Sunday, August 9.

World.title: Halo BPO sweetens the deal: $10 an hour plus commission for home based sales agents
World.content:
Halo BPO sweetens the deal: $10 an hour plus commission for home based sales agents

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Halo BPO is back on the hiring trail, and the terms have improved. The company’s latest recruitment drive for work from home sales agents offers $9.00 BZD per hour during training, rising to $10.00 BZD per hour after training, plus commission and bonuses, with pay issued weekly, an upgrade on the $8.50 flat rate advertised earlier this month.

The role is full time outbound sales, done entirely from home anywhere in Belize. The qualifying bar has risen alongside the pay: applicants now need two or more years of sales experience, and credit repair experience is listed as a plus, suggesting the campaign involves the credit services market.

The technical requirement is the other significant change. Home internet must deliver at least 85 Mbps download and 45 Mbps upload, a specification that in practice points to fibre-grade service, so applicants should run a speed test before applying.

For experienced sellers with strong connections, the package is among the more competitive remote offers advertised locally: guaranteed hourly pay, weekly payout, and commission upside on top.

Applications go to [email protected], and the standing instruction applies: include your full name in the email subject line.

World.title: The weekend keeps its promise: sunshine across Belize
World.content:
The weekend keeps its promise: sunshine across Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The forecast made the promise on Friday, and Saturday is delivering it in full. Mainly fair weather conditions prevail across Belize, with sunshine overhead, gentle seas, and inland heat reaching 95 degrees, and Sunday is set to repeat the performance.

According to the National Meteorological Service, skies will be sunny with a few cloudy spells today and clear to partly cloudy tonight. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated, with a medium chance of a few more mostly over the Toledo District tonight, the weekend’s lone exception to the fair pattern.

Temperatures along the coast will reach a high of 89 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius) and a low of 82 (28 Celsius). Inland areas will be the hottest in the country, climbing to 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 Celsius) before dropping to 73 (23 Celsius). In the hills, expect a high of 83 degrees Fahrenheit (28 Celsius) and a cool low of 67 (19 Celsius). With the mercury at 95 inland, the weekend checklist stays simple: water close and shade often.

At sea, conditions remain at their friendliest, with easterly winds of 5 to 15 knots, a light chop, and waves of 2 to 4 feet, fine water for the weekend’s boaters, snorkelers, and fishing trips.

On the tropical front, the calm holds. Tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the region over the next 48 hours.

Looking ahead to Sunday and Sunday night, similar weather conditions are expected to prevail, carrying the sunshine through the full weekend.

Today’s low tides are at 1:06 PM and 11:32 PM, with a high tide at 7:41 PM and another high at 6:11 AM tomorrow. The sun sets this evening at 6:22 PM and rises tomorrow at 5:34 AM. The forecast was issued by forecaster Tareek Matthews.

World.title: Santander clarifies operations following reports of fish kill in Belize River
World.content:
Santander clarifies operations following reports of fish kill in Belize River

By Zoila Palma: On August 7, 2026, Santander Sugar Group (SSG) released a statement clarifying its operations following reports of aquatic life deaths in the Belize River Valley.

The release states that Santander Sugar Group is “deeply saddened by the loss of aquatic life recently reported in the Belize River Valley.” The company said it recognizes the importance of the Belize River to surrounding communities, the environment and Belize as a whole.

Santander said protecting natural resources remains a core principle of its operations. The company explained that it operates under an approved Environmental Compliance Plan and continuously monitors its operations while implementing measures to minimize runoff and protect surrounding waterways.

The company also said it has fully cooperated with the Department of the Environment (DoE) and other relevant government agencies since the incident was reported. According to SSG, the DoE was granted unrestricted access to its facilities and operations to support the ongoing investigation.

Santander further stated that its processing facility is designed to operate as a closed-loop system and does not operate with a continuous process effluent stream returning to the Belize River. The company said it remains committed to providing any additional information or assistance that may be required as authorities continue their investigation.

World.title: Belize City featured in Commonwealth Study
World.content:
Belize City featured in Commonwealth Study

By BBN Staff: Belize City is being featured in a new Commonwealth study examining how cities and local governments can close the urban finance gap and secure sustainable funding for infrastructure and essential services. The city was selected as one of only three case studies highlighted in the research, alongside Kerala State in India and Kigali, Rwanda.

On Wednesday, August 5, Belize City Mayor Bernard Wagner participated in the Commonwealth Local Government Forum’s webinar, “The Urban Finance Gap: Practical Pathways for Local Government Finance across the Commonwealth.” The discussion explored practical approaches to strengthening local government finance, improving resilience and ensuring cities have the resources needed to deliver critical services.

During the webinar, Wagner emphasized that financing infrastructure projects cannot end once construction is completed. He noted that projects such as drainage systems and roads must be designed to withstand changing conditions while also having adequate funding for operation, maintenance and eventual renewal. The Yarborough Pumping Station was highlighted as an example, having proven effective in draining the city’s waterways during flooding but also requiring significant recurring costs for continued operation and maintenance.

The Belize City Council said the city’s inclusion in the study highlights its fiscal administration, innovative approach to municipal finance and experience with its Municipal Bond Programme. It added that closing the urban finance gap will require greater decentralization, sustainable financing frameworks and increased trust in capable local governments to invest in their communities. Belize City’s experience is being presented as an example of what local leadership can achieve despite limited fiscal space.

World.title: Department of the Environment provides update on Fish Kill in the Belize River Valley area
World.content:
Department of the Environment provides update on Fish Kill in the Belize River Valley area

INVESTIGATION INTO THE FISH KILL IN THE BELIZE RIVER VALLEY AREA

Belmopan, Belize. August 7, 2026: The public is hereby informed that, as part of the ongoing investigation into the fish kill in the Belize River Valley area, the Department of the Environment (DOE) has conducted visual observations and water quality assessments from near Banana Bank, upstream of Santander Farms, to the Burrell Boom Village bridge. Significant fish mortality and changes in water conditions were observed particularly along the approximately 17.5-mile stretch between Isabella Bank and Grace Bank. The Department is also assessing discharge points and other activities along and within the vicinity of the river as part of its investigation into the possible source or sources of the event.

On-site water quality testing and sampling have been conducted at various locations along the river. Preliminary field results recorded extremely low levels of dissolved oxygen in areas where significant fish mortality was observed, together with elevated conductivity, chlorophyll-a and turbidity at certain locations. These conditions can adversely affect aquatic life. Samples have been submitted for laboratory analysis to assist in determining the cause of the observed conditions.

As part of the ongoing investigation, the DOE has also collected water samples from the Santander Farms drainage system and at locations downstream for chemical analysis. Fish and sediment samples are also being collected and analysed to assist in determining the cause of the fish mortality and whether contaminants may have contributed to the event.

The Department is additionally reviewing satellite imagery from before and during the event to assess changes in water conditions, land-clearing activities and other factors that may assist in identifying potential contributing sources. Investigations and assessments are also being conducted in relation to other developments, activities and potential discharge points within the wider area.

At this stage, the Department has not determined the source or responsible party associated with the fish kill. The investigation remains ongoing, and any determination will be based on the results of laboratory analyses and the totality of the scientific and technical evidence collected.

The precautionary advisory issued by the Department on August 5, 2026, remains in effect. The public is therefore advised not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from the affected areas and not to use untreated river water for drinking, cooking, food preparation, livestock or pets until further notice. This advisory applies to untreated water taken directly from the river and does not apply to treated potable water supplied by Belize Water Services Limited.

The DOE continues to coordinate with relevant government agencies and other authorities in monitoring the situation and advancing the investigation. The public will be informed as laboratory results and other verified findings become available.

The Department of the Environment remains committed to protecting Belize’s environment, safeguarding our natural resources and public health, and ensuring that all potential sources are thoroughly investigated and that appropriate action is taken where the evidence establishes a breach of Belize’s environmental laws.

END

For More Information Contact: Anthony Mai, Chief Environmental Officer

Department of the Environment
