World.title: Iraq oil exports drop 75% amid Hormuz closure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Oil Minister Hayan Abdul-Ghani announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, that the nation’s crude oil exports have plummeted by 75% due to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and regional military escalations. The severe drop in oil revenues has triggered a liquidity squeeze across the federal government, causing widespread delays in state employee salary disbursements.

Speaking at a press conference in Baghdad, Abdul-Ghani revealed that Iraq is currently exporting only a quarter of its pre-war volumes, which stood at approximately 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) prior to the outbreak of regional hostilities on February 28. He noted that while Baghdad has engaged in diplomatic talks with Iran to permit the passage of Iraqi oil shipments through the Gulf, no operational agreement has been activated.

Key financial and operational highlights

Export Collapse: Iraq’s crude exports have fallen to ~25% of pre-war capacity, cutting off the primary source of state revenue.

Fiscal Pressure & Salary Delays: Reduced export volumes and below-budget sale prices have caused acute liquidity shortages, delaying public sector payrolls.

Corporate Damage Compensation: Domestic Attacks: Baghdad has agreed to compensate foreign energy companies for damages resulting from attacks originating inside Iraqi territory. External Strikes: The government declared itself legally exempt from compensating firms for damages caused by foreign strikes or broader military actions beyond state control.

Alternative Export Bypasses: Baghdad is fast-tracking pipeline infrastructure projects bypassing the Persian Gulf, including routes south toward Turkey’s Ceyhan port, Syria’s Baniyas terminal, and Jordan’s Aqaba port.

To maintain minimal cash flows, Iraq is currently forced to sell its crude at deep price concessions below the baseline benchmark set in the national budget, compounding treasury deficits.

In response to the prolonged maritime chokehold in the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministry of Oil is accelerating infrastructure development along overland export routes.

Priority has been placed on expanding and constructing pipeline corridors connecting southern production hubs to the Mediterranean via Syria and Turkey, alongside long-term transit planning toward the Red Sea via Jordan.

World.title: Iraq activates Kirkuk oil field development contract with BP
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, the official activation of its Kirkuk oilfield development contract with British energy giant BP. The project aims to elevate crude oil production from its current capacity of 320,000 barrels per day (bpd) to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Ministry of Oil Spokesperson Salim Al-Rikabi stated that the contract—initially signed in September 2025—focuses on expanding crude extraction while capturing associated natural gas to eliminate routine flaring and feed domestic power generation infrastructure.

Key operational targets & metrics

Crude Oil Output: Increasing current production from 320,000 bpd to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Associated Gas Capture: Raising associated gas processing from 255 million standard cubic feet per day (scf/d) to a peak capacity of 400 million scf/d.

Facility Modernization: Upgrading and expanding infrastructure across North Oil Company fields and North Gas Company processing plants.

Power & Social Infrastructure: Constructing a dedicated 400-megawatt (MW) power plant, expanding local employment, funding community development initiatives, and upskilling North Oil and North Gas workforces.

Environmental Impact: Phasing out continuous gas flaring to redirect captured methane directly into national electricity generation.

The activation of the Kirkuk project represents a major component of Iraq’s broader energy strategy to achieve natural gas self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on imported fuel.

By upgrading processing facilities managed by the North Gas Company and constructing a dedicated 400 MW power generation facility, the initiative directly addresses regional electricity shortages while reducing environmental emissions.

The partnership also reinforces BP’s operational footprint in northern Iraq, complementing its long-standing management of the Southern Rumaila field and bolstering state-led efforts to modernize national energy infrastructure.

World.title: India’s Reliance pays record $25 million freight cost for Iraqi crude amid Hormuz crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — India’s Reliance Industries (RELI.NS), operator of the world’s largest refining complex in Gujarat, paid an unprecedented record charter fee of $23 million to $25 million for a Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) to transport 2 million barrels of Basrah crude from Iraq, according to shipping sources cited by Reuters on Friday, August 7, 2026.

The extreme freight surge—marking a jump from a pre-war average of $2 million to 12 times the baseline global freight rate—highlights severe shipping chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Daily vessel transits through the strategic waterway have plummeted from a pre-war average of 125–140 ships to a fraction of normal capacity as shipowners avoid military risks.

Key financial & logistics metrics

Soaring Freight Rates: Reliance chartered the VLCC from South Korea’s Sinokor at 1,200 points on the Worldscale freight index—12 times the reference benchmark—up from pre-war levels of 0.8 to 0.9 times ($2 million total).

Deep SOMO Discounts: To offset soaring shipping costs and attract buyers into the Gulf, the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) offered steep discounts of $25 to $30 per barrel below Dubai regional benchmarks.

Net Margin Offset: Despite the $25 million freight tag, energy analysts estimate Reliance will still save millions on the overall transaction due to Iraq’s heavy crude price reductions.

Limited Carrier Pool: Sinokor remains one of the few international maritime operators willing to navigate the Strait of Hormuz to load cargo at Iraq’s Basra Oil Terminal.

While Asian refiners—particularly across India and China—are actively seeking chartered tankers to capture Iraq’s discounted crude allocations, shipowner reluctance continues to limit available tonnage entering the Gulf.

By offering deep price concessions, Iraq’s oil marketing arm is successfully maintaining crude flow off the Basra coast despite soaring war-risk insurance premiums and maritime transport bottlenecks.

World.title: Kata’ib Sayyid Al Shuhada clarifies delay in retaliatory strikes against U.S.-Saudi targets
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Abu Ala al-Walai, Secretary-General of Kata’ib Sayyid al-Shuhada, commented on Saturday, August 8, 2026, regarding the decision by the “Islamic Resistance in Iraq” to pause planned military responses to recent joint U.S.-Saudi strikes.

Speaking via a statement on social media platform X, al-Walai confirmed that the delay was granted at the direct request of Coordination Framework leaders, led by Badr Organization chief Hadi al-Amiri, alongside several independent political figures. However, the paramilitary commander emphasized that options for retaliation—including the reassessment of its timing, scale, and nature—remain fully on the table. He urged state officials to utilize this temporary window to secure Iraq’s rights through diplomatic and legal channels.

Key developments in the escalation pause

The Deferred Response: The Islamic Resistance in Iraq announced on Friday, August 7, the postponement of retaliatory operations originally scheduled for the 23rd of Safar targeting Saudi Arabia and U.S. military bases.

Al-Amiri’s Appeal: Badr Organization leader Hadi al-Amiri issued an urgent video address early Friday urging armed factions to delay military action following American-Saudi strikes on Iraqi territory, prioritizing national stability while pursuing accountability for casualties via diplomatic means.

High Security Readiness: The political appeal followed a volatile night across Baghdad and multiple governorates, prompting high-level security alerts and military deployments across the capital.

Command Structure On Site: In response to directives from Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi to elevate combat readiness, senior commanders from Baghdad Operations Command were deployed on the ground to enforce military discipline and secure vital sectors.

The brief pause in military operations provides a critical window for Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s administration to manage state security, navigate delicate diplomatic channels with Washington and Riyadh, and prevent further regional escalation.

World.title: Iraq fish deaths: 7 alarming signs of a deepening water and pollution crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Recurring Iraq fish deaths are becoming an increasingly serious environmental and economic warning, with the Green Iraq Observatory describing the phenomenon as an annual pattern that reflects the accumulation of two interconnected crises: worsening water scarcity and persistent pollution.

Rather than representing isolated incidents caused by temporary changes in river conditions, the repeated deaths of large numbers of fish across Iraq’s rivers, canals and marshlands suggest that the country’s aquatic ecosystems are coming under sustained pressure from declining water flows, untreated wastewater, industrial pollution and weaknesses in water management.

The latest incidents, recorded in April and August 2026, have once again raised concerns about the condition of Iraq’s freshwater resources and the government’s ability to protect them. According to the observatory, more than 1,000 tonnes of fish died in the Tigris and Diyala rivers during April, with particularly heavy losses reported in Wasit province, while a separate incident occurred earlier this month in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan.

Although the two incidents were associated with different immediate circumstances, they demonstrate how vulnerable Iraq’s aquatic ecosystems have become when declining water levels interact with pollution and inadequate environmental controls.

Iraq fish deaths are becoming an annual warning sign

The Green Iraq Observatory argues that the recurrence of mass fish deaths should no longer be treated as a series of unrelated environmental emergencies. According to its assessment, similar incidents have occurred repeatedly across different parts of Iraq over the past several years, yet the underlying causes have not been addressed with sufficient consistency to prevent them from returning.

This pattern is particularly concerning because rivers and wetlands are not only ecological assets; they also support fisheries, agriculture and the livelihoods of communities that depend directly on healthy waterways.

The observatory said the April incident involved more than 1,000 tonnes of dead fish in the Tigris and Diyala rivers, with the largest losses concentrated in Wasit. It attributed the event to severe contamination caused by untreated sewage and industrial waste, while also pointing to increased water releases from Hamrin Dam that reportedly moved accumulated pollutants downstream toward the Tigris.

The organization further said that more than 20 people experienced poisoning or skin-related injuries and were taken to hospital, illustrating how deterioration in water quality can potentially extend beyond damage to aquatic life and become a broader public-health concern.

A second incident was reported at the beginning of August in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan. According to the observatory, the agriculture and water committee of the Maysan Provincial Council attributed the fish deaths to a sharp decline in the water releases allocated to the canal.

This episode is significant because it demonstrates that pollution is not necessarily the only immediate trigger for fish mortality; inadequate water flows can also create conditions in which fish become increasingly vulnerable to high temperatures, reduced oxygen levels and the concentration of pollutants already present in the water.

Water scarcity Is only part of the problem

Iraq’s water crisis is frequently discussed in terms of declining river flows, prolonged drought and reductions in water arriving from upstream countries. Those factors are undoubtedly important, but the recent fish deaths suggest that the country’s environmental problems cannot be explained simply by saying that Iraq does not have enough water. The quality, distribution and management of the water available can be just as important as its overall volume.

The Green Iraq Observatory highlighted this distinction by noting that the country’s total water storage had reportedly risen to around 34 billion cubic meters at the time of the latest incident.

From the organization’s perspective, the fact that fish mortality continued despite an increase in total reserves indicates that administrative decisions concerning water distribution may be contributing to the problem alongside genuine resource scarcity.

This does not mean that Iraq’s wider water shortage is unimportant. On the contrary, prolonged drought and declining inflows can weaken the natural ability of rivers and wetlands to dilute pollutants and maintain ecological balance. However, when available water is distributed unevenly or when polluted water is allowed to enter already stressed waterways, the consequences can become significantly more severe.

In other words, the crisis is not simply about how much water Iraq has, but also about where the water goes, what quality it has and how effectively it is managed.

Pollution can turn a water shortage into an ecological emergency

Untreated sewage and industrial waste are among the most serious threats facing Iraq’s waterways because they can fundamentally alter the chemical and biological conditions required for aquatic life. When large quantities of organic material enter a river or canal, microorganisms consume oxygen while breaking that material down, potentially reducing dissolved oxygen to levels that fish and other aquatic organisms cannot tolerate.

The situation can become even more complicated when water temperatures rise or when algae proliferate excessively. Some forms of harmful algae can contribute to oxygen depletion, particularly when large quantities of organic matter subsequently decompose.

At the same time, reduced water flows can prevent pollutants from being dispersed naturally, leaving them concentrated in particular sections of a river, canal or wetland.

This combination of factors helps explain why pollution and water scarcity should not be treated as completely separate problems. A waterway with strong flows may have a greater capacity to dilute certain pollutants, whereas a shallow and poorly circulated waterway can become significantly more vulnerable to contamination.

Consequently, environmental protection requires both adequate water releases and strict control over what is discharged into the country’s rivers.

Iraq has experienced similar fish mortality events for years

The latest incidents are not without precedent. The Green Iraq Observatory cited a long record of mass fish mortality events in Iraq, including a major incident in the Euphrates in Babylon in 2018, when tens of thousands of tonnes of fish were reportedly affected.

This was followed by the death of millions of fish at the Hindiya Barrage and another major incident in Al-Dalm Marsh in Diwaniyah in 2020.

Further incidents were reported in the Al-Ezz River in Maysan in 2023, while extensive fish deaths occurred in Ibn Najm Marsh in Najaf last year. Particularly worrying is the recurrence of fish mortality in the Maysan area where a similar incident had already been recorded, because repeated events in the same geographic location can indicate that the environmental conditions responsible for the original problem have not been adequately corrected.

The observatory argues that the repeated nature of these incidents is difficult to reconcile with a system that relies primarily on temporary investigative committees after environmental damage has already occurred. Investigations can establish causes and responsibility, but they cannot substitute for permanent monitoring mechanisms capable of identifying dangerous changes in water quality before they result in large-scale ecological losses.

Iraq’s Marshlands face particular risks

The Iraqi marshlands are especially sensitive to changes in water availability and quality because their ecological health depends on a delicate relationship between water flows, seasonal conditions and the surrounding environment. These wetlands provide habitat for fish and birds while supporting communities whose economic and cultural lives have developed around them over generations.

When water levels fall sharply, sections of the marshes can become isolated or excessively shallow, increasing temperatures and reducing oxygen circulation. If polluted water enters these already stressed environments, the damage can become significantly more difficult to reverse.

Protecting Iraq’s marshlands therefore requires a long-term approach that connects water policy with environmental policy. Maintaining adequate ecological flows, reducing pollution and establishing continuous monitoring systems would be far more effective than treating each fish mortality event as an isolated emergency.

What Iraq can do to prevent future fish deaths

The Green Iraq Observatory has called for several measures aimed at addressing the structural causes behind recurring fish mortality. Among its recommendations is the establishment of fair and sustainable water allocations for provinces and marshlands, rather than relying on short-term decisions that may leave some waterways dangerously depleted.

The observatory has also called for stronger environmental oversight of wastewater treatment facilities and industrial establishments located near rivers. Effective enforcement would require more than regulations on paper; authorities would need regular inspections, reliable water-quality testing and meaningful consequences for facilities that discharge untreated or inadequately treated waste.

Another important proposal is the creation of an early-warning system that monitors dissolved oxygen and pollution levels. Such a system could bring together government agencies, universities and civil-society organizations, allowing scientific data to be collected continuously and shared quickly when dangerous changes are detected.

Finally, rapid compensation for fish farmers affected by major environmental incidents could provide essential economic relief while investigations determine responsibility and long-term solutions.

No. Water scarcity is an important contributing factor, but pollution and poor water management can also play major roles. Even when overall water reserves increase, individual rivers, canals or marshes may experience insufficient flows or deteriorating water quality.

World.title: US Fed sends $500 million cash shipment to Iraq amid financial pressures
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The United States Federal Reserve has sent a new $500 million cash cargo to the Central Bank of Iraq, providing additional dollar liquidity as Baghdad grapples with rising financial pressures and disruptions to its oil-dependent economy.

The shipment was announced by Iraq’s national news agency, citing an official source who claimed the dollars will be used for permitted overseas transfers and transactions involving Iraqi citizens.

Further supplies are planned each month, with a government official estimating annual cash delivery of $8 billion to $10 billion.

These cash payments are part of Iraq’s peculiar financial relationship with the United States.

Proceeds from Iraqi oil exports are mostly placed in an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, with Baghdad obtaining dollars via permitted transfers and cash shipments administered by the Central Bank of Iraq.

The new supply comes at a critical moment for Iraq’s budget.

The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has increased pressure on a nation that relies significantly on oil exports to support government expenditures and get foreign currency.

Iraq’s enormous public-sector pay bill contributes to this vulnerability.

Millions of Iraqis rely directly or indirectly on government wages, pensions, and social benefits; therefore, stable oil income and liquidity are crucial to the national budget.

Baghdad has lately expressed increased worries about its capacity to fulfill expenditure obligations if oil earnings continue low, strengthening long-standing demands for Iraq to diversify government income and lessen its reliance on petroleum exports.

The most recent dollar cargo should offer further liquidity to Iraq’s banking system, but it also shows the country’s vulnerability to both oil-market shocks and its financial ties with Washington at a time of rising regional tensions.

World.title: Lise Klaveness, the Norwegian thorn in Infantino’s side
World.content:
Oslo – A rare woman in the top echelons of football, the head of Norway’s federation Lise Klaveness has been a thorn in FIFA’s side for years.

Now, some would gladly see her take over the leadership of football’s international governing body from Gianni Infantino.

The 45-year-old lawyer and former footballer who played 73 matches for Norway has been highly vocal about international football’s woes under Infantino.

The Swiss-Italian has been mired in controversy since his plan to open FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors was swiftly rejected last week.

On Friday she called for him to resign.

When he was elected FIFA president in 2016, “he was a candidate who had been elected on a reform programme focused on good governance,” she told AFP.

“Then things quickly deteriorated: from keeping a distance, we moved to giving up, and even backtracking, all against a backdrop of a lack of independence from heads of state and other influential figures, particularly from World Cup host countries,” she said.

She fired her first salvo at Infantino in 2022, just after she was appointed head of the Norwegian federation, about the conditions under which the World Cup was awarded to Qatar.

From Doha, she publicly lamented that “human rights, equality, democracy, the core interests of football, were not in the starting 11”.

The following year, Norway refused to back Infantino in his re-election bid, signalling its dissatisfaction with his leadership.

Klaveness “was in a way the first standard-bearer for much of this criticism that many others now share when it comes to the way Infantino runs FIFA,” said Mina Finsted Berg, a sports commentator for Norwegian channel TV2.

She “is very committed to ensuring that rules and decisions are respected,” she added.

– Trump, Balogun and investors –

The reasons for her outrage against Infantino have piled up in recent months: FIFA’s decision to award a “Peace Prize” to US President Donald Trump, with whom Infantino has a conspicuously close relationship; the lifting of the suspension of US player Folarin Balogun at the 2026 World Cup following an intervention by Trump; and the aborted plan to open FIFA to private investors.

The Norwegian federation has decided to bring all three issues before the Ethics Committee of the world football governing body.

Klaveness’s voice carries all the more weight after Norway, long absent from major international tournaments, enjoyed a strong run in this year’s World Cup before being knocked out in the quarter-finals by England.

Internationally, commentators have praised her “strong moral compass” and consider her a serious candidate to replace Infantino if he were to step down.

He is standing for re-election for a fourth and final term next March and is currently the only declared candidate.

“She was the only one who always took a clear stand and did not go along with the mainstream. And at FIFA, the time is right for a woman to take the lead,” former FIFA head Sepp Blatter — himself disgraced after a corruption scandal — wrote on social network X.

– Ballot box obstacles –

Klaveness herself has insisted that the crisis in world football should not be reduced to a simple “Game of Thrones” power struggle and has instead called for a renewed focus on good governance.

“For us, it has never been a personal issue against Gianni Infantino,” she told AFP. “The problems go beyond the person of the president.”

And while she “has registered” that her name is being tossed around as a possible successor, she brushed aside questions about whether she was a candidate: “We’re not there yet.”

Many obstacles remain.

“In addition to being seen as extremely radical in many places, especially outside Europe, she is a woman. That is also likely to count against her in many regions of the world,” Mina Finsted Berg said.

Even within Europe’s governing body UEFA, which one could presume would be most favourable to her, Klaveness failed to win election to the Executive Committee in 2023.

She only joined in 2025, when she was the sole candidate for the seat reserved for women.

“If she already has such a hard time getting elected in Europe, how could she convince Africans and South Americans?” asked Erik Thorstvedt, a former goalkeeper for the Norwegian national team turned commentator.

World.title: Clinton compares Trump’s White House to former Iraqi dictator Saddam’s palaces
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has compared President Donald Trump’s White House renovations to former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein’s palaces, remembering her own travels to Baghdad after his ouster.

Clinton, speaking on journalist Kara Swisher’s podcast, compared Trump’s White House decor to meetings she attended in Saddam Hussein’s former palaces while serving as a US senator.

“They were quite reminiscent of what we are seeing in our own White House,” she said.

Her remarks come amid wider criticism of Trump’s renovations and architectural decisions, such as heavy gold décor within the Oval Office, plans for a new White House ballroom, and a projected triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

Clinton called the improvements “tacky” and suggested that the president was focusing too much on cosmetic initiatives when the US confronts substantial foreign policy, economic, and technological issues.

She also criticized the process around Trump’s planned ballroom, stating that she was not opposed to the White House having such a facility but was concerned about the architecture and how the project had been handled.

Given Clinton’s past with Iraq, the connection to Saddam was especially relevant.

She was a member of the United States Senate during the 2003 war that deposed Saddam Hussein and subsequently became Secretary of State under President Barack Obama.

During his reign, Saddam was noted for building multiple extravagant presidential palaces around Iraq, many with elaborate interiors and significant use of marble, chandeliers, and gold-colored décor, despite the country’s international sanctions and economic difficulty.

Trump has defended his White House restoration plans, which are part of a larger push to renovate and enhance Washington’s important federal buildings and sites.

Clinton’s parallel brings Iraq and one of Saddam’s most recognizable emblems into the increasingly heated political argument over Trump’s White House moves.

World.title: 'Should have gone to Ranchi': Rijiju takes dig at Rahul Gandhi over Prayagraj event
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Union minister

on Saturday took a dig at leader of opposition in Lok Sabha

over 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' programme in Uttar Pradesh's Prayagraj, saying he should have travelled to Ranchi, where students are protesting over alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations.

In a post on X, Rijiju said, "Rahul Gandhi ji should have gone to Ranchi instead of Prayagraj."

The remarks came after Rahul, during his address at the event, attacked the government over what he described as a lack of jobs, expensive education, paper leaks, poor access to credit and the growing use of artificial intelligence, which he said were holding India's youth back.

"You are told to watch as many reels as you like, send as many WhatsApp messages as you wish, and browse or create content on Instagram.

This is the addiction of the 21st century, and then you are told to work for Blinkit or Uber, or to do manual labour. You can indulge in this 21st-century addiction, but you cannot get a job; you cannot find employment in this country," Rahul said.

He also criticised the government's economic policies, arguing that demonetisation and what he called "wrong GST" had damaged India's manufacturing sector.

"The first door is manufacturing. Today, in the world, you'll see 'Made in China', 'Made in Vietnam', 'Made in Bangladesh', but you won't see 'Made in India'.





The reason is that demonetisation and the wrong GST have destroyed our manufacturing system. Small businessmen who used to provide employment, and industries like leather, textile, and automobile that used to manufacture in India... all that has been finished.

The first door is closed," he added.

Meanwhile, in Jharkhand, the state government held talks with several student groups amid protests over alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations but failed to break the deadlock, with the protesting aspirants deciding to continue their agitation until their demands are met.

A five-member government panel, comprising state ministers, first met a faction of protesters led by JLKM leader Devendra Nath Mahto, whose hunger strike over the issue entered its seventh day. The panel then separately met delegations of the Congress-backed NSUI, Adivasi Chhatra Sangh (ACS) and Jharkhand Chhatra Morcha (JCM).

World.title: ‘Gangstran Te Vaar’: Punjab Police acts against over 58,000 criminals in 200-day crackdown
World.content:
Punjab Policeâs flagship anti-gangster campaign âGangstran Te Vaarâ has completed 200 days, with the force claiming a major crackdown on organised crime networks across the state.

During the campaign, police conducted 1,09,087 raids, arrested 1,532 proclaimed offenders and initiated action against 58,212 criminals and their associates, according to official sources.

Crackdown targets entire organised crime ecosystem

Launched under the Bhagwant Mann government, the intelligence-driven campaign has focused not only on gangsters but also on their associates, financial networks, weapons supply, logistics and overseas handlers.

Police said preventive action was taken against 28,201 people, while another 18,514 were verified and released.

Overall, the campaign covered 1,04,927 persons, including gangsters, their associates and wanted criminals.

DGP Gaurav Yadav said the operation had evolved into a multi-dimensional campaign aimed at dismantling the ecosystem supporting organised crime.

âOur strategy goes beyond arrests to dismantling the ecosystem that enables organised crime by targeting associates, finances, logistics, communication channels and overseas linkages,â Yadav said.





Weapons, drugs and criminal infrastructure seized

The campaign also targeted the firepower and financial networks of organised gangs. Punjab Police recovered 990 illegal firearms, 242 sharp-edged weapons, 2,739 rounds of ammunition, 315 magazines, 2.5 kg of explosives and 15 hand grenades.

In its action against the crime-drug nexus, police seized 774.38 kg of heroin, 480.23 kg of opium, 7,266.26 kg of poppy husk and more than 26.91 lakh intoxicant tablets.

Authorities also seized Rs 1.73 crore in drug money, Rs 1.80 crore in cash and 413.85 grams of gold.

Overseas gangsters brought back

The Anti-Gangster Task Force (AGTF) also pursued fugitives operating from abroad. Police highlighted the deportation of gangster Bhuvnesh Chopra alias Ashish Chopra from Central Asia and Jobanjit Singh alias Joban Billa from Jakarta, Indonesia.

AGTF chief Pramod Ban said the campaign increasingly combines field operations with financial investigations, digital intelligence and coordination with central agencies to track foreign-based handlers and criminal networks.

Tipline launched for public intelligence

Punjab Police said 4,978 mobile handsets, 1,781 vehicles and 61 drones linked to criminal activities were also seized, while 64,402.77 litres of illicit liquor was recovered and destroyed.

To strengthen public participation, the AGTF has launched a dedicated anonymous tipline at 93946-93946 for information about gangsters, wanted criminals and related activities. A reward policy has also been introduced for credible information leading to action against wanted criminals, with authorities promising confidentiality for informants.

World.title: Bihar should withdraw alcohol ban as it failed to curb crimes against women: Report
World.content:
Representative image

Ban failed to reduce crimes against women, says paper

Prohibition has also hit state revenues

Education, health and jobs among Bihar's priorities

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Bihar should withdraw its prohibition on alcohol as the ban has failed to reduce crimes against women and has been accompanied by a rise in illicit liquor and alternative intoxicants, according to a research paper by economic think tank National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER).The paper, titled âMacro Perspective of Bihar's Development Achievements, Unfinished Agenda, and the Way Forwardâ, also said restoring liquor excise duty to pre-ban levels could increase the state's own revenues by 14-15 per cent while reducing expenditure on enforcement and anti-smuggling operations.Prepared by a team of economists led by Ratna Sahay and presented at the India Policy Forum, the paper examined the economic and social impact of Bihar's prohibition, introduced in April 2016.The paper said the primary reasons for introducing prohibition were the belief that alcohol consumption contributed significantly to domestic violence and that households would redirect money previously spent on alcohol towards more productive uses.Women's groups and activists had also strongly backed the ban, arguing that prohibition would reduce alcohol-related abuse.However, the NCAER researchers said available data now allows an assessment of whether those objectives were achieved.âWe now have sufficient data and information to assess if the ban was effective. Reported crimes against women in Bihar have not declined following the introduction of prohibition. Instead, total reported crimes against women increased over the post-2016 period,â the paper said.According to the study, the available evidence does not show a broad-based reduction in crimes against women after prohibition. Instead, it said the ban coincided with concerns over the expansion of illicit liquor networks, enforcement difficulties and corruption.The paper also pointed to increased use of alternative intoxicants, including illicit drugs.âIn tandem, there was a significant rise in illegal liquor trade leading to higher alcohol consumption, increased crime and corruption, and an increase in the use of alternative additive substances, such as illicit drugs,â it said.The NCAER paper said Bihar suffered significant fiscal consequences after the ban. Before prohibition, excise duty on alcohol accounted for about 14 per cent of the state's own revenues in the three years preceding the ban.At the same time, the government incurred higher expenditure on monitoring, enforcement and anti-smuggling operations, which the paper said added to fiscal pressures.The researchers argued that reinstating liquor excise duty at historical levels could help restore the contribution of the tax to around 14 per cent of state revenues.The paper concluded that the prohibition had not achieved its intended objectives and had instead coincided with higher reported crimes against women, loss of state revenue and increased enforcement expenditure.Beyond prohibition, the paper identified six interconnected areas that it said should form the core of Bihar's development strategy: education, health, governance and law and order, flood mitigation, private-sector development and women's empowerment.It said reforms in these areas were necessary to improve productivity, accelerate structural transformation and create better-quality jobs for Bihar's young population.The study also examined the state's public debt and fiscal sustainability, and assessed the financing required for different reform scenarios. It called for a combination of stronger own-revenue mobilisation, more efficient public spending, additional central government support and, where necessary, further borrowing.The paper noted that improvements in law and order had played an important role in Bihar's economic recovery after 2005, when the state government under Nitish Kumar placed greater emphasis on policing, criminal prosecution, judicial reforms and administrative accountability.It also highlighted Bihar's significance for India's broader development goals, noting that the state is the country's second most populous and remains its poorest.Bihar's population is estimated at 13.2 crore in 2026, according to the paper, accounting for more than 9 per cent of India's population. It noted that the state's population is larger than that of all but 10 sovereign countries.

World.title: Safety vs privacy: How domestic-help platforms are building a two-way support system
World.content:
Indiaâs instant domestic help economy is expanding faster. App-based platforms promise cleaners, cooks and household workers within minutes. However, the real contest here is no longer just about speed, convenience or pricing.

It is increasingly about trust.

A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprises women.

For years, domestic work in India has operated through informal neighbourhood networks, word-of-mouth referrals and personal recommendations. The new generation of platforms is attempting to formalise that ecosystem by adding identity verification, digital payments, ratings, training, insurance and customer support.

But unlike food delivery or ride-hailing, these services involve something far more intimate: a stranger entering a private home.

That has forced platforms to solve an unusually difficult problem. They must simultaneously protect women who enter unfamiliar homes for work and women who may be home alone when they invite those workers inside.

The result is a rapidly evolving safety architecture built around background checks, restricted service hours, real-time monitoring, SOS systems, human escalation teams and, increasingly, AI-assisted risk detection.





Formalising trust in an informal workforce

Indiaâs domestic work sector employs millions of workers, many of them women, and remains overwhelmingly informal. Instant domestic help platforms have created new income opportunities by offering structured onboarding, predictable payments and access to a larger customer base.

But formalisation has also brought safety concerns into sharper focus.

A spokesperson for Pronto shared the measures it takes to ensure transparency, saying that every worker completes criminal court record verification and police verification before joining the platform.

Customers, too, verify their name, phone number and address through OTP authentication and must agree to a code of conduct before placing a booking.

Pronto's workers, for example, receive training before taking their first assignment, and that low customer ratings are investigated by trainers rather than triggering automatic deactivation.

âEvery hub we operate doubles as a training centre, and a professional takes her first booking only after she is trained, background-verified and dispatch-ready, a process that takes about four days,â the spokesperson said.

Similarly, Snabbit, whose workforce consists entirely of women professionals, said it has built a multi-layered safety framework supported by a dedicated Trust & Safety team.

A spokesperson said the system includes âmandatory KYC and background checks for all experts on the platform, verified customers, address-level traceability and controlled job allocation.â

Safety vs surveillance divide

The sharpest divide between platforms and customers is emerging around body-worn cameras.

Pronto has begun experimenting with optional recorded bookings designed to protect workers from false allegations in cases of disputes with customers.

For many users, however, the presence of a camera inside a private home changes the nature of the interaction. âI know some platforms are starting to equip their workers with chest-mounted bodycams for transparency, and while I understand it protects the worker from false claims, it completely freaks me out as a customer,â a Delhi resident said.

âMy home is my private sanctuary. The idea of a stranger walking through my living room with an active lens, recording the exact layout of my home, my entrances, my exits, my personal belongings, and where my work setup or valuables are, feels like an extreme invasion of privacy.â

Her concerns extend beyond the recording itself. âWhere is that video footage stored? Who at the tech company has access to it? Could that footage leak or be hacked?â she said.

âI would honestly think twice before booking a service that mandates live video recording inside my private space. There has to be a boundary between physical safety and digital surveillance.â

Pronto, however, ensured that the sole mechanism of this process is to ensure safety and privacy.

It said that additional video data is collected only on opt-in verified bookings. According to its spokesperson, customers choose the feature during booking and confirm it again when the worker arrives.

The camera is tilted downward to capture only the work area, records no audio, blurs faces and personal information on the device itself, deletes raw footage immediately, and retains only an anonymised encrypted version for a limited review period and AI training.

Safety by design

One of the most striking trends across the sector is that many safety measures are designed not around responding to incidents, but around preventing high-risk situations from arising in the first place.

Several platforms have restricted service hours, particularly avoiding late-evening and night bookings when women workers may be required to enter unfamiliar homes after dark.

Snabbit said its safety system monitors active jobs in real time and can identify anomalies that may require intervention. According to its spokesperson, âActive jobs are monitored in real time, with the dedicated Trust & Safety team supporting rapid escalation and incident response.â

What women check before opening the door

For many women, however, trust begins long before a worker arrives.

A 24-year-old student in Jaipur said she has developed a consistent checklist before booking any on-demand domestic service. She checks whether the app displays a verified profile with a photograph, ID verification, ratings and reviews, and prefers platforms that offer real-time tracking and OTP-based service verification.

âThe first thing I check is whether the app shows a verified profile with a photo, ID verification, ratings, and reviews from other women,â she said.

âReal-time tracking and an OTP-based start and end of the service also make me feel more comfortable.â

Before the worker arrives, she follows a set of precautions that have become almost automatic. She keeps her phone fully charged, informs at least one friend that someone is coming over, avoids leaving valuables or personal documents in plain sight, and stays in a part of the house where she can easily monitor what is happening.

âI usually make sure my phone is fully charged and I let at least one friend know that someone is coming over,â she said. âIf itâs a longer service, I stay in a part of the house where I can easily see whatâs happening.â

She is also careful about digital privacy. âI prefer apps that mask phone numbers, and I never share extra details unless theyâre necessary for the service,â she said. âI avoid mentioning that I live alone or discussing my schedule.

Once the job is done, Iâm careful not to continue communication outside the platform.â

For her, safety is not just about preventing a crime; it is about minimising information that could make her vulnerable later.

The rituals of being home alone

Minal, a 26-year-old professional in Delhi described a different set of habits that have emerged through repeated use of instant service platforms. While the agent is at home, she stays in the hall rather than a closed bedroom, keeps her phone in her hand, and deliberately leaves a pair of her partnerâs or male flatmateâs shoes near the entrance.

âI never sit in my bedroom with the door shut. I stay in the main living area, usually at the dining table with my laptop,â she said. âI also leave a pair of my male flatmateâs or partnerâs shoes near the entryway. Itâs a small mental trick, but it makes me feel less exposed.â

She and two close friends have an informal safety protocol built around messaging apps.

âI have a private WhatsApp group with two close friends. We have a tacit rule: whenever an instant maid or repair person is assigned, I drop the tracking link, their name, and a quick âExpected time: 45 mins,ââ she said.

âI donât overthink it, but it gives me a safety net.â

When asked what app features actually make her feel secure, she was sceptical of marketing labels.

âHonestly, badges and âpolice verifiedâ tags on an app screen donât mean much to me anymore. Anyone can upload a document,â she said. âWhat actually makes me feel safe is seeing a real-time, live selfie of the person taken right when they accept the job, matching the photo on their profile.

Plus, knowing thereâs a strict OTP entry system where they canât start billing until I give them a code at the door.â

Her distinction is important: she is less interested in historical verification and more interested in real-time authentication.

The older customerâs definition of trust

For older users, digital verification often feels less persuasive than physical verification.

, a 52-year-old homemaker in Delhi-NCR, said she places greater trust in tangible indicators such as uniforms, identity cards and residential security systems.

âA professional now gets to share her version of events and any relevant information before a decision is taken, and we work to keep investigations balanced and transparent,â Pronto spokesperson said.

That shift, from treating workers merely as service providers to treating them as rights-bearing participants in the platform ecosystem, may prove as important as any technological innovation.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The next phase of trust

As instant domestic help services expand beyond metropolitan cities into smaller urban centres, safety may become the industryâs primary competitive differentiator.

Speed is easy to advertise. Trust is harder to build.

Women are asking for features that combine digital verification with human accountability: live identity confirmation, female-worker filters, trusted-contact notifications, residential gate integration, discreet exit mechanisms, neighbourhood-level reputation and transparent data governance.

Platforms, meanwhile, are investing in training hubs, background verification, restricted service hours, SOS networks, counselling, insurance and AI-assisted monitoring.

World.title: Pests, mould, live insects: FSSAI suspends license of two food units
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has suspended the licences of two food manufacturers in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra after inspections uncovered serious food safety violations, including live insects in pistachios, rodent droppings, fungal growth, unhygienic processing conditions and ineffective pest control.

The action was taken against VKC Nuts Private Limited (Uttar Pradesh) and Chheda Specialities Foods Pvt Ltd (Maharashtra), with FSSAI saying the deficiencies posed a potential risk to public health.

At VKC Nuts, inspectors found live insects in stored pistachios, heavy black mould on storage walls and ceilings, rodent droppings across the premises, rusted machinery, damaged flooring, houseflies on food products and a live lizard near open crates of figs.

They also found a food handler sorting figs with a bandaged hand and another handling dry fruits without prescribed corrective spectacles. The unit scored 38% in FSSAI's compliance assessment, following which its licence was partially suspended with immediate effect.

At Chheda Specialities Foods, inspectors found workers mixing besan dough with bare hands and peeling bananas on contaminated floors beside decomposing waste.





The inspection also found fungal growth around edible oil tanks, wastewater on the processing floor, broken insect-proof mesh, dead houseflies, poor waste management and raw materials stored on wet, dusty floors. Multiple food samples collected during earlier inspections had already been declared unsafe or misbranded, with legal proceedings still underway.

The unit recorded a compliance score of 42%.

FSSAI said the licences have been suspended in the interest of public health and food safety. Chheda Specialities Foods will remain under suspension until it implements corrective measures and demonstrates full compliance with food safety regulations, while VKC Nuts' partial suspension will continue until further orders.

World.title: Supriya Sule opposes FCRA Bill, urges Centre to withdraw it or send it to JPC
World.content:
NEW DELHI: NCP (SP) working president

on Saturday opposed the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 in its present form, urging the Centre either to withdraw the proposed legislation or refer it to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for wider discussion.

Sule, the Lok Sabha MP from Baramati, said all political parties should be given an opportunity to examine the contentious legislation before Parliament takes it up for consideration. She cautioned the government against rushing the bill through Parliament, amid reports that it could be discussed and passed next week.

âWe reject and disagree with the present form of the FCRA bill. If the government is not ready to withdraw the bill, then it should send it to a JPC.

In a strong democracy, merely opposing something is not enough; we also have to sit together and discuss it,â she said.

The proposed legislation seeks to establish a designated authority for the vesting, supervision, management and disposal of foreign contributions and assets in cases involving cancellation, surrender or expiry of an organisationâs FCRA registration.

The bill also provides for provisional and permanent vesting of such assets.





Critics have argued that the proposed changes could give the government greater control over organisations receiving foreign contributions.

â Foreign funding cannot always be viewed with suspicionâ

Sule said foreign funding should not automatically be treated with suspicion, arguing that overseas contributions can support legitimate work in areas such as healthcare and education.

She said action should be taken if foreign funds are linked to illegal activities such as drug trafficking or terrorism, but questioned the rationale for viewing every foreign-funded organisation negatively.

âThere are organisations such as the Gates Foundation and USAID that have been doing good work for many years. Why should we look at every foreign-funded organisation with a bad eye?â she said.

She also compared foreign funding with money sent home by Indians living abroad, arguing that the source of money alone should not determine whether it is viewed negatively.

According to official figures, 13,520 entities received foreign remittances totalling Rs 55,741 crore between 2019 and 2022.

As of July 15, 2026, there were 14,449 active FCRA registrations, while 22,498 registrations had been cancelled and 15,212 had expired.

The FCRA regulates the receipt and utilisation of foreign contributions by NGOs, charitable institutions, educational bodies, religious trusts and other organisations.

Sule backs youth protests, questions party symbol decisions

Sule also commented on the ongoing protests by students, saying young people should not face such treatment while seeking education.

âWhat happened at Jantar Mantar should not happen anywhere in the country. Our children want to study and this is happening to them. I read that ministers from Jharkhand have ordered an inquiry into it,â she said.

She also backed Uddhav Thackeray in the dispute over the Shiv Sena's name and election symbol, arguing that party organisations and constitutions should be considered while deciding control of political parties.

On the NCP dispute, Sule said the legal battle remained unresolved and alleged that her party had been waiting for a hearing.

âSharad Pawar is the founder president of the NCP and injustice has been done to him. We have been asking for a date for a long time, but why are we not getting a date?â she said.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Sule also criticised the Maharashtra government's approach to farm loan waivers and called for political criticism to remain focused on issues rather than becoming personal.

On the proposed delimitation legislation, Sule said it would be premature to comment before the bill was introduced. She added that the NCP (SP) would discuss the legislation with its alliance partners once it came before Parliament.

Sule further said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had agreed to meet NCP (SP) MPs on Monday to discuss issues concerning their constituencies, amid the opposition's contention that Parliament was not functioning properly.

World.title: Explainer: What changes as Parliament passes Registration of Births and Deaths Bill
World.content:
What does the Bill change?

What is the significance of a birth certificate?

What happened in the Parliament?

The country now wants to get rid of ghosts. There are govts in some states that look for an opportunity and welcome those (who were not born in India) and register their births who are not eligible to be registered here. Now, we will not allow this to happen.

Union minister of state for home Nityanand Rai

World.title: Indian-flagged vessel comes under attack in Red Sea
World.content:
An Indian-flagged merchant vessel with 13 Indian nationals aboard came under attack off the coast of Yemen on Tuesday (August 4, 2026), the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said.

All the Indians have been rescued, it said.

New Delhi condemned the attack and said targeting of commercial shipping in the region must stop.

"We condemn the attack on the Indian-flagged commercial vessel, MSV Faize Noore Oliya that sank in the Red Sea, off the coast of Yemen on August 4," the MEA said.

"All 13 Indian nationals have been rescued. Our Embassy in Riyadh is closely monitoring the situation and proactively coordinating with the Yemeni authorities for the safety and security of the crew," it added.

The MEA thanked the Yemeni authorities for their support in rescuing the Indians.

"The continuing incidents of attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply worrisome," it said.

"The targeting of commercial shipping in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways in the region, in keeping with international law, must be restored at the earliest," the MEA said in a statement.

World.title: Kerala to set up an independent AYUSH University
World.content:
The Kerala government has initiated steps to establish an independent AYUSH University to coordinate education, research, clinical services and drug development across the State’s AYUSH systems of medicine.

Health Minister K. Muraleedharan said in an official release on Tuesday (August 4, 2026) that a four-member committee has been constituted to prepare the draft legislation for the proposed university.

The committee will have the Principal Secretary, AYUSH department as the chairperson and the State mission director of the National AYUSH Mission as convener. The other members of the committee are the director of Ayurveda medical education and the principal and controlling officer of the Government Homoeopathic Medical College.

‘A historic step’

Mr. Muraleedharan said the State was taking a historic step by moving to create a new academic framework for the AYUSH sector.

The proposed AYUSH University will bring all AYUSH educational institutions, currently under the Kerala University of Health Sciences, under a single umbrella and strengthen education, research and comprehensive academic collaboration in the field.

The proposed university will be based at the School of Fundamental Research in Ayurveda at Tripunithura.

The committee will prepare the draft legislation for a separate AYUSH University after examining the existing functioning of AYUSH educational institutions, the proposed university’s organisational structure, academic infrastructure, research projects and administrative framework. The draft Bill for the university is expected to be submitted within two months.

To raise standards

The government is seeking to establish the university to raise the academic standards of Ayurveda, Homoeopathy, Siddha, Unani and other AYUSH systems, expand research opportunities and to develop academic programmes that meet international standards.

Mr. Muraleedharan said that once an independent AYUSH University is established, AYUSH education, research, clinical studies and drug development will improve and that this will help Kerala’s traditional systems of medicine gain wider national and international acceptance.

World.title: Lack of long-term plans to mitigate rain-induced calamities worrying for Kerala
World.content:
Under fire for the sluggish response to the rain-related calamities in the State over the last few days, the State government on Monday sought to blame the India Meteorological Department (IMD) for a delay in relaying the weather forecast. But experts say it also unravels the absence of long-term mitigation plans to tackle increasingly frequent rain-induced calamities in the State.

Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan on Monday said the flooding was triggered by extremely heavy rainfall, with some places receiving more than 350 mm of rain. He said the State received the IMD’s warning of an extreme rainfall event only around midnight, leaving little time for authorities to carry out large-scale evacuations.

However, the IMD’s 125-year rainfall dataset, covering 110 weather stations across Kerala from 1901 to 2025, shed enough light on the State’s most vulnerable regions during the monsoon, including areas prone to extreme rainfall. Using this historical dataset with machine learning and Geographic Information System (GIS) techniques, weather scientists have prepared a rainfall vulnerability map that highlights several disaster-prone regions.

Colour-coded zones

The map shows that many parts of north Kerala, Idukki and Pathanamthitta, particularly areas along the Western Ghats, are highly susceptible to extreme rainfall events. The map categorises the State into different colour-coded zones based on rainfall intensity. Areas marked in red have experienced extreme rainfall events repeatedly over the past 125 years, while orange zones receive heavy rainfall of lower intensity. Green, blue and light blue represent progressively lower rainfall categories.

Notably, the recent weather events in Idukki, Pathanamthitta and Kottayam, as well as the debris slip in Wayanad last month that claimed eight lives, occurred in areas classified as red zones. According to weather experts, these regions become particularly vulnerable whenever the offshore trough extends up to Kerala along India’s west coast. Their geographical characteristics, combined with prevailing monsoon conditions, make them highly susceptible to heavy and very heavy rainfall, they say. The State need not wait for weather alerts to be upgraded before initiating preparedness measures.

The challenges

According to Thara K.G., a geologist and disaster management expert, rainfall warnings are only one component of disaster preparedness. Kerala’s biggest challenge is the absence of a long-term disaster mitigation strategy. “The State cannot evacuate an entire population solely based on rainfall alerts,” she said. “What Kerala lacks is a comprehensive long-term plan to reduce the impact of extreme weather events. This problem is further aggravated by the absence of effective land-use planning,” said Ms. Thara.

A senior official associated with the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority said implementing major policy reforms remains difficult in a densely populated State like Kerala. Measures such as enforcing land-use regulations or removing accumulated silt, sand and soil from rivers and other waterbodies often face significant resistance. “Strong policy-level intervention is essential to bring about meaningful reforms in the sector,” the official said.

World.title: Student body polls to be held in Madhya Pradesh universities after nine years
World.content:
The student union elections in Madhya Pradesh’s educational institutions are slated to be held in September, after a gap of nine years, the State Government has told the High Court.

On Monday (August 3), the government shared the academic calendar of 2026-27 with a Division Bench of Acting Chief Justice Vivek Rusia and Justice Pradeep Mittal in Jabalpur, in which student body polls are schedules for September.

The High Court was hearing two petitions filed in 2024 and 2025 that sought that elections be conducted in colleges and universities.

Student body elections in the State’s higher education institutions were last held in 2017, with a petition alleging that lack of student unions has affected the democratic representation of students.

“The State Government has filed a reply along with the Academic Calendar for the academic session 2026–27. In the said Academic Calendar, the month of September 2026 has been fixed for conducting the Student Body Elections (Chhatra Sangathan),” the court order read, while disposing the pleas.

The court also directed the State authorities and various public universities of Madhya Pradesh to hold the elections in every college.

Meanwhile, various universities sought directions for the State authorities to ensure adequate police arrangements for the elections. The court said that each college or university could read out to the district administration and local police for security measures.

State’s Higher Education Minister Inder Singh Parmar said that his department is examining the court’s directions and a decision will be taken soon.

“The Court has issued certain directions regarding the student union elections. Our department is examining them, and I have discussed the matter with the Chief Minister. We will take a decision soon,” Mr. Parmar said, speaking to reporters in capital Bhopal.

During the previous hearing on July 15, the government had told that the 2026-27 academic calendar was under preparations and that provisions will be made for student body polls.

World.title: Iran denies negotiating with U.S. after Trump announces talks
World.content:
Iran denied any negotiations were taking place with the United States after President Donald Trump said new talks would begin Monday (August 3, 2026) in an effort to end their war, now in its sixth month.

Aslo Read: West Asia updates on August 3, 2026

The rebuttal by the Iranian Foreign Ministry follows Mr. Trump saying he had held off launching new strikes on the Islamic republic to allow for further diplomatic efforts, a familiar pattern in the conflict.

Washington and Tehran have been at war since February 28, when the U.S. and Israel launched surprise strikes against Iran, though months of on-off diplomacy have led to periods of relative calm.

Mr. Trump last week threatened to hit Iran “very hard”, with the U.S. leader reportedly considering renewed attacks, including against energy infrastructure.

But the President pulled back from that threat Saturday, saying the “perimeters” of a deal were there.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry however denied there were currently negotiations taking place.

“We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz,” said foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei during a weekly press briefing.

The Hormuz shipping route is a major sticking point in efforts to end the war. Iran has obstructed vessels attempting to pass the critical trade corridor, firing on commercial ships.

Before the war, there was free passage through the strait, but Iran now insists on retaining control and charging fees, something the U.S. rejects.

Tehran has refused to let ships travel any route other than one which hugs the Iranian coast.

On Sunday (August 2), Baqaei told state television that a deal was close on managing Hormuz together with Oman, which sits on the other side of the narrow waterway.

“We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides — neither the northern route nor the southern route — but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said.

But he insisted that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait.

‘It begins tomorrow’

On Sunday (August 2), a tanker off the coast of Oman reported hearing an explosion nearby, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported, but the ship and crew were all reported safe.

Mr. Trump told reporters on Sunday that the new talks with Iran would cover Hormuz and ultimately the denuclearisation of Iran.

The U.S. President said at the start of the conflict that the war was necessary to deal with Iran’s nuclear programme. Western nations accuse Iran of seeking a bomb, though Tehran insists the programme is entirely civilian in nature.

“Now what we’re doing is we’re talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon,” Mr. Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, without providing details of the venue or participants.

The President said he had been asked by Iran as well as U.S. partners Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to hold off on further strikes, which he claimed would have been “the biggest attack since World War II”.

Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Mr. Trump not to strike.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly claimed a settlement to end the war is near, only for fighting to resume. He has previously issued apocalyptic warnings to Tehran, only to later backtrack by saying diplomacy was underway.

A previous ceasefire deal between the foes fell through last month. It was supposed to open the Strait of Hormuz to ships carrying vital energy exports from the Gulf to feed the global economy.

Iranian lawmaker Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the parliament’s national security commission, said on Sunday that mediators were trying to revive the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June.

That agreement was not intended as a final peace deal, but as a stepping stone to negotiations on a comprehensive agreement, though it did include provisions on Hormuz.

“They know that the main issue and, in fact, the key to the matter right now is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, so yes, there is an exchange of views,” Mr. Ghashghavi said.

Posting on X, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said: “We must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed.”

World.title: A. Kanyakumari’s unique year-long Tyagaraja series comes to a close
World.content:
What does a musician do when the repertoire well before him has run nearly dry? That was the question facing Delhi P. Sunderrajan as he stepped up to deliver the 13th and final concert of the monthly series ‘Ekaika Raga Kritis of Tyagaraja’, curated and launched by violin maestro A. Kanyakumari last June. Over the preceding 12 editions at the Arkay Convention Center, the series had systematically exhausted about a hundred kritis — compositions that are solitary in their ragas — leaving Sunderrajan with very little to choose from. This meant repetition was almost inevitable.

Yet the violinist-turned-vocalist and guru of repute transformed this constraint into an opportunity. Accompanied by M.A. Sundareswaran (violin), Tiruvarur Vaidyanathan (mridangam) and K.V. Gopalakrishnan (kanjira), Sunderrajan presented a vocal recital that was less about novelty of selection than about the depth of its interpretation. The focus was rightly on the kritis, and the fare was an enchanting mix of the familiar and the rare. Nine compositions were presented, with manodharma kept to the essentials.

‘Padavi ni sadbhaktiyu’ in Salagabhairavi — a kriti that critiques hollow piety while championing genuine devotion — provided a brisk start. A short swara segment capped it. Sunderrajan’s sublime artistry came to the fore in his alapana of Bhushavali, a shadava-sampurna raga (nishada-varja in the ascent) derived from Vachaspathi. He maintained the raga’s identity throughout, with characteristic phrases flowing with elegance. Sundareswaran’s response on the violin was sweet and silken. The vocalist’s rendition of ‘Tanamidane’, a composition in which Tyagaraja owns up to his faults rather than complaining to Rama, made one wonder why it is not heard more often in concerts. Deftly presented kalpanaswaras added value.

The Vasanthabhairavi kriti ‘Nee dayarada’ (in Rupakam) showcased the beauty of sangatis — with familiar ones in the one-phrase pallavi, and a few intriguing variations rendered in the charanam. Sunderrajan then moved on to Swarabhushani, a rare shadava-shadava raga with an asymmetric scale (omits ‘ri’ in the ascent and ‘ga’ in the descent) derived from Kharaharapriya, and rendered ‘Varadaraja ninnu kori’, also set in Rupaka tala. The kriti paints a vivid portrait of the iconic Garuda Seva festival, comparing the Lord’s radiance on the moving Garuda mount to the bright moon shining among the stars.

Subhapantuvarali ushered in a reflective mood. Sunderrajan’s exploration of the raga, particularly in the mandhra sthayi, was marked by measured and meditative phrases. Long, loopy ones towards the end served as a perfect foil. ‘Ennalu urake’ is a typically expressive kriti whose dominant sentiment is one of mock indignation and loving confrontation, born from a deep sense of intimate devotion. Tyagaraja takes on the role of a lawyer presenting a case, questioning the Lord’s apparent unconcern and indifference by reminding him of his own divine track record. The niraval at ‘Satatamu tyagaraju nammaga leda?’ — the rhetorical question “Didn’t Tyagaraja forever keep faith in you?” — sustained the emotional arc beautifully. The ensuing swara passages sparkled with seamless team sync, the top-octave forays rising above the rest.

‘Manavyala kincha ratade’ in Nalinakanti and ‘Evvare Ramayya’ in Gangeyabhushani followed, with contrasting musical contours. A short delineation of raga Andolika — whose literal meaning is ‘palanquin’ or ‘swing’ — led into the kriti ‘Raga sudha rasa’, which proved true to the raga’s name. Like a palanquin bearing a sovereign, Andolika lifted the kriti’s theology — sacrifice, union, enjoyment — carrying Tyagaraja’s ecstatic vision of Omkara in a single melodic procession. Synergy was the reigning element in another burst of engaging swara exchanges. Vaidyanathan’s energy and experience were an asset, and his tani avartanam in two-kalai Adi tala alongside his percussion partner Gopalakrishnan was crisp and lively.

‘Kamalaptakula’ in Brindavana Saranga was the concluding composition. On the day, ‘Pavamana’ served as the mangalam not just for the concert, but for the series itself.

World.title: Maharashtra CM orders fresh investigation of Siddhivinayak Temple donation case
World.content:
Days after Siddhivinayak Temple Trustees raised irregularities in the collection of donations, Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis instructed a fresh investigation into the case.

Mr. Fadnavis gave directions to the Home Affairs Department to investigate the temple’s records from 2022 to 2026.

Maharashtra Navnirman Sena chief Raj Thackeray raised the issue on August 2, claiming that every year from 2023, irregularities of at least ₹18 crore had appeared. He made accusations, saying, “After the accused were caught, the weekly donation amount increased from ₹50 lakh to about ₹1.5 crore.”

Nine employees of the temple have been arrested.

Siddhivinayak Temple embezzlement allegations come after the controversies over irregularities in donations at the Ram Mandir in Uttar Pradesh’s Ayodhya.

On August 3, the trustees sought an investigation by the Anti-Corruption Bureau and the Maharashtra Law and Judiciary Department.

World.title: Security beefed up as Congress, PDP, NC to observe August 5 as 'Black Day'
World.content:
Security has been intensified across the Jammu region, particularly along the Jammu-Srinagar and Jammu-Pathankot national highways, as the National Conference (NC), the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the Congress have announced separate protests to observe August 5 as ‘Black Day’.

August 5 marks the seventh anniversary of the Centre's decision to abrogate the special status of the erstwhile Jammu and Kashmir State under Article 370 and reorganise it into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.

Police, the Army and the CRPF have stepped up security arrangements by increasing vehicle checking, frisking and surveillance at sensitive locations across the region, officials said.

Special checkpoints have been placed on high alert along the Jammu-Srinagar and Jammu-Pathankot highways, with security personnel conducting searches of vehicles and verifying the identity of commuters, they said.

Security has also been strengthened in border areas, where patrolling and area domination exercises have been intensified as a precautionary measure, the officials said, adding that additional deployments have been made at vulnerable locations.

The National Conference leadership will assemble outside the party headquarters in Jammu and stage a protest on Wednesday, party leaders said.

The Congress will hold a demonstration outside its Shaheedi Chowk headquarters, demanding restoration of statehood to Jammu and Kashmir, along with constitutional safeguards for land, jobs and natural resources, party leaders said.

The PDP will also hold a protest at its Gandhi Nagar headquarters to mark the occasion, its leaders said.

World.title: Mir Raza Ali case: Family, lawyer allege 25-year-old was murdered after torture
World.content:
Advocate Jibran Nasir, representing the family of slain businessman Mir Raza Ali, alleged on Saturday evening that Raza had been tortured before being murdered, hours after his second post-mortem was conducted, and demanded that the entire investigation team be replaced.

Raza, owner of eatery Wafflix, had gone missing on July 28. The 25-year-old’s body was found a day later with a gunshot wound in bushes near Shahi Qila Ground in Gulistan-i-Jauhar.

His body was exhumed earlier today, the family’s lawyer confirmed, after the Sindh government restored the original medical board.

Speaking to the media in the evening, Nasir said the medical report of the second post-mortem answered “14 questions” and detailed some of the alleged injuries Raza had sustained before his death.

“This was murder following torture — the murder of a happy, ambitious and educated young man from Karachi,” he alleged.

“He had an injury on his chin,” the advocate said, adding that Raza’s eye sockets were compressed and that traces of a foreign substance were found.

“Samples were taken and sent to a lab to see if there are any chemical traces,” he told reporters.

The lawyer also claimed that Raza had wounds to his forehead and a fractured nose, as well as swelling and congealed blood around his lower jaw, consistent with having been punched.

“There is a fracture to his temple above his ear, indicating he was struck,” he alleged.

“In the tongue area, a congealed black substance was discovered, which is not naturally found in the body. This substance has been taken and sent to a lab to see what he was forced to ingest.”

Continuing the description, he also claimed that internal muscles in Raza’s throat were covered in the same black substance, and that a broken hyoid bone and muscle damage suggested that he also was strangled.

“Now we come to the firearm injury, where it was earlier said that he was shot in the chest and the bullet exited through his back,” Nasir said.

“We have now proven 110 per cent that the bullet entered his back and exited after breaking and fracturing his ribs.”

The family’s lawyer also criticised senior police officials, alleging that they “do not want to investigate, but rather humiliate, harass and exhaust the family”.

“They are finding months-old recordings and frustrating, emotionally exhausting and humiliating Mir Hussain and Maryam Hussain. Are you investigating or harassing them? They sat them in their offices and told them repeatedly, ‘It’s a suicide, accept it’. Our city’s AIG was saying this,” the advocate claimed further.

Nasir added that he and the family had “no faith” in the AIG or the SSP’s investigation team and that they wanted the entire team changed, including senior officers.

“If they appoint the same kind of officers, such as those doctors from Jamshoro and Hyderabad, then we will approach the court,” he added.

“But have no doubts about it: senior officers spent 10 days with the parents and misguided them into believing it was a suicide,” Nasir alleged.

Raza’s father, Mir Hussain, told reporters that he had maintained since July 30 that his son’s death was a brutal murder.

“We saw the body and told them [that it was murder], but they kept saying, ‘Suicide, suicide, suicide,’” he said. “Sometimes the SSP would talk to us; the IG would say that the matter had been resolved but there was a problem in the report.

“If your entire police station investigates based on post-mortem reports, then how can someone in such a position of responsibility say something like this?”

Mir Hussain said it “brought us peace” to learn that their claims that Raza had been attacked before his death were true.
