"My writing is cartoonish and always satirical.

"Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone. Its purpose was never to be taken literally."

The film has been removed from the ABC's platforms and will be replaced with an edited video without the material subject to the complaint.

World.title: Trump announces $560m critical minerals investment in tiny NSW town
World.content:
The Pentagon is investing more than half a billion dollars to expand an Australian critical mineral project poised to become the world's first scandium mine, US President Donald Trump has announced.

The $US400 million ($560m) loan to Sunrise Energy Metals' Syerston scandium project in central west NSW is expected to shore up America's supply of the "increasingly critical mineral" used in aerospace, defence and automotive sectors.

Scandium is already used widely for defence, aerospace and energy applications, but nearly all supply comes from China, Russia and Ukraine. The US has not mined scandium since 1969.

The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) said while there was currently no primary mine-source scandium supply globally, it was harvested through by-products of other industrial or resource extraction processes.

Donald Trump's announcement was part of a slew of investments in critical minerals and battery projects. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

It said "foreign competitors" accounted for about 80 per cent of the world's mining production and nearly all scandium processing.

The OSC said the mine's production would "support warfighting capabilities" as well as "strategically important economic sectors" including data centres, semiconductors and automotives.

Under the proposed financing, the US Department of War would receive a right of first offer on the mine's output.

Sunrise Energy Metals said its project near Fifield, about 350 kilometres west north-west of Sydney, aimed to deliver "the world's first primary source of mine-able, high-grade scandium".

It is set to have an initial capacity of 60 tonnes a year of scandium oxide, starting production in the first half of 2028.

In February, the company's chief executive Sam Riggall said the project, backed by mining billionaire Robert Friedland, was expected to contribute to a US critical minerals stockpile worth $US12 billion ($16.9b).

Last year, the company signed a five-year deal with US defence contractor Lockheed Martin granting it to buy up to 15 tonnes of scandium oxide from its Syerston project.

The deal came days after Mr Trump and Anthony Albanese inked a critical minerals pact during the prime minister's visit to Washington.

Albanese and Trump ink deal for 'dominance' of critical minerals Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have inked a deal for "critical mineral and energy dominance" in a new partnership that will tip billions into mining projects in the US and Australia.

Resources Minister Madeleine King welcomed the decision, calling it a "significant vote of confidence" in Australia's capacity to supply the US and its partners with the critical minerals they need.

"The Sunrise scandium project hosts the world's largest and highest-grade known scandium resource, which has a range of vital aerospace, defence and clean energy applications," she said.

"No one country alone can create secure, end-to-end supply chains in critical minerals and rare earths.

"In working together, Australian mining companies can create more jobs and investment opportunities here at home, and more jobs and investment in the United States."

Madeleine King says the Sunrise project has the world's largest and highest-grade known scandium resource. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

OSC's senior managing director Peter B Zuckerman said the conditional loan was a "decisive step toward creating a US-aligned scandium value chain, ensuring our warfighters and manufacturers no longer depend on adversaries".

Mr Trump announced the loan on Friday, local time, alongside a slew of other local investments in critical minerals and battery projects totalling $US3 billion ($4.2b).

Speaking at a State Department event in Washington involving more than 200 mining executives, educators and investors, Mr Trump said the US was reclaiming its place as "the minerals superpower of the world".

"Critical minerals are the raw materials of American strength that power everything from advanced weaponry to automobiles, and we want these essential products to be mined, refined and made right here in the USA," he said.

The US has burned through large numbers of precision-guided missiles and air-defence interceptors during its five-month-long war against Iran.

Defence officials and lawmakers have warned that replenishing some inventories could take years given existing production constraints, even as the Trump administration has disputed reports of significant shortages.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Rockliff adviser, ex-minister chosen as Liberal Senate replacements
World.content:
A senior adviser to Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff has been chosen to replace outgoing Liberal Senator Wendy Askew, while a former state minister will replace Senator Jonno Duniam when he finishes up at the end of the year.

Former party president Chris Gatenby will top the Liberals Senate ticket at the next federal election, with former minister Sarah Courtney coming in second and Latrobe councillor Jacki Martin third.

Brad Stansfield, a former chief of staff to Will Hodgman, missed out on a spot on the ticket.

Senators Askew and Duniam announced earlier this year they would not be seeking preselection.

Their resignations create casual vacancies, allowing the party to appoint new senators in their place, rather than go through a by-election.

The Senate spots were determined by about 60 Liberal Senate selectors at a meeting in Launceston today.

Long-term staffer gets his chance

Mr Gatenby is a senior adviser to Premier Jeremy Rockliff and has been involved with the Liberals for years, having previously served as party president.

He was raised on a farm in northern Tasmania, and then lived in Launceston.

He has had a broad career including senior roles in policy development, advocacy and government across Australia and the UK.

The father of two ran unsuccessfully in Bass during the last election.

"I think having two attempts at the state level gives you a great grounding at the door step, understanding what people's issues are, and I'm looking forward to getting in there and making a difference," Mr Gatenby said on Saturday.

Premier Rockliff said in July 2025, during the election campaign, Mr Gatenby "brings a wealth of experience to the table, in government, in small business, in policy advocacy and in the Liberal Party, including as our previous party president.

"Chris is the next generation of the party, putting his hand up to represent his community in parliament. He already volunteers in his community, including on the board of the Launceston Harvest Market," he said.

Sarah Courtney was Tasmania's first-ever female primary industries minister, in the government of Peter Gutwein. (ABC News: Scott Ross)

Sarah Courtney was elected to the Tasmanian parliament in 2014 and appointed to cabinet in 2018.

Ms Courtney, a moderate Liberal, was viewed as a talented minister with leadership potential.

She was Tasmania's first female primary industries minister, but stepped down after starting a relationship with her department secretary, who is now her husband.

She is a trained engineer and owns a boutique vineyard in the Tamar Valley.

Ms Courtney held the health portfolio throughout the COVID pandemic, and listed the guiding of voluntary assisted dying through the parliament as a key achievement.

In 2022, Ms Courtney quit Tasmanian politics after returning from a European holiday during which she caught COVID-19.

Ms Courtney, who was education minister, was forced to isolate in France just days out from school resuming in Tasmania.

When asked on Saturday if she had learnt from that time, Ms Courtney would not comment, instead telling reporters she had a wealth of experience.

"I have enjoyed being a minister, it gave me a thorough understanding of a range of portfolios and that's the experience I bring here today," she said.

"I've got experience as a minister plus I've worked in the real world across a range of industries and that coupled together means I'm good at finding solutions.

"I'm good at working with the community and small business to make sure the policies we have here in Tasmania — and that we're advocating for in Canberra — make a meaningful difference."

Not quite for Martin, Stansfield

Jacki Martin who came third in the vote, has been a Latrobe councillor since 2022 and is currently a parliamentary adviser to Wendy Askew.

Jacki Martin has been a Latrobe councillor since 2022 and is currently a parliamentary advisor to Wendy Askew. (Facebook: Jacki Martin)

She nominated for preselection in June and said on her social media page that she would "bring energy, discipline and relentless determination" to the role.

Representing the north of the state, she has been outspoken recently on the closure of Boags Brewery in Launceston, the Liberty Bell Bay smelter and the sale of Tasmania's largest farm, Rushy Lagoon.

Ms Martin helped campaign for Education Minister Jo Palmer, Senator Claire Chandler and Health Minister Bridget Archer.

"Small business drives me, I'm the child of a small business owner … my family drives me, your family drives me, and I'll be working every day to see that this generation that's coming up underneath us isn't any worse off than what we have been," Ms Martin said.

Brad Stansfield was unsuccessful in his bid for a place high on the ticket.

Mr Stansfield was chief of staff to former Liberal premier Will Hodgman for eight years, and former Liberal senator Eric Abetz between 2007 and 2010.

Brad Stansfield has missed out on a spot. (Supplied: Font PR)

He also advised the Tasmanian Liberals through successful state election campaigns from 2014 to 2024.

Mr Stansfield was a partner in a public relations and lobbying firm before leaving to become the owner of a polling firm and co-owner in a stable of regional newspapers.

He also commentated on Tasmanian and federal politics on a podcast which he co-hosted.

Mr Stansfield has also spoken against the federal coalition doing preference deals with One Nation, and in February wrote that the "increased voter support for One Nation is a symptom of the federal coalition’s dysfunction for much of last year".

World.title: On the front line of WA’s fight against bird flu as fears grow for endangered species
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWABird flu On the front line of WA’s fight against bird flu as fears grow for endangered species Michael Philipps August 9, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia is the last continent on earth to experience cases of H5 bird flu, but with that unique status comes the key advantage of several years to formulate a plan for when the disease hits – particularly when it comes to protecting and preparing our most at-risk wildlife. In Western Australia, several programs have been quietly progressing to protect endangered species including the western ground parrot and the Australian lesser noddy. Australian sea lions are an endangered species. On the Abrolhos Islands off the coast of Geraldton, a program to boost Australian sea lion pup health through building shelters and trialling hookworm treatment hopes to keep the population resilient ahead of bird flu taking hold in the area. Dr Holly Raudino, a senior research scientist with the marine science program of the WA Department of Biodiversity Conservation and Attractions, has been working with the sea lion population along the state’s coast, focusing on species around the Abrolhos Islands near Geraldton.



Raudino said there was serious concern for the population due to the severe impact the virus has had on other sea lion colonies around the world. Related Article Bird flu ‘Biggest threat is from the sky’: How Victoria is preparing for bird flu “South American sea lions have been really affected, as have elephant seals in South America, but also more recently on Heard Island, which is one of the South Antarctic islands,” she said. “We’re seeing tens of thousands of pups dying in one breeding season. “To put that into perspective, the Australian sea lions we think there’s 12,000 or less across the species range, and they’re restricted just to South Australia and Western Australia.



“So there’s definitely the potential that we could lose the whole species.” Raudino and the team have been busy on the islands trying to build shore up the population ahead of any potential incursion of the virus, building shelters and checking the sea lion pups for hookworm, a parasite that has led to high mortality rates among South Australian colonies. “The idea is that it reduces other stresses ahead of avian influenza getting into those colonies,” Raudino said. “The pups are definitely susceptible to bird flu as are the older age classes too,” she said. “But the main concern is that when they are pupping, they are all in close proximity together.



“We know this highly pathogenic avian influenza is spreading mammal to mammal, so once it gets in it could be catastrophic.” Recently, the first inland case of H5N1 bird flu in Australia was detected in western NSW at the junction of the Murray and Darling rivers on the Victorian border, in a sign the virus will spread rapidly across the continent. The NSW government announced two more cases of the virus on Saturday, one in Narooma on the South Coast and one near Wentworth in the far west, bringing the total number of confirmed detections across Australia to 215. Federal Environment and Water Minister Murray said the best way to protect vulnerable species in the wild from H5 bird flu was to make sure there were strong and healthy populations. Sea lions are found along the coast from south of Esperance to north of the Abrolhos Islands.



“Protective action is giving species the best chance of withstanding and recovering from the potential impacts of H5 bird flu,” he said. “These projects have not only helped us prepare for H5 bird flu, they will also have enduring conservation benefits for many of the species that rely on these habitats.” Raudino said the best-case scenario for bird flu spreading among the sea lion population – which ranges from the coast to the south of Esperance up to north of the Abrolhos – is that the virus reached an equilibrium and did not wipe out the population. “I really hope that we don’t get local extinctions and that we’re able to kind of preserve the species across their range,” she said. “It is important to record and report, and the community has been doing a good job of that.



“We can’t underestimate the power of people looking and seeing things first, and then hopefully we can get measures in place.” WA Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn was confident the conservation initiatives would put the state in a good position to boost native species. “Given H5 bird flu detections in Australia, this work is now more important than ever,” he said. “This funding is fundamental in strengthening resilience in our most threatened species.” The Abrolhos Islands are a key focus for scientists looking to prepare wildlife populations for bird flu incursions.



Raudino said her key concern was how quickly bird flu spread across the sea lion population, and whether it was established. “We have known for the last few years that it is a real threat, and we have been trying to do as much as we can” she said. “Even if we get mortalities we have been testing, at least to my knowledge, since 2023 and we have had time to prepare. “I think we’re relieved that it’s happened after the main pupping season for the Abrolhos. It would be great if we could get to the end of the year, and [the virus] wasn’t established. “In WA, it’s still only been detected in the migratory seabirds.



“There’s no local transmission, which has been a huge relief.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Rose had two heartbreaking IVF losses. Then her specialist clocked one crucial detail
World.content:
Exclusive NationalIVF Rose had two heartbreaking IVF losses. Then her specialist clocked one crucial detail Kate Aubusson August 9, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One child in 16 is now conceived via IVF in Australia as success rates creep up, but would-be parents face a high-stakes numbers game in which age, and the clinic they choose, can determine success – or otherwise. More than 50,000 women in Australia had IVF treatment in 2024, totalling 104,721 IVF cycles, according to the latest analysis of the database tracking every cycle performed at every IVF clinic in Australia and New Zealand. Rose and Brendan Larkin with their children Theodore and Maia. George Chan There were 18,509 IVF babies born in 2024, equating to one baby for every five to six cycles, says the report published on Sunday by UNSW’s National Perinatal Epidemiology and Statistics Unit (NPESU). Success rates varied widely between IVF clinics. One clinic – its identity was not revealed– reported just over 5 per cent of its initiated cycles resulted in a live birth. At the other end of the scale was a clinic with a 38 per cent success rate.



Male infertility was a factor for one in four IVF cycles. The specific cause in the majority of these cases was unknown. Related Article IVF Suzanne froze her eggs – then a calculator gave her a reality check Of all the causes of infertility among people undergoing IVF, women diagnosed only with endometriosis had the highest chance of success. More than one in three (36.3 per cent) of initiated cycles resulted in a live birth. Rose Larkins was 27 when she and her husband, Brendon, started trying for a baby. After a procession of increasingly intensive fertility treatments, she started IVF at 33. Her only egg retrieval resulted in four embryos. It was heartbreaking when her first two embryo transfers failed. “IVF was extremely overwhelming,” Larkins said.



She recalled her first IVF specialist’s pro-forma PowerPoint presentation. “Then he put me on an IVF treatment plan he said he starts all his patients on … there was no consideration of my medical history,” Larkins said. Her second fertility specialist spent the first appointment taking a detailed history and put her on a fraction of the medication dosage previously prescribed, which she lowered after Larkins almost developed ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. Rose Larkin with Theodore: “IVF was extremely overwhelming.” George Chan The couple had addressed Brendon’s treatable condition causing male infertility, and Rose’s benign tumour of the pituitary gland. But the specialist picked up on a crucial component that Rose had raised years earlier with other doctors. “I had always had painful periods to the point where [at work] I was crawling under my desk and half passing out,” Larkins said. “She asked me, ‘Have you ever had a laparoscopy?’”



The procedure revealed Larkins had severe, widespread and deep infiltrating endometriosis. Three months after surgery to remove endometrial lesions, her specialist transferred the embryo that would become her son, Theodore, now 3. Her 14-month-old daughter, Maia, was conceived with her last embryo. “I have two beautiful little miracles that I wouldn’t otherwise have,” she said, but the all-consuming experience took a toll. She has joined the NPESU’s consumer advisory group in the hopes of improving the sector. IVF clinic medical directors said aggregated success rates are misleading because they penalised clinics that treated the most complex or older patients.



Related Article IVF ‘Patients deserve to know’: The IVF clinics and the missing success rates Professor Georgina Chambers, the director of NPESU and the report’s lead author, agreed but said there may be unwarranted variation between clinics. She hoped an independent regulator for the IVF sector would make publishing success rates mandatory for all IVF clinics. Overall, 37 per cent of women had a live birth from their first complete cycle. By the sixth complete cycle, that rose to 57.6 per cent, but age was a powerful predictor. The chance of having a baby per frozen embryo cycle when women used their own eggs was 38.4 per cent among those aged 30 to 34. This dropped to 12.2 per cent for women 45 and older, many of whom would have frozen their eggs when they were younger. For fresh embryo transfers, the chance of having a baby per initiated cycle dropped from 28.7 per cent in the 30-34 cohort to 1.4 per cent in those over 45.



“If a woman isn’t successful in her first cycle, the report provides reassuring data that after multiple cycles, she had a very good chance of having a baby,” Chambers said. After three complete IVF cycles and using their own eggs, women starting IVF under 30 have a 70 per cent chance of having a baby, falling to 21 per cent for women between 40 and 44, and 3 per cent after 45. “But every woman is different,” Chambers said, urging anyone considering IVF to use the calculator on Your IVF Success for an individualised estimate. Michael Chapman, co-founder of IVF Australia and Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at UNSW, said Australia was leading the world in terms of transferring just one embryo at a time.



“When I started in the ’80s, we would put back two, three or four embryos at once, got a 10 per cent pregnancy rate and thought we were doing pretty well,” Chapman said. Quick statistics from the Australian and New Zealand Artificial Reproduction Database Report 2024 51,303 women in Australia had IVF treatment in 2024

Roughly 94 per cent of women in Australia and New Zealand used their own eggs (56,245 women)

Of these women, 14.4 per cent were single, and 4.6 per cent were female couples

Almost 10 per cent of cycles involved pre-implantation genetic testing (9.7 per cent)

The single embryo transfer rate was 94.4 per cent Dr Petra Wale, president of the Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand, which funded the report, said single embryo transfers and freezing embryos allowed clinics to reduce the risks of multiple pregnancies and gave patients the best possible chance of building a healthy family. Frozen embryos accounted for roughly 70 per cent of embryos transferred in 2024. Freezing embryos allows women to recover from ovarian stimulation before a transfer, and in some cases for those embryos to undergo preimplantation genetic testing. World.title: ‘Big Brother was watching’: Ex-students recall life at Opus Dei-linked Sydney school
World.content:
NationalNSWOperation Rosny ‘Big Brother was watching’: Ex-students recall life at Opus Dei-linked Sydney school Ben Cubby August 9, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Big brother was always watching you.” This is how a former student recalled Redfield College, the Opus Dei-linked Sydney school that has featured in the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s inquiry into secret political donations. Four targets in ICAC’s Operation Rosny – Robert Assaf, Jeremy Greenwood and Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet – received their Catholic education at Redfield before starting their activities with the Reformers, a Christian activist group in the NSW Liberal Party. Redfield College in Dural. Wolter Peeters In 2000, the school captain was Dominic Perrottet. The former premier, who is not accused of any wrongdoing by ICAC, reportedly spoke at a recruitment event run by the Reformers. Ex-students told the Herald that the school, at Dural in the city’s north-west, cultivated a strictly conservative atmosphere that guided students into Opus Dei-run study centres and in some cases prepared them for celibacy within the priesthood.



“It really felt like Orwell’s Big Brother, in that you were just constantly monitored,” said Tim Pocock, who attended Redfield at the same time as Dominic Perrottet and Assaf and briefly trained to be a priest. “Half of the teaching staff were members of Opus Dei. There was the mentoring system, where each student is assigned these mentors who would monitor them. And everywhere there are parents, cousins, brothers, uncles. It’s a very close-knit, very conservative community.” Tim Pocock, in his school days and as an adult. Another ex-student named Alex, who withheld his family name as he is still involved with members of the school community, said he felt he was being steered in the direction of the priesthood by mentors assigned by the school and at study centres, attended by many students after school hours. “You’re essentially surrounded by people who are either supportive of Opus Dei or are members of it, so it’s inevitable that you sort of absorb that worldview, including being suspicious of outsiders,” Alex said. “The wider world is seen as full of sin.”



Opus Dei, a secretive and highly conservative organisation within the Catholic Church, has only 600 to 700 members in Australia – a sliver of the Catholic population of just over 5 million, according to religious historian Paul Collins. Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny The self-styled Braveheart crusader now accused of branch stacking Redfield was founded in 1986 by the Parents for Education Foundation, or PARED, a registered charity formed in part by Opus Dei members. Opus Dei supplies chaplains to the school. “It was established by parents inspired by the educational philosophy of St Josemaría Escrivá, the founder of Opus Dei,” a school spokesperson said. “The school is independently governed by its own board and is not owned or operated by Opus Dei.” PARED runs three other schools in Sydney – Tangara in Cherrybrook, Montgrove College in Orchard Hills and Wollemi College in Werrington.



The charity’s annual financial report for 2025 shows it in a healthy financial position, with an annual operating surplus of $4.4 million and more than $111 million in net assets. The charity received $24.2 million in commonwealth funding and $6.3 million in state funding last year, the report says. Former Redfield student Robert Assaf arrives to give evidence at the ICAC inquiry. James Brickwood The Redfield spokesman distanced the school from the ICAC inquiry, saying it “has had very little impact on the day-to-day life of the school”. “The matters before ICAC concern a small number of former students acting in their personal capacities many years after leaving Redfield and are not in any way connected with the operation of the school.”



But even before the ICAC put the Reformers’ Redfield connections in the public domain in counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer’s opening address to the corruption inquiry, the schools were “in a bit of a state of siege”, Alex said. “They are very sensitive to media coverage and criticism from outsiders,” he said. Related Article Education War of words erupts between Opus Dei schools and the ABC Redfield, an all-boys school, and its sister school Tangara, were investigated by the NSW Education Standards Authority in 2023 after former students publicly raised allegations, including that the schools were recruiting grounds for Opus Dei, that female students were advised against receiving the HPV cervical cancer vaccine, and that homophobia was rife. The NESA inquiry findings are unpublished, but no adverse findings were recorded against the schools.



“Both continue to be fully registered, have an unblemished regulatory record with both NESA and the Australian Government Department of Education, and continue to maintain the highest standards of student wellbeing, safeguarding and governance,” a Redfield spokesman said. Asked if the school welcomed gay students, the spokesperson said: “Redfield welcomes all students whose families seek a Catholic education and who are willing to participate in the life of the school. Every student is entitled to be treated with dignity, respect and care. The school expects all members of its community to treat one another with respect.” The school rejected claims its mentoring system is, in part, a recruiting tool for Opus Dei. Loading “Its purpose is to support parents and to assist students academically and personally, including in areas such as goal setting, study habits, character development and wellbeing,” the spokesman said.



“Participation in religious activities is voluntary, consistent with Catholic schools generally. The suggestion that mentoring exists as a recruitment mechanism for Opus Dei or the priesthood does not reflect the school’s purpose or practice.” Pocock, who is gay, remembers his mentoring experience at Redfield differently. “Once every two or three weeks, we’d leave class, walk around the school grounds and talk about my development as a young man. There was a concerted effort to make me more ‘masculine’. They talked about how I talked, how I walked. When I was being bullied, the inference was always that it was my fault. I was told, ‘Stop making yourself a target’. Liberal MP Damien Tudehope arrives at the ICAC inquiry to give evidence. Steven Siewert “The bullying I experienced at school was very much targeted towards the fact that I was gay,” said Pocock, a nephew of Damien Tudehope, who has not been accused of any wrongdoing at the ICAC inquiry but has stood down from the NSW opposition frontbench when he was called to give evidence.



“It was clear that they felt it was legitimate because they felt backed up in their minds by scripture and God himself. Whenever the Mardi Gras was on, there would be 24-hour vigils in church. There was a lot of talk about the gay agenda. “There was a lot of emphasis on ‘purity’. Even kissing – we had a guest speaker come to address the class about how it is immoral to kiss before marriage because kissing leads to arousal. “We were taught there are sins everywhere, basically. You can’t avoid them.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan Jonathan Drennan August 8, 2026 — 11:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aidan Ross 5.5 The Wallabies are still struggling to provide a regular tag-team partner for Angus Bell, and the search continues. Ross was busy in defence with 11 tackles, but was barely used in open play, making just four metres with the ball. Josh Nasser 6 Nasser was strong from the set piece and provided a solid lineout with his throwing. Didn’t let anyone down, especially after the recent impressive form of Brandon Paenga Amosa. Harry Wilson leads his team around the field. Getty Images



Allan Alaalatoa 5.5 It was brutal conditions for any front rower in Osaka, and, like Ross, was busy in defence as the Wallabies struggled to deal with early Japanese onslaughts. Made nine tackles and had little chance to do much else. Josh Canham 8 Canham just keeps getting better and better as a Test second-rower. Athletic, great hands and even put in a clearing kick from the Wallabies line. Won five lineouts, including a crucial steal off Japan ball. Canham is beginning his Test career but already is looking like he has been a Wallaby for years.



Miles Amatosero 3 Amatosero was given a big opportunity with his first Test start and was red-carded for a high shot on Japan captain Warner Dearns. Amatosero could argue that Dearns’ body height changed dramatically, but it was still careless and could have proven far more costly to the Wallabies. Rob Valetini 6 A quieter outing for Valetini, who struggled in brutal conditions. Made 14 tackles but only made 12 metres, far below what the breakaway would normally make in a Test.



Fraser McReight 6.5 Wasn’t able to dominate at the breakdown, but did lead his team with 21 tackles and scored a try in a tireless performance. McReight put in a tireless performance. Getty Images Harry Wilson 5.5 Had 10 carries but only made 8 metres, in simple maths, averaging 0.8 metres per carry. Also seemed to get on the wrong side of Irish referee Eoghan Cross and conceded two penalties. The captain’s effort can never be faulted, but it wasn’t an easy night.



Ryan Lonergan 6 Lonergan has had an outstanding season so far for the Wallabies, but it was a very tough night with a slippery ball for a halfback. Provides the Wallabies with an accurate goal kicker, which proved crucial in the end. Missed four tackles. Declan Meredith 4 The playmaker struggled badly with his kicking on exits, getting low metres and leaving the Wallabies under pressure. Showed his inexperience when taking a quick tap and completely mis-kicking it to himself, when the Wallabies were putting Japan under huge pressure in the scrum near their try line, and a yellow card was possible. Harry Potter 8.5



The Wallabies’ best on the night. Potter struggled with the Waratahs this season, but was the pick of the Wallabies backline. Scored a try and looked dangerous with the ball, beating four defenders with three line breaks. Difficult to drop now. Harry Potter makes a break for the Wallabies Getty Images Hunter Paisami 7 Some huge defensive hits from Paisami, even if he does sometimes shoot out of the line too quickly. Also made a brilliant pass for Tom Wright’s try and was dangerous with the ball in his hands. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii 5



Just could not get himself into the game, making a poor pass early, which Harry Potter did well to scoop off the ground and still score a try. Made a ruck turnover and didn’t stop trying, but did look vulnerable against quick Japanese attack in defence. Surely it is time to give him a go on the wing to utilise his strengths aerially and in attack. A huge talent that needs another chance to show it somewhere else on the field. Max Jorgensen 6 Scored a try and was solid when he attacked. Also made a ruck turnover. Tom Wright 7



Made a huge play, putting his body on the line to win a ruck turnover on 38 minutes with Japan certain to score. Scored a try, although also guilty of some handling errors on a humid night. Tom Wright scored a try, but was also guilty of some handling errors. Getty Images REPLACEMENTS Billy Pollard 5.5 Made a mess of a set play with a pass with the Wallabies pressuring the Japanese defence, but played a role in a strong bomb squad scrum that caused havoc for Japan.



Angus Bell 7 Gave away two penalties, but also made a crucial turnover on the ruck and played his part in a strong scrum. Carried the ball for 22 metres and was exactly what was needed to take the game to Japan late. Taniela Tupou 7 Made a huge hit at the end of the game to knock the ball out of Japanese hands and win the game; also ended up scoring the decisive try. Tupou was having a field day in the scrum and would have loved an opportunity to do more of them. Provided the perfect ballast off the bench. Isaac Henry, Tate McDermott, Hunter Paisami, Taniela Tupou and Angus Bell await the national anthem. Getty Images



Jeremy Williams 6.5 Brought a desperately needed calmness to the Wallabies and the Force second rower is clinical in his work; it was his clean-out that paved the way for the Tupou try. Charlie Cale 6 Finally given a chance to wear the Wallabies jersey and was busy, topping the Wallabies carries per minute with 0.22. Tate McDermott 6



Had looked rusty in his previous Tests, but was back with his sniping best against Japan. Busy and helped fight the Japanese speed with his own blistering tempo. Ben Donaldson 6 Came on at fullback, but would have liked to have been given more time to impress at five-eighth after Meredith’s wobbles. Isaac Henry N/A Wallaby 999 was desperate to make an impression, but only had eight minutes to do it. Will have lots more opportunities in Test rugby. World.title: Mistakes abound, but Wallabies’ win provides plenty of satisfaction
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion Mistakes abound, but Wallabies’ win provides plenty of satisfaction Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author August 8, 2026 — 11:00pm

August 8, 2026 — 11:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Get that up yer, Eddie. The Wallaby win over Japan in Osaka was satisfying on a dozen levels at once. Most importantly, of course, is the fact that it was indeed a WIN, a victory if not a triumph, but that rarest of breed in recent times, a (W) next to the Wallaby name on the scoring ledger as the final whistle blew. And it was terrific that it came in the first match of new Wallaby coach Les Kiss’s tenure. The Wallabies’ lineouts were excellent, and Josh Canham turned in a near Man of the Match performance. Getty Images But right up there in terms of satisfaction was that it was against a side coached by Eddie Jones, who in fact was negotiating to take that very position while having carriage of the Australian team in the 2023 World Cup. The result was that our side was a complete shambles, and he left behind the smoking ruins of what might have been.



But here, three years later, our blokes registered a small payback against a Japanese side good enough to have easily defeated Italy and even threatened Ireland in recent times. The win to the Goodies, came despite several things not going the Wallabies’ way. The first thing was playing in such heat and humidity; it was clear from the first that in terms of sheer energy expended, not to mention hugely skilful play, the habituated locals were always going to be a handful. We were also a man down for twenty minutes – following lock Miles Amatosero being dispatched for high contact - which exhausted the surviving fourteen further. Ryan Lonergan kicks the ball. Getty Images And finally, we had an error rate that would kill a brown dog. Balls were kicked out on the full, knocked on and dropped behind with alarming regularity, even while the Japanese kicks were twice allowed to bounce and we kept making mistakes just when the try-line beckoned. Against that?



Related Article Wallabies ‘We found a way’: Wallabies defy heat, red card to get home over Eddie’s Japan Well, against that both our scrum and lineouts were excellent, and the surviving lock, Josh Canham – sort of rhymes with CANNON - turned in a near Man of the Match performance, stealing balls in the lineout, winning his own, ripping the balls off them in the maul, and constantly penetrating their line with death-or-glory charges. In the back row, Fraser McReight had his usual strong game while, off the bench, Taniela Tupou scored a great try which – if I were him – I’d describe as “a 50-metre carry, sidestepping my way through,” but was closer to a five-centimetre carry, followed by falling over the line with the ball in hand. The point was, after marvellous lead-up work by the entire team, it was Tupou who was there at the death to finish the job against a valiant Cherry Blossoms team that simply refused to quit. It was also Tupou who pulled off a massive tackle in the final seconds, making his opponent spill the ball, which finally put the game to rest. Angus Bell also had a great game off the bench, as did Jeremy Williams, and in some ways Kiss’s bench might have been stronger than the starting side they replaced, which saw the Wallabies finish strongly and not fade badly, which they have also been wont to do in recent times. In our back-line we saw the virtues of new coach Les Kiss’s stated desire to have less structured play, to have his charges work less with zones and channels and more with – stop me if this is too complex – running to where the bloody gaps are! Related Article Wallabies Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan



Time and again they did that, led by Max Jorgensen, and the results were there for all to see. The diminutive winger – and Tom Wright at fullback – were standouts for us, while the other winger Harry Potter had another strong game, as did Ryan Lonergan at halfback. When Tate McDermott came on to replace him at half in the final twenty minutes, he did what he does best, launching a series of darting runs from the base of the scrums, rucks and mauls and always laying the ball back. At fly-half, Declan Meredith struggled, and it was frankly a surprise that he played the full eighty minutes, as hard as he did try. (Carter Gordon, who was a revelation against Ireland last month, before injuring himself, will likely be back next week, in the return bout against Japan in Townsville.) Joseph Suaalii also struggled at times to hold on to the ball, though as captain Harry Wilson noted at game’s end, in those conditions the ball was like soap. Whatever. It was a WIN, did I mention? And not only that, the Wallabies second in succession! Get that up yer, Eddie. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Rabbitohs deny Eels greatest comeback in NRL history
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Rabbitohs deny Eels greatest comeback in NRL history Jasper Bruce and Justin Chadwick Updated August 8, 2026 — 10:12pm ,first published 5:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Parramatta have come within a sliver of the greatest comeback in NRL history, but have gone down 28-24 to South Sydney, who moved one step closer to a top-eight finish. But the manic victory looks to have come at a cost as young Souths halfback Ashton Ward injured his hamstring attempting a sideline conversion in Saturday’s first half. Loading Alex Johnston crossed for three tries as Souths took an imperious 28-0 halftime lead in the veteran winger’s first game at Allianz Stadium since breaking the NRL’s tryscoring record. The Eels lost Brian Kelly to the sin bin for a professional foul after just 92 seconds and conceded three tries without him, then watched as gun fullback Isaiah Iongi went down with a knee injury just before the break.



But against all odds, and with no realistic finals hopes to play for, Parramatta were hoisted back into the contest by off-contract journeyman Ronald Volkman. Ronald Volkman celebrates a try. Getty Images With Josh Addo-Carr deputising at fullback and hooker Ryley Smith in the centres, five-eighth Volkman’s attacking nous threatened to help the Eels pass the standing record for biggest NRL comeback (26 points). After Tallyn Da Silva crossed for the Eels’ first try, Volkman kicked through for Smith to nab their second before spinning past Matt Dufty for a four-pointer of his own. When Jordan Samrani soared over makeshift winger Jye Gray and slammed Volkman’s kick down, Parramatta were within four points.



After forcing a dropout in the final minutes, the Eels looked set to go for the killer blow, but the returning Tallis Duncan regathered the Rabbitohs’ short restart. In the same set, veteran Cody Walker kicked a 40/20 to put Souths out of trouble and on the attack for the final exchanges of a calamitous game. Brandon Smith celebrates a Rabbitohs try. Getty Images In Indigenous Round, Walker had been integral to the Rabbitohs’ early lead, most memorably slamming a kick into the goalposts that Tevita Tatola regathered for a fantastic try. The win lifts Souths back into seventh place to finish a weekend during which top-eight rivals Manly and Canterbury suffered potentially costly defeats.



They will likely make finals if they win two of their remaining four games, but have tough matches against Canterbury, the Warriors and Sydney Roosters on the run home. Earlier, Manly endured a dark day in Perth, conceding a whopping 42 consecutive points as their finals hopes took an almighty hit in a 42-20 loss to Melbourne. The Storm were horrible early on Saturday, with their completion rate sitting at just five of 12 as the Sea Eagles scored the opening two tries of the match to race out to a 14-0 lead. Loading But it was all one way traffic from that point on, with Melbourne piling on six unanswered tries either side of half-time to turn the contest on its head.



Manly’s fifth loss on the trot leaves their finals hopes on life support. Kieran Foran’s men now nurse a 9-11 record, meaning they will have to win their last four games to have a legitimate chance of making finals. In a further blow for the Sea Eagles, prop Taniela Paseka limped off in the first half after suffering a suspected MCL injury. Sualauvi Fa’alogo celebrates a try for Melbourne. Getty Images The Storm snapped a three-game losing streak, but at 9-12 they need to win their remaining three games and rely on other results to go their way in order to sneak into the post-season.



Fittingly, Melbourne’s Nick Meaney was a perfect nine-of-nine with the boot in a place he will soon call home. Related Article Updated

Perth coach Mal Meninga led around 1000 supporters on a pre-match ‘Bear Walk’ in the rain to HBF Park to signify the venue will soon become a ‘Bear Pit’. The NRL’s newest franchise launched their home jersey on Friday, with the red-and-black hooped strip paying tribute to the first-ever North Sydney Bears side of 1908, when the club was a foundation member of the NSW Rugby Football League. World.title: On the front line of WA’s fight against bird flu as fears grow for endangered species
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWABird flu On the front line of WA’s fight against bird flu as fears grow for endangered species Michael Philipps August 9, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia is the last continent on earth to experience cases of H5 bird flu, but with that unique status comes the key advantage of several years to formulate a plan for when the disease hits – particularly when it comes to protecting and preparing our most at-risk wildlife. In Western Australia, several programs have been quietly progressing to protect endangered species including the western ground parrot and the Australian lesser noddy. Australian sea lions are an endangered species. On the Abrolhos Islands off the coast of Geraldton, a program to boost Australian sea lion pup health through building shelters and trialling hookworm treatment hopes to keep the population resilient ahead of bird flu taking hold in the area. Dr Holly Raudino, a senior research scientist with the marine science program of the WA Department of Biodiversity Conservation and Attractions, has been working with the sea lion population along the state’s coast, focusing on species around the Abrolhos Islands near Geraldton.



Raudino said there was serious concern for the population due to the severe impact the virus has had on other sea lion colonies around the world. Related Article Bird flu ‘Biggest threat is from the sky’: How Victoria is preparing for bird flu “South American sea lions have been really affected, as have elephant seals in South America, but also more recently on Heard Island, which is one of the South Antarctic islands,” she said. “We’re seeing tens of thousands of pups dying in one breeding season. “To put that into perspective, the Australian sea lions we think there’s 12,000 or less across the species range, and they’re restricted just to South Australia and Western Australia.



“So there’s definitely the potential that we could lose the whole species.” Raudino and the team have been busy on the islands trying to build shore up the population ahead of any potential incursion of the virus, building shelters and checking the sea lion pups for hookworm, a parasite that has led to high mortality rates among South Australian colonies. “The idea is that it reduces other stresses ahead of avian influenza getting into those colonies,” Raudino said. “The pups are definitely susceptible to bird flu as are the older age classes too,” she said. “But the main concern is that when they are pupping, they are all in close proximity together.



“We know this highly pathogenic avian influenza is spreading mammal to mammal, so once it gets in it could be catastrophic.” Recently, the first inland case of H5N1 bird flu in Australia was detected in western NSW at the junction of the Murray and Darling rivers on the Victorian border, in a sign the virus will spread rapidly across the continent. The NSW government announced two more cases of the virus on Saturday, one in Narooma on the South Coast and one near Wentworth in the far west, bringing the total number of confirmed detections across Australia to 215. Federal Environment and Water Minister Murray said the best way to protect vulnerable species in the wild from H5 bird flu was to make sure there were strong and healthy populations. Sea lions are found along the coast from south of Esperance to north of the Abrolhos Islands.



“Protective action is giving species the best chance of withstanding and recovering from the potential impacts of H5 bird flu,” he said. “These projects have not only helped us prepare for H5 bird flu, they will also have enduring conservation benefits for many of the species that rely on these habitats.” Raudino said the best-case scenario for bird flu spreading among the sea lion population – which ranges from the coast to the south of Esperance up to north of the Abrolhos – is that the virus reached an equilibrium and did not wipe out the population. “I really hope that we don’t get local extinctions and that we’re able to kind of preserve the species across their range,” she said. “It is important to record and report, and the community has been doing a good job of that.



“We can’t underestimate the power of people looking and seeing things first, and then hopefully we can get measures in place.” WA Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn was confident the conservation initiatives would put the state in a good position to boost native species. “Given H5 bird flu detections in Australia, this work is now more important than ever,” he said. “This funding is fundamental in strengthening resilience in our most threatened species.” The Abrolhos Islands are a key focus for scientists looking to prepare wildlife populations for bird flu incursions.



Raudino said her key concern was how quickly bird flu spread across the sea lion population, and whether it was established. “We have known for the last few years that it is a real threat, and we have been trying to do as much as we can” she said. “Even if we get mortalities we have been testing, at least to my knowledge, since 2023 and we have had time to prepare. “I think we’re relieved that it’s happened after the main pupping season for the Abrolhos. It would be great if we could get to the end of the year, and [the virus] wasn’t established. “In WA, it’s still only been detected in the migratory seabirds.



“There’s no local transmission, which has been a huge relief.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Rose had two heartbreaking IVF losses. Then her specialist clocked one crucial detail
World.content:
Exclusive NationalIVF Rose had two heartbreaking IVF losses. Then her specialist clocked one crucial detail Kate Aubusson August 9, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One child in 16 is now conceived via IVF in Australia as success rates creep up, but would-be parents face a high-stakes numbers game in which age, and the clinic they choose, can determine success – or otherwise. More than 50,000 women in Australia had IVF treatment in 2024, totalling 104,721 IVF cycles, according to the latest analysis of the database tracking every cycle performed at every IVF clinic in Australia and New Zealand. Rose and Brendan Larkin with their children Theodore and Maia. George Chan There were 18,509 IVF babies born in 2024, equating to one baby for every five to six cycles, says the report published on Sunday by UNSW’s National Perinatal Epidemiology and Statistics Unit (NPESU). Success rates varied widely between IVF clinics. One clinic – its identity was not revealed– reported just over 5 per cent of its initiated cycles resulted in a live birth. At the other end of the scale was a clinic with a 38 per cent success rate.



Male infertility was a factor for one in four IVF cycles. The specific cause in the majority of these cases was unknown. Related Article IVF Suzanne froze her eggs – then a calculator gave her a reality check Of all the causes of infertility among people undergoing IVF, women diagnosed only with endometriosis had the highest chance of success. More than one in three (36.3 per cent) of initiated cycles resulted in a live birth. Rose Larkins was 27 when she and her husband, Brendon, started trying for a baby. After a procession of increasingly intensive fertility treatments, she started IVF at 33. Her only egg retrieval resulted in four embryos. It was heartbreaking when her first two embryo transfers failed. “IVF was extremely overwhelming,” Larkins said.



She recalled her first IVF specialist’s pro-forma PowerPoint presentation. “Then he put me on an IVF treatment plan he said he starts all his patients on … there was no consideration of my medical history,” Larkins said. Her second fertility specialist spent the first appointment taking a detailed history and put her on a fraction of the medication dosage previously prescribed, which she lowered after Larkins almost developed ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. Rose Larkin with Theodore: “IVF was extremely overwhelming.” George Chan The couple had addressed Brendon’s treatable condition causing male infertility, and Rose’s benign tumour of the pituitary gland. But the specialist picked up on a crucial component that Rose had raised years earlier with other doctors. “I had always had painful periods to the point where [at work] I was crawling under my desk and half passing out,” Larkins said. “She asked me, ‘Have you ever had a laparoscopy?’”



The procedure revealed Larkins had severe, widespread and deep infiltrating endometriosis. Three months after surgery to remove endometrial lesions, her specialist transferred the embryo that would become her son, Theodore, now 3. Her 14-month-old daughter, Maia, was conceived with her last embryo. “I have two beautiful little miracles that I wouldn’t otherwise have,” she said, but the all-consuming experience took a toll. She has joined the NPESU’s consumer advisory group in the hopes of improving the sector. IVF clinic medical directors said aggregated success rates are misleading because they penalised clinics that treated the most complex or older patients.



Related Article IVF ‘Patients deserve to know’: The IVF clinics and the missing success rates Professor Georgina Chambers, the director of NPESU and the report’s lead author, agreed but said there may be unwarranted variation between clinics. She hoped an independent regulator for the IVF sector would make publishing success rates mandatory for all IVF clinics. Overall, 37 per cent of women had a live birth from their first complete cycle. By the sixth complete cycle, that rose to 57.6 per cent, but age was a powerful predictor. The chance of having a baby per frozen embryo cycle when women used their own eggs was 38.4 per cent among those aged 30 to 34. This dropped to 12.2 per cent for women 45 and older, many of whom would have frozen their eggs when they were younger. For fresh embryo transfers, the chance of having a baby per initiated cycle dropped from 28.7 per cent in the 30-34 cohort to 1.4 per cent in those over 45.



“If a woman isn’t successful in her first cycle, the report provides reassuring data that after multiple cycles, she had a very good chance of having a baby,” Chambers said. After three complete IVF cycles and using their own eggs, women starting IVF under 30 have a 70 per cent chance of having a baby, falling to 21 per cent for women between 40 and 44, and 3 per cent after 45. “But every woman is different,” Chambers said, urging anyone considering IVF to use the calculator on Your IVF Success for an individualised estimate. Michael Chapman, co-founder of IVF Australia and Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at UNSW, said Australia was leading the world in terms of transferring just one embryo at a time.



“When I started in the ’80s, we would put back two, three or four embryos at once, got a 10 per cent pregnancy rate and thought we were doing pretty well,” Chapman said. Quick statistics from the Australian and New Zealand Artificial Reproduction Database Report 2024 51,303 women in Australia had IVF treatment in 2024

Roughly 94 per cent of women in Australia and New Zealand used their own eggs (56,245 women)

Of these women, 14.4 per cent were single, and 4.6 per cent were female couples

Almost 10 per cent of cycles involved pre-implantation genetic testing (9.7 per cent)

The single embryo transfer rate was 94.4 per cent Dr Petra Wale, president of the Fertility Society of Australia and New Zealand, which funded the report, said single embryo transfers and freezing embryos allowed clinics to reduce the risks of multiple pregnancies and gave patients the best possible chance of building a healthy family. Frozen embryos accounted for roughly 70 per cent of embryos transferred in 2024. Freezing embryos allows women to recover from ovarian stimulation before a transfer, and in some cases for those embryos to undergo preimplantation genetic testing. World.title: ‘Big Brother was watching’: Ex-students recall life at Opus Dei-linked Sydney school
World.content:
NationalNSWOperation Rosny ‘Big Brother was watching’: Ex-students recall life at Opus Dei-linked Sydney school Ben Cubby August 9, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Big brother was always watching you.” This is how a former student recalled Redfield College, the Opus Dei-linked Sydney school that has featured in the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s inquiry into secret political donations. Four targets in ICAC’s Operation Rosny – Robert Assaf, Jeremy Greenwood and Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet – received their Catholic education at Redfield before starting their activities with the Reformers, a Christian activist group in the NSW Liberal Party. Redfield College in Dural. Wolter Peeters In 2000, the school captain was Dominic Perrottet. The former premier, who is not accused of any wrongdoing by ICAC, reportedly spoke at a recruitment event run by the Reformers. Ex-students told the Herald that the school, at Dural in the city’s north-west, cultivated a strictly conservative atmosphere that guided students into Opus Dei-run study centres and in some cases prepared them for celibacy within the priesthood.



“It really felt like Orwell’s Big Brother, in that you were just constantly monitored,” said Tim Pocock, who attended Redfield at the same time as Dominic Perrottet and Assaf and briefly trained to be a priest. “Half of the teaching staff were members of Opus Dei. There was the mentoring system, where each student is assigned these mentors who would monitor them. And everywhere there are parents, cousins, brothers, uncles. It’s a very close-knit, very conservative community.” Tim Pocock, in his school days and as an adult. Another ex-student named Alex, who withheld his family name as he is still involved with members of the school community, said he felt he was being steered in the direction of the priesthood by mentors assigned by the school and at study centres, attended by many students after school hours. “You’re essentially surrounded by people who are either supportive of Opus Dei or are members of it, so it’s inevitable that you sort of absorb that worldview, including being suspicious of outsiders,” Alex said. “The wider world is seen as full of sin.”



Opus Dei, a secretive and highly conservative organisation within the Catholic Church, has only 600 to 700 members in Australia – a sliver of the Catholic population of just over 5 million, according to religious historian Paul Collins. Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny The self-styled Braveheart crusader now accused of branch stacking Redfield was founded in 1986 by the Parents for Education Foundation, or PARED, a registered charity formed in part by Opus Dei members. Opus Dei supplies chaplains to the school. “It was established by parents inspired by the educational philosophy of St Josemaría Escrivá, the founder of Opus Dei,” a school spokesperson said. “The school is independently governed by its own board and is not owned or operated by Opus Dei.” PARED runs three other schools in Sydney – Tangara in Cherrybrook, Montgrove College in Orchard Hills and Wollemi College in Werrington.



The charity’s annual financial report for 2025 shows it in a healthy financial position, with an annual operating surplus of $4.4 million and more than $111 million in net assets. The charity received $24.2 million in commonwealth funding and $6.3 million in state funding last year, the report says. Former Redfield student Robert Assaf arrives to give evidence at the ICAC inquiry. James Brickwood The Redfield spokesman distanced the school from the ICAC inquiry, saying it “has had very little impact on the day-to-day life of the school”. “The matters before ICAC concern a small number of former students acting in their personal capacities many years after leaving Redfield and are not in any way connected with the operation of the school.”



But even before the ICAC put the Reformers’ Redfield connections in the public domain in counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer’s opening address to the corruption inquiry, the schools were “in a bit of a state of siege”, Alex said. “They are very sensitive to media coverage and criticism from outsiders,” he said. Related Article Education War of words erupts between Opus Dei schools and the ABC Redfield, an all-boys school, and its sister school Tangara, were investigated by the NSW Education Standards Authority in 2023 after former students publicly raised allegations, including that the schools were recruiting grounds for Opus Dei, that female students were advised against receiving the HPV cervical cancer vaccine, and that homophobia was rife. The NESA inquiry findings are unpublished, but no adverse findings were recorded against the schools.



“Both continue to be fully registered, have an unblemished regulatory record with both NESA and the Australian Government Department of Education, and continue to maintain the highest standards of student wellbeing, safeguarding and governance,” a Redfield spokesman said. Asked if the school welcomed gay students, the spokesperson said: “Redfield welcomes all students whose families seek a Catholic education and who are willing to participate in the life of the school. Every student is entitled to be treated with dignity, respect and care. The school expects all members of its community to treat one another with respect.” The school rejected claims its mentoring system is, in part, a recruiting tool for Opus Dei. Loading “Its purpose is to support parents and to assist students academically and personally, including in areas such as goal setting, study habits, character development and wellbeing,” the spokesman said.



“Participation in religious activities is voluntary, consistent with Catholic schools generally. The suggestion that mentoring exists as a recruitment mechanism for Opus Dei or the priesthood does not reflect the school’s purpose or practice.” Pocock, who is gay, remembers his mentoring experience at Redfield differently. “Once every two or three weeks, we’d leave class, walk around the school grounds and talk about my development as a young man. There was a concerted effort to make me more ‘masculine’. They talked about how I talked, how I walked. When I was being bullied, the inference was always that it was my fault. I was told, ‘Stop making yourself a target’. Liberal MP Damien Tudehope arrives at the ICAC inquiry to give evidence. Steven Siewert “The bullying I experienced at school was very much targeted towards the fact that I was gay,” said Pocock, a nephew of Damien Tudehope, who has not been accused of any wrongdoing at the ICAC inquiry but has stood down from the NSW opposition frontbench when he was called to give evidence.



“It was clear that they felt it was legitimate because they felt backed up in their minds by scripture and God himself. Whenever the Mardi Gras was on, there would be 24-hour vigils in church. There was a lot of talk about the gay agenda. “There was a lot of emphasis on ‘purity’. Even kissing – we had a guest speaker come to address the class about how it is immoral to kiss before marriage because kissing leads to arousal. “We were taught there are sins everywhere, basically. You can’t avoid them.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan Jonathan Drennan August 8, 2026 — 11:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Aidan Ross 5.5 The Wallabies are still struggling to provide a regular tag-team partner for Angus Bell, and the search continues. Ross was busy in defence with 11 tackles, but was barely used in open play, making just four metres with the ball. Josh Nasser 6 Nasser was strong from the set piece and provided a solid lineout with his throwing. Didn’t let anyone down, especially after the recent impressive form of Brandon Paenga Amosa. Harry Wilson leads his team around the field. Getty Images



Allan Alaalatoa 5.5 It was brutal conditions for any front rower in Osaka, and, like Ross, was busy in defence as the Wallabies struggled to deal with early Japanese onslaughts. Made nine tackles and had little chance to do much else. Josh Canham 8 Canham just keeps getting better and better as a Test second-rower. Athletic, great hands and even put in a clearing kick from the Wallabies line. Won five lineouts, including a crucial steal off Japan ball. Canham is beginning his Test career but already is looking like he has been a Wallaby for years.



Miles Amatosero 3 Amatosero was given a big opportunity with his first Test start and was red-carded for a high shot on Japan captain Warner Dearns. Amatosero could argue that Dearns’ body height changed dramatically, but it was still careless and could have proven far more costly to the Wallabies. Rob Valetini 6 A quieter outing for Valetini, who struggled in brutal conditions. Made 14 tackles but only made 12 metres, far below what the breakaway would normally make in a Test.



Fraser McReight 6.5 Wasn’t able to dominate at the breakdown, but did lead his team with 21 tackles and scored a try in a tireless performance. McReight put in a tireless performance. Getty Images Harry Wilson 5.5 Had 10 carries but only made 8 metres, in simple maths, averaging 0.8 metres per carry. Also seemed to get on the wrong side of Irish referee Eoghan Cross and conceded two penalties. The captain’s effort can never be faulted, but it wasn’t an easy night.



Ryan Lonergan 6 Lonergan has had an outstanding season so far for the Wallabies, but it was a very tough night with a slippery ball for a halfback. Provides the Wallabies with an accurate goal kicker, which proved crucial in the end. Missed four tackles. Declan Meredith 4 The playmaker struggled badly with his kicking on exits, getting low metres and leaving the Wallabies under pressure. Showed his inexperience when taking a quick tap and completely mis-kicking it to himself, when the Wallabies were putting Japan under huge pressure in the scrum near their try line, and a yellow card was possible. Harry Potter 8.5



The Wallabies’ best on the night. Potter struggled with the Waratahs this season, but was the pick of the Wallabies backline. Scored a try and looked dangerous with the ball, beating four defenders with three line breaks. Difficult to drop now. Harry Potter makes a break for the Wallabies Getty Images Hunter Paisami 7 Some huge defensive hits from Paisami, even if he does sometimes shoot out of the line too quickly. Also made a brilliant pass for Tom Wright’s try and was dangerous with the ball in his hands. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii 5



Just could not get himself into the game, making a poor pass early, which Harry Potter did well to scoop off the ground and still score a try. Made a ruck turnover and didn’t stop trying, but did look vulnerable against quick Japanese attack in defence. Surely it is time to give him a go on the wing to utilise his strengths aerially and in attack. A huge talent that needs another chance to show it somewhere else on the field. Max Jorgensen 6 Scored a try and was solid when he attacked. Also made a ruck turnover. Tom Wright 7



Made a huge play, putting his body on the line to win a ruck turnover on 38 minutes with Japan certain to score. Scored a try, although also guilty of some handling errors on a humid night. Tom Wright scored a try, but was also guilty of some handling errors. Getty Images REPLACEMENTS Billy Pollard 5.5 Made a mess of a set play with a pass with the Wallabies pressuring the Japanese defence, but played a role in a strong bomb squad scrum that caused havoc for Japan.



Angus Bell 7 Gave away two penalties, but also made a crucial turnover on the ruck and played his part in a strong scrum. Carried the ball for 22 metres and was exactly what was needed to take the game to Japan late. Taniela Tupou 7 Made a huge hit at the end of the game to knock the ball out of Japanese hands and win the game; also ended up scoring the decisive try. Tupou was having a field day in the scrum and would have loved an opportunity to do more of them. Provided the perfect ballast off the bench. Isaac Henry, Tate McDermott, Hunter Paisami, Taniela Tupou and Angus Bell await the national anthem. Getty Images



Jeremy Williams 6.5 Brought a desperately needed calmness to the Wallabies and the Force second rower is clinical in his work; it was his clean-out that paved the way for the Tupou try. Charlie Cale 6 Finally given a chance to wear the Wallabies jersey and was busy, topping the Wallabies carries per minute with 0.22. Tate McDermott 6



Had looked rusty in his previous Tests, but was back with his sniping best against Japan. Busy and helped fight the Japanese speed with his own blistering tempo. Ben Donaldson 6 Came on at fullback, but would have liked to have been given more time to impress at five-eighth after Meredith’s wobbles. Isaac Henry N/A Wallaby 999 was desperate to make an impression, but only had eight minutes to do it. Will have lots more opportunities in Test rugby. World.title: Mistakes abound, but Wallabies’ win provides plenty of satisfaction
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion Mistakes abound, but Wallabies’ win provides plenty of satisfaction Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author August 8, 2026 — 11:00pm

August 8, 2026 — 11:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Get that up yer, Eddie. The Wallaby win over Japan in Osaka was satisfying on a dozen levels at once. Most importantly, of course, is the fact that it was indeed a WIN, a victory if not a triumph, but that rarest of breed in recent times, a (W) next to the Wallaby name on the scoring ledger as the final whistle blew. And it was terrific that it came in the first match of new Wallaby coach Les Kiss’s tenure. The Wallabies’ lineouts were excellent, and Josh Canham turned in a near Man of the Match performance. Getty Images But right up there in terms of satisfaction was that it was against a side coached by Eddie Jones, who in fact was negotiating to take that very position while having carriage of the Australian team in the 2023 World Cup. The result was that our side was a complete shambles, and he left behind the smoking ruins of what might have been.



But here, three years later, our blokes registered a small payback against a Japanese side good enough to have easily defeated Italy and even threatened Ireland in recent times. The win to the Goodies, came despite several things not going the Wallabies’ way. The first thing was playing in such heat and humidity; it was clear from the first that in terms of sheer energy expended, not to mention hugely skilful play, the habituated locals were always going to be a handful. We were also a man down for twenty minutes – following lock Miles Amatosero being dispatched for high contact - which exhausted the surviving fourteen further. Ryan Lonergan kicks the ball. Getty Images And finally, we had an error rate that would kill a brown dog. Balls were kicked out on the full, knocked on and dropped behind with alarming regularity, even while the Japanese kicks were twice allowed to bounce and we kept making mistakes just when the try-line beckoned. Against that?



Related Article Wallabies ‘We found a way’: Wallabies defy heat, red card to get home over Eddie’s Japan Well, against that both our scrum and lineouts were excellent, and the surviving lock, Josh Canham – sort of rhymes with CANNON - turned in a near Man of the Match performance, stealing balls in the lineout, winning his own, ripping the balls off them in the maul, and constantly penetrating their line with death-or-glory charges. In the back row, Fraser McReight had his usual strong game while, off the bench, Taniela Tupou scored a great try which – if I were him – I’d describe as “a 50-metre carry, sidestepping my way through,” but was closer to a five-centimetre carry, followed by falling over the line with the ball in hand. The point was, after marvellous lead-up work by the entire team, it was Tupou who was there at the death to finish the job against a valiant Cherry Blossoms team that simply refused to quit. It was also Tupou who pulled off a massive tackle in the final seconds, making his opponent spill the ball, which finally put the game to rest. Angus Bell also had a great game off the bench, as did Jeremy Williams, and in some ways Kiss’s bench might have been stronger than the starting side they replaced, which saw the Wallabies finish strongly and not fade badly, which they have also been wont to do in recent times. In our back-line we saw the virtues of new coach Les Kiss’s stated desire to have less structured play, to have his charges work less with zones and channels and more with – stop me if this is too complex – running to where the bloody gaps are! Related Article Wallabies Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed against Japan



Time and again they did that, led by Max Jorgensen, and the results were there for all to see. The diminutive winger – and Tom Wright at fullback – were standouts for us, while the other winger Harry Potter had another strong game, as did Ryan Lonergan at halfback. When Tate McDermott came on to replace him at half in the final twenty minutes, he did what he does best, launching a series of darting runs from the base of the scrums, rucks and mauls and always laying the ball back. At fly-half, Declan Meredith struggled, and it was frankly a surprise that he played the full eighty minutes, as hard as he did try. (Carter Gordon, who was a revelation against Ireland last month, before injuring himself, will likely be back next week, in the return bout against Japan in Townsville.) Joseph Suaalii also struggled at times to hold on to the ball, though as captain Harry Wilson noted at game’s end, in those conditions the ball was like soap. Whatever. It was a WIN, did I mention? And not only that, the Wallabies second in succession! Get that up yer, Eddie. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Rabbitohs deny Eels greatest comeback in NRL history
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Rabbitohs deny Eels greatest comeback in NRL history Jasper Bruce and Justin Chadwick Updated August 8, 2026 — 10:12pm ,first published 5:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Parramatta have come within a sliver of the greatest comeback in NRL history, but have gone down 28-24 to South Sydney, who moved one step closer to a top-eight finish. But the manic victory looks to have come at a cost as young Souths halfback Ashton Ward injured his hamstring attempting a sideline conversion in Saturday’s first half. Loading Alex Johnston crossed for three tries as Souths took an imperious 28-0 halftime lead in the veteran winger’s first game at Allianz Stadium since breaking the NRL’s tryscoring record. The Eels lost Brian Kelly to the sin bin for a professional foul after just 92 seconds and conceded three tries without him, then watched as gun fullback Isaiah Iongi went down with a knee injury just before the break.



But against all odds, and with no realistic finals hopes to play for, Parramatta were hoisted back into the contest by off-contract journeyman Ronald Volkman. Ronald Volkman celebrates a try. Getty Images With Josh Addo-Carr deputising at fullback and hooker Ryley Smith in the centres, five-eighth Volkman’s attacking nous threatened to help the Eels pass the standing record for biggest NRL comeback (26 points). After Tallyn Da Silva crossed for the Eels’ first try, Volkman kicked through for Smith to nab their second before spinning past Matt Dufty for a four-pointer of his own. When Jordan Samrani soared over makeshift winger Jye Gray and slammed Volkman’s kick down, Parramatta were within four points.



After forcing a dropout in the final minutes, the Eels looked set to go for the killer blow, but the returning Tallis Duncan regathered the Rabbitohs’ short restart. In the same set, veteran Cody Walker kicked a 40/20 to put Souths out of trouble and on the attack for the final exchanges of a calamitous game. Brandon Smith celebrates a Rabbitohs try. Manly’s fifth loss on the trot leaves their finals hopes on life support.
